tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Maya has finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday.
Our hiking club has met every Saturday since April.
While the band was rehearsing, the lights suddenly went out.
Leo used to swimming before school every morning.
By next Friday, the volunteers will plant fifty saplings.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A finished time marker such as "last Tuesday" calls for past simple ("finished"), not present perfect.

Tip: Spot calendar anchors (yesterday, last week, in 2019) — they usually kill present perfect.

TRUE — Present perfect with "since" correctly signals a habit that began in the past and continues now.

Tip: Pair "since + starting point" with present perfect, not past simple.

TRUE — Past continuous sets the background rehearsal; past simple marks the sudden blackout.

Tip: Longer background → continuous; shorter interrupt → simple past.

FALSE — Past habit needs "used to" + base verb: "used to swim," not "used to swimming."

Tip: "Used to" + V1 for habits; "be used to" + -ing for familiarity.

FALSE — Completion before next Friday needs future perfect: "will have planted," not plain "will plant."

Tip: "By + future time" often flags future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Warm up on classic tense traps: finished time versus "since," background continuous versus a short interrupt, "used to" form, and future perfect with "by." Read each verb against its time cue before you tick true or false.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guests already left when the dessert trolley arrived.
They had already left when the dessert trolley arrived.
Nina is knowing every lyric in the musical.
I am used to cycling through the park in the rain.
We visited the science museum in March.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The departure happened first, so past perfect is needed: "had already left."

Tip: When two past events stack, mark the earlier one with past perfect.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly shows that leaving preceded the trolley’s arrival.

Tip: "Already" often sits comfortably with past perfect in sequenced past narratives.

FALSE — Stative "know" resists continuous form; use "knows."

Tip: Mental-state verbs (know, believe, own) rarely take -ing in exam English.

TRUE — "Be used to" + gerund correctly means "accustomed to" a recurring activity.

Tip: "Am/is/are used to + -ing" ≠ "used to + V1."

TRUE — Past simple with "in March" correctly places a finished outing in a closed time frame.

Tip: Closed past time → past simple is the safe default.
tasks.solution_overview: This set contrasts past simple with past perfect, tests a stative continuous trap, and separates "used to" habit from "be used to" familiarity. Match the verb form to the timeline before you decide.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach has changed the starting line-up yesterday evening.
By the time the ferry docks tomorrow, we will pack our bags.
She has been a library volunteer here in 2016.
This scarf is belonging to my grandmother.
We used to camp by the lake before the path flooded.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Yesterday evening" is finished time, so write "changed," not present perfect.

Tip: Present perfect hates explicit finished-time adverbs.

FALSE — Completion before a future ferry arrival needs future perfect: "will have packed," not plain "will pack."

Tip: "By the time + future" often invites "will have + past participle."

FALSE — "In 2016" closes the period; use past simple: "was a library volunteer here in 2016."

Tip: "In + year" usually blocks present perfect for a finished role.

FALSE — "Belong" is stative; prefer "belongs," not continuous.

Tip: Possession and membership verbs stay simple in formal exam prose.

TRUE — "Used to camp" correctly reports a discontinued past habit.

Tip: "Used to + base verb" = past habit that no longer holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Only one sentence survives here. Hunt finished-time clashes with present perfect, demand future perfect with "by the time," and reject stative continuous — the lone survivor is clean past habit with "used to."

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The gallery has displayed local artists since the renovation.
While the neighbours were gardening, a fox slipped through the fence.
By year-end, the choir will have learned twelve new pieces.
Children used to play outdoors until dusk in this street.
Omar is owning three vintage cameras.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect + "since" correctly links an ongoing practice to its start point.

Tip: "Since" points to a start that still matters now — present perfect territory.

TRUE — Continuous background plus simple interrupt is the standard past pairing.

Tip: Ask which action was "in progress" when the other struck.

TRUE — Future perfect places learning completion before year-end.

Tip: Deadlines with "by" love future perfect.

TRUE — "Used to play" correctly describes a past habit that has changed.

Tip: Preferences and habits both take "used to + V1."

FALSE — Stative "own" should be "owns," not continuous.

Tip: Ownership verbs almost never take continuous in exam English.
tasks.solution_overview: Four sentences are clean; only the stative continuous fails. Confirm "since," background continuous, future perfect with "by," and past habit before you hunt the ownership trap.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The weather presenter explained the storm path at last week's briefing.
Runners are used to training before sunrise in winter.
The club has published three newsletters this semester.
By Friday noon, the caterers will have prepared the picnic baskets.
When the teacher entered, the class had already finished the quiz.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past simple correctly anchors a finished talk to "last week."

Tip: Explicit past time → past simple is rarely wrong.

TRUE — "Are used to training" correctly means runners are accustomed to the routine.

Tip: "Be used to + -ing" = familiarity, not past habit.

TRUE — Present perfect fits an unfinished period ("this semester") with present relevance.

Tip: "This week / this year / this semester" often keep present perfect alive.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places preparation before Friday noon.

Tip: Clock deadlines with "by" are classic future-perfect cues.

TRUE — Past perfect shows the quiz ended before the teacher walked in.

Tip: Earlier past action → had + past participle.
tasks.solution_overview: All five lines are sound. Use this card as a model set: closed past time, "be used to," unfinished-period present perfect, future perfect with "by," and past perfect sequencing.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I have seen that documentary twice already this month.
They are believing the rumours about the new café.
By dawn, the rescue team will have reached the ridge.
Sam used to hate spicy food, but now he loves it.
We are knowing each other since primary school.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect with "already" and an unfinished month fits repeated experience with present relevance.

Tip: "Already / yet / so far" often pair with present perfect.

FALSE — "Believe" is stative here; write "believe," not continuous.

Tip: Opinion verbs (believe, think = opinion) stay simple in careful English.

TRUE — Future perfect places arrival before dawn.

Tip: "By + future point" → will have + V3.

TRUE — "Used to hate" correctly marks a past taste that no longer holds.

Tip: Contrast "used to" with a present change to show discontinued habit.

FALSE — "Know" is stative and needs present perfect for a continuing relationship: "have known," not "are knowing."

Tip: Duration with "since" → present perfect simple for stative verbs.
tasks.solution_overview: Three survivors, two stative continuous fails. Trust present perfect for unfinished time, future perfect for "by," and "used to" for abandoned habits — then reject -ing on believe and know.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Priya has lived in Lisbon for six years.
The trail was still wet when we have arrived.
I am used to the noise from the tram line.
He used to be afraid of public speaking.
By the time the concert starts, we will have found our seats.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect + "for + duration" correctly shows a situation that continues now.

Tip: "For + length of time" with present perfect = still true.

FALSE — A completed arrival in a past narrative needs past simple: "when we arrived," not present perfect.

Tip: Do not mix a past continuous/simple story with present perfect for the same closed past.

TRUE — "Be used to" + noun correctly means accustomed to something.

Tip: After "be used to," a noun or -ing form both work.

TRUE — "Used to be" correctly describes a past state that has changed.

Tip: "Used to + be + adjective" is fine for former feelings or identities.

TRUE — Future perfect places finding seats before the concert begins.

Tip: "By the time + present" for future reference still wants will have in the main clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch the one timeline clash: a finished past arrival cannot wear present perfect. Everything else — "for," "be used to," "used to be," and future perfect — is clean.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bakery closed early last Sunday because of the heatwave.
She has just baked a loaf of sourdough.
Tom is preferring tea to coffee these days.
We will have walked ten kilometres by lunchtime.
My cousins used to visit us every summer.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past simple with "last Sunday" correctly closes a finished event.

Tip: Day/date anchors → past simple.

TRUE — Present perfect with "just" marks a recent action with present relevance.

Tip: "Just / already / yet" are classic present-perfect companions.

FALSE — "Prefer" is stative; write "prefers," not continuous.

Tip: Likes and preferences stay simple unless you force a temporary "acting" sense (rare in exams).

TRUE — Future perfect correctly projects distance covered before lunchtime.

Tip: Distance or quantity "by" a future point → will have + V3.

TRUE — "Used to visit" correctly reports a repeated past habit.

Tip: Frequency phrases (every summer) sit naturally with "used to."
tasks.solution_overview: Four good lines and one stative continuous. Separate closed past ("last Sunday") from recent present perfect ("just"), then reject "is preferring."

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Did you ever climb a volcano?
Have you ever climbed a volcano?
While I was reading on the balcony, it started to snow.
They are used to get up early for rowing practice.
By next winter, she will have completed her first marathon.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Life experience up to now needs present perfect: "Have you ever climbed…?" Past simple "Did you ever" is non-standard in careful exam English for open experience.

Tip: "Ever" for lifetime experience → Have you ever + V3?

TRUE — Present perfect correctly asks about experience at any time up to now.

Tip: "Ever / never" + present perfect = life experience.

TRUE — Past continuous background + past simple interrupt is textbook.

Tip: Reading was in progress; snow was the interrupt.

FALSE — Familiarity needs "be used to" + -ing: "are used to getting up," not "are used to get."

Tip: After "be used to," add a gerund or a noun — never a bare infinitive.

TRUE — Future perfect places marathon completion before next winter.

Tip: "By next + season/year" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Compare the two experience questions side by side, keep the continuous–simple pair, fix "be used to" + -ing, and lock future perfect with "by next winter."

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The app update has crashed twice since midnight.
I was understanding the lecture until the fire alarm rang.
We used to take the coastal path before the landslide.
By eight o’clock, the photographer will have set up the lights.
Hana has known her climbing partner for a decade.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect with "since midnight" fits repeated crashes still relevant now.

Tip: Tech glitches with "since" stay in present perfect.

FALSE — "Understand" is stative; use "understood" (past simple) for the background sense before the alarm.

Tip: Stative verbs rarely take past continuous in exam answers.

TRUE — "Used to take" correctly marks a discontinued route habit.

Tip: Past habit blocked by a later change → used to + V1.

TRUE — Future perfect places set-up before eight o’clock.

Tip: Clock "by" + future perfect.

TRUE — Present perfect of stative "know" with "for" correctly shows a continuing relationship.

Tip: "Have known … for" beats "am knowing."
tasks.solution_overview: Four keepers and one stative continuous. Trust "since," "used to," future perfect, and "have known" — reject "was understanding."

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: When we reached the summit, the sun has already risen.
When we reached the summit, the sun had already risen.
She is seeming tired after the long rehearsal.
I am getting used to the new keyboard layout.
They will have reheated the soup by the time you arrive.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Both events are in the past; the earlier sunrise needs past perfect, not present perfect.

Tip: Closed past narrative → had + V3 for the earlier action.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly places sunrise before the summit arrival.

Tip: "Already" + past perfect marks the prior completed state.

FALSE — "Seem" is stative; write "seems," not continuous.

Tip: Appearance verbs (seem, appear = look like) stay simple.

TRUE — "Get used to" + noun correctly means becoming accustomed.

Tip: "Get used to" = the process of adapting; "be used to" = already adapted.

TRUE — Future perfect places reheating before your arrival.

Tip: "By the time you arrive" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast the two summit lines carefully, reject stative "seeming," and accept "get used to" plus future perfect as clean.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: How long are you waiting for the night bus?
How long have you been waiting for the night bus?
The river flooded the towpath three times last winter.
Jonas used to living near the botanical gardens.
By Thursday evening, we will have curated the exhibition labels.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Duration up to now with "how long" needs present perfect continuous: "have you been waiting."

Tip: "How long …?" for ongoing action → have/has been + -ing.

TRUE — Present perfect continuous correctly asks about waiting that started earlier and continues.

Tip: Visible temporary activity + duration → present perfect continuous.

TRUE — Past simple with "last winter" correctly counts finished floods in a closed season.

Tip: Numbered past events in a finished period → past simple.

FALSE — Past habit needs "used to live," not "used to living."

Tip: Never put -ing after "used to" for habit.

TRUE — Future perfect places curation before Thursday evening.

Tip: Art-deadline "by" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Duration questions need present perfect continuous, closed seasons need past simple, and "used to" never takes -ing for habit. Future perfect with "by" stays solid.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I have been meaning to call you all week.
This jacket is fitting me perfectly today.
We had finished dinner before the guests rang the doorbell.
She is used to cook for large family gatherings.
By the time the podcast drops, the host will have recorded three more episodes.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect continuous of "mean" is an accepted fixed pattern for delayed intention.

Tip: "Have been meaning to…" is a rare continuous that exams often accept.

FALSE — "Fit" as a size/state is stative; prefer "fits" (or "fit" in AmE past) — not continuous for a permanent/current size fact.

Tip: Clothing size → simple: It fits me.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly shows dinner ended before the doorbell.

Tip: "Before" often helps you spot the earlier past action.

FALSE — Familiarity needs "is used to cooking," not "is used to cook."

Tip: Be used to + -ing / noun, never bare infinitive.

TRUE — Future perfect places recording before the podcast release.

Tip: Media schedules with "by the time" invite will have.
tasks.solution_overview: Accept the idiomatic "have been meaning," keep past perfect and future perfect, and reject stative "fitting" plus the bare infinitive after "be used to."

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Since moving abroad, Lara is making friends more easily.
Since moving abroad, Lara has been making friends more easily.
The museum used to open only on weekdays.
I am tasting the soup to check the seasoning.
By noon tomorrow, the drones will have mapped the whole coastline.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Since" with a continuing change needs present perfect (continuous), not present continuous alone.

Tip: "Since + -ing / since + time" → have/has (been) + verb.

TRUE — Present perfect continuous correctly links the move to an ongoing social change.

Tip: Process + since → have been + -ing.

TRUE — "Used to open" correctly reports a former schedule.

Tip: Former rules and timetables take used to + V1.

TRUE — "Taste" here is a deliberate action (sampling), so continuous is allowed.

Tip: Dynamic sense of sense verbs (taste/smell/feel on purpose) can take -ing.

TRUE — Future perfect places mapping completion before noon tomorrow.

Tip: Science deadlines with "by" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Pair the "since" lines carefully, keep "used to" and future perfect, and notice when a sense verb becomes dynamic ("am tasting") so continuous is fine.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He has gone to the allotment — he should be back by dusk.
He has been to the allotment three times this week.
We are loving this new pottery class.
They will have been travelling for fourteen hours by the time they land.
I used to be used to the cold winters, but I am not any more.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Has gone" correctly means he went and is still away.

Tip: Has gone = left and not back yet.

TRUE — "Has been to" correctly means visited and returned (experience/count).

Tip: Has been to = visited; has gone to = still there.

FALSE — In careful exam English, "love" stays stative: "We love this class," not continuous (marketing "I’m loving" is informal).

Tip: Exam default: like/love/hate → simple forms.

TRUE — Future perfect continuous correctly stresses duration before landing.

Tip: "By the time" + duration → will have been + -ing.

TRUE — The sentence deliberately contrasts "used to be" (past state) with "be used to" (familiarity) — both forms are used correctly.

Tip: Used to be ≠ be used to; you can combine them when meaning requires it.
tasks.solution_overview: Master "gone" versus "been," reject informal continuous "loving," accept future perfect continuous for duration, and parse the double "used to" contrast carefully.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This is the first time I have ever tried paddleboarding.
This is the first time I ever tried paddleboarding.
While the barista was frothing milk, the espresso machine jammed.
People are depending on the coastal path for weekend walks.
By the end of the festival, performers will have given forty shows.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "This is the first time" requires present perfect for the new experience.

Tip: First/second/third time + present perfect.

FALSE — Past simple after "this is the first time" breaks the pattern; use "have ever tried."

Tip: If the sentence starts with "This is the first time," expect have/has + V3.

TRUE — Continuous background + simple interrupt works for café chaos too.

Tip: Machine jam = short interrupt.

TRUE — "Depend" here describes a current community pattern; continuous is acceptable for a temporary/current reliance (and simple "depend" would also work).

Tip: Some verbs allow continuous when you stress a current situation.

TRUE — Future perfect totals shows before the festival ends.

Tip: Quantity completed "by the end" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Lock the "first time" + present perfect rule, keep the café interrupt pair and future perfect, and treat "are depending" as an acceptable current-situation continuous.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish I would have packed a warmer coat yesterday.
I wish I had packed a warmer coat yesterday.
She has been working on the mural all morning and still isn’t finished.
The soup is smelling of garlic and thyme right now.
By next spring, we will have been volunteering at the shelter for five years.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — After "I wish" for a past regret, use past perfect: "I wish I had packed," not "would have packed."

Tip: Wish + past perfect for past regrets; save would for present wishes about others’ behaviour.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly expresses a regret about yesterday’s packing.

Tip: I wish + had + V3 = past counterfactual.

TRUE — Present perfect continuous correctly stresses ongoing unfinished mural work.

Tip: All morning + still going → have been + -ing.

TRUE — "Smell" here reports a temporary sensory impression, so continuous is natural.

Tip: Dynamic sense (how something smells now) can take continuous; stative "It smells of garlic" is also fine.

TRUE — Future perfect continuous correctly projects five years of volunteering completed by next spring.

Tip: Duration up to a future point → will have been + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Fix the wish-regret pattern, then accept present perfect continuous, a dynamic sensory continuous, and future perfect continuous for long-running volunteering.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It’s high time we have updated the club website.
It’s high time we updated the club website.
After the storm had passed, birds began singing again.
I am seeing what you mean about the plot twist.
They will finish the crossword by tonight — in fact, they will have finished it by six.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "It’s high time" takes a past-simple form with present meaning: "updated," not present perfect.

Tip: High time / about time + past simple (unreal present).

TRUE — Past simple after "It’s high time" correctly marks overdue action.

Tip: Treat "high time" like a mini-unreal: past form, present urgency.

TRUE — Past perfect for the earlier storm, past simple for the later singing — clean sequence.

Tip: After + past perfect, then simple past for the next event.

TRUE — "See" here means "understand," and continuous "am seeing" is accepted in modern careful English for gradual understanding (simple "see" is also fine).

Tip: Mental "see" can take continuous when understanding unfolds.

TRUE — The second clause correctly upgrades to future perfect for a clearer "by six" completion.

Tip: "Will finish by" is ok; "will have finished by" is more precise for completion.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the "high time" + past simple rule, keep past-perfect sequencing, accept gradual "am seeing," and prefer future perfect for precise "by" completion.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No sooner the train had left than the platform announcement began.
No sooner had the train left than the platform announcement began.
I have yet to try the new climbing wall downtown.
We are having a brilliant time at the street festival.
By the time you read this postcard, we will already arrive in Lisbon.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "No sooner" needs inversion: "No sooner had the train left…," not subject–verb order without the auxiliary fronted.

Tip: No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than…

TRUE — Inverted past perfect correctly pairs with "than" for immediate sequence.

Tip: Inversion after no sooner / hardly / scarcely is exam gold.

TRUE — "Have yet to" is a present-perfect pattern meaning "still haven’t done."

Tip: Have yet to + V1 = still outstanding.

TRUE — "Have" for experiences/enjoyment is dynamic, so continuous is fine.

Tip: Having a good time / having lunch = action; owning = stative.

FALSE — "By the time" with a future reading needs future perfect: "will already have arrived," not "will already arrive."

Tip: By the time + present → will have + V3 in the main clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Force inversion after "no sooner," keep "have yet to" and dynamic "having," and repair the broken future perfect after "by the time."

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly I had sat down when my phone buzzed.
Hardly had I sat down when my phone buzzed.
She has been wanting a pottery wheel for months.
I’m thinking that the gallery closes too early on Mondays.
In two hours’ time, the tide will have turned and the rock pools will be underwater.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Hardly" needs inversion with past perfect: "Hardly had I sat down…"

Tip: Hardly / scarcely + had + subject + V3 + when…

TRUE — Correct inverted past perfect for an immediate follow-up event.

Tip: Match hardly … when with had + V3 after the fronted adverb.

TRUE — "Want" occasionally takes present perfect continuous for a long-standing desire; this is accepted in modern exam-tolerant English.

Tip: Have been wanting = desire lasting up to now.

FALSE — Opinion "think" (= believe) is stative: "I think that…," not "I’m thinking that…" Continuous "thinking" is for mental process ("I’m thinking about a title").

Tip: Think = opinion → simple; think about = considering → continuous ok.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places the turn of the tide before the two-hour mark, with a clear present-result consequence.

Tip: Nature deadlines with "in … time" + will have work well.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with inversion after "hardly," accept long-running "has been wanting," reject opinion continuous "I’m thinking that," and keep future perfect for the tide.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If you heat ice, it melts.
If the library opens early, Maya will finish her essay before lunch.
If it rains tomorrow, we will cancels the picnic.
If Leo studies tonight, he passes the quiz for certain next week.
If the oven is ready, Sara will bakes the muffins.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Zero conditional: present simple in both clauses for a general scientific fact that always holds.

Tip: Rules and natural facts → present + present, not will.

TRUE — First conditional: a real future plan takes present simple after if and will + base verb in the result.

Tip: Real near-future plans → if + present, main clause will + V1.

FALSE — After will the verb must stay bare: will cancel, not will cancels.

Tip: Modals never take a third-person -s on the following verb.

FALSE — A real future result needs will pass (or similar), not a bare present "passes" when you mean next week's outcome.

Tip: Open future results after a real condition usually take will, not plain present.

FALSE — Will takes the base form bake, not bakes.

Tip: Scan will + verb: if you see an -s, the line is broken.
tasks.solution_overview: Warm up on zero versus first: facts keep present + present; real plans keep present + will. Three lines fail on form — will + -s, and a bare present where a future result needs will.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If plants get no water, they die.
If Nora books the tickets today, we will sit together on the train.
If the bus is late, Tom will misses his lecture.
If you mix red and blue, you will get purple every time as a law of nature.
If the gym opens at six, Ana will train before work.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Zero conditional correctly states a general consequence with present simple on both sides.

Tip: Habitual or scientific truths prefer zero, not will.

TRUE — First conditional correctly links a real booking decision to a future seating plan.

Tip: Present in the if-clause; will in the result for open futures.

FALSE — Will misses is ungrammatical; use will miss.

Tip: After will, always use the bare infinitive.

FALSE — A timeless colour fact belongs in zero conditional (you get purple), not first with will.

Tip: If the result is always true, drop will and keep present + present.

TRUE — Clean first conditional for a real morning plan.

Tip: Real timetable + real intention → present + will.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate always-true rules (zero) from open future plans (first). Reject will + -s, and reject will when the sentence is really stating a permanent fact.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If I were you, I would take the earlier train.
If the weather were better, we would cycle to the lake.
If she would have more free time, she would join the choir.
If Dan lived closer, he would walk to campus every day.
If I was the team captain tomorrow in this hypothetical, I would change the formation.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional with formal were after if I, plus would + base verb for unreal advice.

Tip: Exams prefer If I were … would … for hypothetical roles.

TRUE — Past simple/were in the if-clause plus would marks an unreal present wish about the weather.

Tip: Unreal now → if + past, result would + V1.

FALSE — Do not put would in the if-clause; use If she had more free time…

Tip: Keep would in the result only; the if-clause wants past simple.

TRUE — Standard second conditional for a counterfactual present about distance and commuting.

Tip: Past simple + would is the default unreal-present frame.

FALSE — Careful exam English prefers were for unreal be after if, not was, especially in formal true/false items.

Tip: Hypothetical be → were is the safe exam choice.
tasks.solution_overview: These lines introduce unreal present (second conditional). Watch for would inside the if-clause and prefer were over was in careful hypothetical be.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Unless it rains, the match will go ahead.
As long as you water the herbs, they will stay fresh.
Unless you will hurry, we will miss the opening credits.
If only I knew her phone number now.
I wish I can speak Italian fluently this semester.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Unless (= if not) + present simple pairs cleanly with will for a real future sports plan.

Tip: Treat unless like if not: present in the condition, will in the result.

TRUE — As long as (= provided that) takes present simple for a real ongoing condition, then will in the result.

Tip: As long as / provided that → present + will for open conditions.

FALSE — After unless, avoid will; use present: Unless you hurry…

Tip: Unless / if / as long as rarely take will in the condition clause.

TRUE — If only + past simple correctly wishes about an unreal present lack of knowledge.

Tip: Present regrets with wish / if only → past simple.

FALSE — Wish about present ability needs past form: I wish I could speak…, not can.

Tip: After wish, shift the tense back one step from reality.
tasks.solution_overview: Meet unless, as long as, and wish / if only at entry level. Keep will out of the condition clause, and shift tenses back after wish for present unreal situations.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the cinema had more evening slots, we would go more often.
If I had known about the sale, I would have bought the jacket.
If they would practise every day, they would improve faster.
Unless Mia finishes her lab report, she will not watch the film.
As long as the neighbours keep quiet, I can revise until midnight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional for an unreal present about the cinema timetable.

Tip: Unreal present → past simple + would.

TRUE — Third conditional: past perfect in the if-clause and would have + past participle for a missed past opportunity.

Tip: Unreal past → if + had + V3, result would have + V3.

FALSE — Would does not belong in the if-clause; use If they practised…

Tip: Ban would from the condition; leave it for the result.

TRUE — Unless + present correctly sets a real study condition before a future plan.

Tip: Unless + present + will / will not is exam-safe for real futures.

TRUE — As long as + present states a real proviso that enables present ability.

Tip: As long as can support present results (can / may) as well as will.
tasks.solution_overview: Blend second, third, unless, and as long as. The only clear fail is would inside the if-clause; everything else keeps the condition form clean.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the ferry had left on time, we would have reached the island before dusk.
Had she set an alarm, she would not have overslept.
If Ben had trained harder, he will have won the race.
I wish I had packed an umbrella yesterday.
If only the Wi-Fi worked in this café right now.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Classic third conditional for a missed travel outcome in the past.

Tip: Past unreal → had + V3 / would have + V3.

TRUE — Inverted third conditional (Had she set…) correctly replaces If she had set…

Tip: Had + subject + V3 is a formal shortcut for if + past perfect.

FALSE — The result must stay in the unreal past: would have won, not will have won.

Tip: Third conditional results use would have, never will have.

TRUE — Wish + past perfect correctly regrets a past packing choice.

Tip: Past regrets after wish / if only → past perfect.

TRUE — If only + past simple correctly wishes about an unreal present problem.

Tip: Present inconvenience → past simple after if only.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on unreal past: third conditional, Had-inversion, and wish / if only. Reject will have where would have is required.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.
Unless you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.
As long as students submit drafts on Friday, the tutor will give feedback on Monday.
I wish the neighbours would stop drilling at dawn.
If only she will listen to the podcast before the seminar.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — First conditional with a negative if-clause correctly predicts a real future result.

Tip: If + present (affirmative or negative) + will is fine for open futures.

FALSE — Unless already means if not, so Unless you don't creates a messy double negative; use Unless you water… or If you don't…

Tip: Avoid stacking unless with another negative.

TRUE — As long as + present correctly sets a real academic condition for a future result.

Tip: Provided / as long as behave like if for real conditions.

TRUE — Wish + would correctly complains about someone else's annoying present habit.

Tip: Wish + would = desire for a change in someone else's behaviour.

FALSE — If only for a present/future wish needs past or would, not will: If only she would listen… / If only she listened…

Tip: After if only, do not keep ordinary will.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch polarity with unless, keep as long as in present for real plans, and use wish / if only + would for behaviour you want to change — not will.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the trail were less muddy, we would hike further.
If prices fall next month, more families will switch to seasonal produce.
If I would be taller, I would reach the top shelf easily.
Unless the museum closes early, we will see the sculpture wing.
I wish I were better at mental arithmetic.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional with were for an unreal present outdoor scenario.

Tip: Unreal be → were is preferred in careful English.

TRUE — First conditional: a real possible price change pairs with will switch. One everyday-economy line is fine among lifestyle topics.

Tip: Real future possibility → present + will.

FALSE — Never write If I would be; use If I were / If I was (exam: were).

Tip: Would stays out of the if-clause in standard conditionals.

TRUE — Unless + present + will correctly frames a real museum visit plan.

Tip: Unless = if not; keep present in the condition.

TRUE — Wish + were correctly marks an unreal present ability.

Tip: Wish I were is the formal pattern for present counterfactuals with be.
tasks.solution_overview: Consolidate second conditional, unless, wish + were, and one real first-conditional lifestyle/price line. The trap is If I would be.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she had taken the earlier bus, she would be at the theatre now.
If he were more organised, he would have handed in the portfolio last Friday.
If they had left earlier, they would arrive yesterday evening.
If I had more patience as a child, I would have learned piano sooner.
If you heated the soup now, it would taste better.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed conditional: past unreal cause (had taken) with present result (would be).

Tip: Past perfect in if + would + V1 = past cause, present effect.

TRUE — Mixed conditional: unreal present character (were) with past result (would have handed).

Tip: If + past / were + would have + V3 = present unreal trait, past consequence.

FALSE — A finished past result needs would have arrived, not would arrive, after a past perfect condition.

Tip: Past condition + past result → third, not first-looking would + V1 with yesterday.

FALSE — A childhood past state needs past perfect: If I had had more patience as a child…

Tip: Pure past regrets need had + past participle in the if-clause.

TRUE — Second conditional can use past simple heated for an unreal/unlikely present suggestion.

Tip: Soft hypothetical now → past + would.
highlights: If I had more patience as a child
tasks.solution_overview: Enter mixed conditionals: match the time of the cause to the time of the result. Reject would + V1 with clear past time markers, and reject weak past-perfect gaps in childhood regrets.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: As long as you will follow the recipe, the cake will rise.
Provided that the pool is open, we will swim after class.
I wish I didn't have to revise tonight.
If only they hadn't cancelled the outdoor concert last Saturday.
Unless she had missed the call, she would answer it now.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — As long as takes present for real conditions: As long as you follow…, not will follow.

Tip: Keep will out of as long as / provided that clauses.

TRUE — Provided that + present + will is a clean real-future proviso.

Tip: Provided that ≈ if / as long as for open conditions.

TRUE — Wish + past simple correctly regrets a present obligation.

Tip: Present annoyance after wish → past simple (didn't have to).

TRUE — If only + past perfect correctly regrets a finished past cancellation.

Tip: Closed past regrets → past perfect after if only / wish.

FALSE — The timelines clash: a past-perfect unless-clause wants a past result (would have answered), or rephrase as Unless she misses… she will answer / If she hadn't missed… she would answer now with matching mixed forms carefully.

Tip: Align condition time and result time; don't paste past perfect onto a plain would + V1 present without a clear mixed pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Tighten connectors (as long as / provided that) and wish / if only tense shifts. Reject will after as long as and messy unless + past perfect with a simple present result.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the tutor explained the theorem more slowly, more students would have passed last week's test.
If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly, more students would pass the resit next month.
If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly last term, more students would understand it now.
Had the trail been clearer, we would not have got lost.
If it weren't for the fog, we could see the harbour lights.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed conditional: unreal present teaching style (explained) with a finished past result (would have passed).

Tip: If + past + would have + V3 = present unreal trait, past consequence.

FALSE — A finished past explanation (had explained) does not pair cleanly with a plain future would pass next month; use would have passed for a past test, or If she explained… would pass for unreal present/future.

Tip: Align the time of the condition with the time of the result.

TRUE — Mixed: past unreal teaching (had explained) with present result (would understand now).

Tip: Had + V3 / would + V1 = past cause, present effect.

TRUE — Inverted third conditional correctly reports a past hiking mishap avoided in an alternate past.

Tip: Had + subject + been / V3 replaces If + past perfect.

TRUE — If it weren't for + noun correctly introduces an unreal present obstacle, with could in the result.

Tip: If it weren't for X = without X (unreal present).
tasks.solution_overview: Drill mixed timelines with a lifestyle pricing example, plus inversion and If it weren't for. Only the clearly time-aligned mixed line and the two standard patterns survive.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish you wouldn't leave your shoes in the hallway.
I wish you don't leave your shoes in the hallway.
If only the semester break were longer.
If water freezes, it will expands.
If water freezes, it expands.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Wish + would correctly asks for a change in habitual annoying behaviour.

Tip: Wish + would = stop doing that / please change.

FALSE — Wish does not take present simple like a command; use wouldn't leave or didn't leave.

Tip: After wish, shift the tense; don't keep ordinary present.

TRUE — If only + were correctly wishes for an unreal present length of break.

Tip: If only + past / were = present counterfactual.

FALSE — A scientific fact belongs in zero conditional, and will expands is doubly wrong (will + -s).

Tip: Zero facts: present + present; never will expands.

TRUE — Clean zero conditional for a physical law.

Tip: Permanent truths keep both clauses in present simple.
highlights: If only the semester break were
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast wish + would with the illegal wish + present, refresh if only + were, and return to zero conditional form for natural facts.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she studied abroad next year, she would improve her Spanish dramatically.
If she will study abroad next year, she improves her Spanish dramatically.
Should you need extra towels, the reception desk will help.
Were the path safer, children would use it after dark.
Had we known the gallery was free on Mondays, we would visit yesterday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional can mark an unlikely or tentative future plan (studied / would improve).

Tip: Unlikely future → past + would, even with next year.

FALSE — Will in the if-clause plus bare present improves is a broken first-conditional attempt.

Tip: Real future: If she studies… she will improve…

TRUE — Should you need… is a polite inverted first-conditional alternative to If you need…

Tip: Should + subject + V1 ≈ if + present for formal offers.

TRUE — Were the path safer… correctly inverts a second-conditional if-clause.

Tip: Were + subject + complement replaces If + subject + were.

FALSE — Inverted past perfect needs would have visited for a past result, not would visit yesterday.

Tip: Had we known… → would have + V3 for finished past outcomes.
tasks.solution_overview: Raise the bar with unlikely futures, Should/Were inversion, and Had-inversion. Keep will out of if-clauses and keep past results in would have.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If it had not been for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.
But for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.
If it was not for the flat tyre, we would have arrived hours ago.
As long as nobody objects, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.
Unless anyone will complain, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed pattern: past obstacle (had not been) with present/future-facing result (would be camping tonight).

Tip: If it had not been for X + would + V1 = past cause, present effect.

TRUE — But for + noun is a compact equivalent of if it were not / had not been for.

Tip: But for X ≈ without X / if not for X.

FALSE — Prefer If it hadn't been for… would have arrived… (past) or If it weren't for… would be… (present); was not for with would have is non-standard here.

Tip: Keep If it weren't for (present) and If it hadn't been for (past) distinct.

TRUE — As long as + present + can correctly sets a real group condition.

Tip: As long as supports present modal results as well as will.

FALSE — Unless + will is wrong; use Unless anyone complains…

Tip: No will after unless in standard condition clauses.
highlights: If it had not been for
tasks.solution_overview: Practise If it had not been for / But for, keep weren't for versus hadn't been for distinct, and strip will from unless.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish I would have more free evenings.
I wish I had more free evenings.
If only the train hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.
If the coach hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.
Supposing the café closed early, where would we study?
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Wish + would have is wrong for a present lack; use wish + past simple (had).

Tip: Wish I would have… is a classic exam error for present wishes.

TRUE — Wish + past simple correctly expresses an unreal present desire.

Tip: Present wish about states → past simple after wish.

TRUE — If only + past perfect cause with wouldn't be now is a valid mixed regret linking past delay to present queue.

Tip: Past perfect after if only can feed a present would/wouldn't result.

TRUE — Same mixed pattern with ordinary if instead of if only.

Tip: Past unreal cause → present continuous-looking result with would/wouldn't + be + -ing.

TRUE — Supposing + past simple introduces a second-conditional hypothesis with would in the question.

Tip: Supposing / suppose ≈ if for tentative scenarios.
tasks.solution_overview: Kill the wish I would have trap, keep wish + past for present states, and confirm mixed past→present with if / if only plus supposing.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Even if the tickets are expensive, we will still go to the festival.
Even if the tickets were free, we will still stay home.
Whether or not it rains, the charity run will start at nine.
If so be the weather improves, we will hike.
If need be, we can share taxis after the concert.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Even if + present + will correctly means the result holds despite the condition.

Tip: Even if ≠ if; the main clause still follows real-future will here.

FALSE — Even if + past (were) wants would stay, not will stay.

Tip: Match even if tense to the result: past → would; present → will.

TRUE — Whether or not + present + will correctly says the run happens regardless of rain.

Tip: Whether or not = no matter if.

FALSE — If so be is archaic and not exam-standard; use If the weather improves…

Tip: Stick to standard if + present for real futures.

TRUE — If need be is an accepted fixed phrase meaning if it is necessary, here with can.

Tip: If need be is a set idiom; don't "correct" it to if needs be in formal keys.
highlights: Even if the tickets were, we will
tasks.solution_overview: Cover even if, whether or not, and fixed if need be, while rejecting tense clashes and archaic if so be.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she were to apply for the scholarship, she would need two references.
If she was to have applied last term, she would need two references now.
Were he to practise daily, his serve would improve within weeks.
If I knew then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.
If I had known then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — If she were to apply is a formal second-conditional way to mark a hypothetical future step.

Tip: If + were to + V1 ≈ unlikely/formal if + past.

FALSE — Was to have applied mixed with would need now is over-stacked and non-standard for this item.

Tip: Prefer clear mixed or third forms; avoid was to have + mismatched results.

TRUE — Were he to practise… correctly inverts were to for a hypothetical training plan.

Tip: Were + subject + to + V1 replaces If + subject + were to.

FALSE — Knew then is underpowered for a clear past knowledge gap; the standard line uses had known then.

Tip: Past counterfactual knowledge → past perfect in the if-clause.

TRUE — Classic form: past perfect for past ignorance, would have chosen for the past decision.

Tip: Had known then… would have + V3 is the polished exam form.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced were to / Were … to inversion and the had known then pattern. Reject tangled was to have stacks and underpowered knew then for past counterfactuals.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'd rather you didn't stream loud videos while I'm revising.
I'd rather you don't stream loud videos while I'm revising.
It's time we left for the airport.
It's time we leave for the airport.
Suppose you won free concert tickets — what would you do?
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Would rather + past simple correctly softens a present preference about someone else's behaviour (conditional-adjacent).

Tip: I'd rather you + past = polite present preference.

FALSE — After I'd rather you, use past simple, not present don't.

Tip: Same backshift habit as wish: prefer past after I'd rather you.

TRUE — It's time + past simple is the standard formal pattern for a present urgency.

Tip: It's time we left = we should leave now.

FALSE — Careful exam keys usually want It's time we left, not leave.

Tip: It's time + past is the marked formal choice.

TRUE — Suppose + past + would correctly frames a second-conditional daydream.

Tip: Suppose / supposing pattern like if + past.
tasks.solution_overview: Extend conditional logic into I'd rather you, it's time + past, and suppose. These share the same backshift instinct as wish and second conditionals.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the inflation rate drops, household budgets will feel less pressure next quarter.
Had the storm not hit, the outdoor market would still be open this afternoon.
If only I could have attended the reunion last month.
I wish I could have attended the reunion last month.
Unless having finished the essay, she will not join us.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — First conditional with a real possible macro change and a future lifestyle effect.

Tip: Real future → present + will.

TRUE — Mixed: past unreal storm (Had … not hit) with present result (would still be open).

Tip: Negative inversion Had … not + V3 can feed a present would result.

TRUE — If only + could have + V3 correctly regrets a missed past ability/opportunity.

Tip: If only I could have… = past inability regret.

TRUE — Wish + could have + V3 matches the same past missed opportunity.

Tip: Wish I could have… parallels if only for past regrets about ability.

FALSE — Unless needs a finite clause (Unless she has finished…), not Unless having finished…

Tip: Unless + subject + verb; avoid dangling -ing after unless.
tasks.solution_overview: Combine one light economy first conditional, mixed Had-not inversion, wish / if only + could have, and reject non-finite unless having.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It's high time we booked the campsite.
If you come to the hike, bring a reusable bottle.
I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather holds.
I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather will hold.
No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm would go off.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — It's high time + past simple correctly marks present urgency with the same backshift as wish / it's time.

Tip: It's (high) time + past = we should do it now.

TRUE — Clear first-conditional imperative result: if + present, imperative bring…

Tip: Imperatives are fine as first-conditional results.

TRUE — Provided + present (holds) correctly sets a real weather condition for a future plan with will come.

Tip: Provided / providing + present, not will.

FALSE — Provided the weather will hold wrongly inserts will into the condition.

Tip: Same rule as if / as long as: no will in the proviso clause.

FALSE — No sooner… than needs a simple past result (went off), not conditional would go off.

Tip: No sooner is past sequencing, not a conditional frame.
highlights: If you come to the hike, bring
tasks.solution_overview: Finish with it's high time, imperative first conditionals, and provided + present, while rejecting will after provided and would forced onto a no sooner sequence.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of overdue library books has risen since March.
A number of neighbours was unable to join the street clean-up.
Neither the coach nor the players were copied on the match email.
Each of the flatmates have filed a chore preference form.
There are several typos in the potluck recipe list.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "The number of" treats the quantity as a single total, so the singular verb "has" is the right match.

Tip: Mentally replace "the number of X" with "that total" — singular almost always follows.

FALSE — "A number of" means "several," so it needs a plural verb: "were unable," not "was."

Tip: Flip the article test — "a number" ≈ many; "the number" ≈ one figure.

TRUE — With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject; "players" is plural, so "were" is correct.

Tip: Ignore the first noun and check only the one sitting next to the verb.

FALSE — "Each of" is always singular: "has filed," not "have filed."

Tip: "Each" picks out one member at a time, even when "of the flatmates" looks plural.

TRUE — "Typos" is plural, so "there are" agrees correctly.

Tip: After there is/are, locate the real subject that follows the verb and match its number.
tasks.solution_overview: This set drills the core agreement traps: the number versus a number, neither…nor proximity, each, and there is/are. Read past the distracting nouns and ask what the true subject is before you choose the verb.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Every applicant for the baking class receives a starter kit.
The chef, along with two helpers, were present at the tasting.
There is a backlog of laundry waiting for the dryer.
Neither the twins nor their aunt has signed the permission slip.
A number of guests have requested a later checkout.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Every" forces a singular verb, so "receives" is correct even though many applicants are implied.

Tip: Treat every/each like "one person at a time."

FALSE — "Along with two helpers" is a parenthetical add-on; the subject remains singular "The chef," so use "was present."

Tip: Cross out along with / as well as / together with and re-check the leftover subject.

TRUE — The delayed subject "a backlog" is singular, so "there is" agrees.

Tip: Do not let plural ideas inside the of-phrase steal the agreement — here "backlog" is the head.

TRUE — The nearer subject after neither…nor is singular "aunt," so "has" is right.

Tip: Proximity, not the first noun, decides the verb after neither…nor.

TRUE — "A number of guests" behaves as a plural group, so "have requested" is correct.

Tip: "A number of" ≈ several → plural verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch how add-ons like "along with" never change the head subject's number, while "every" and "a number of" pull in opposite directions. Confirm the grammatical subject first, then lock the verb.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of complaints have fallen after the repair.
Neither the kitchen nor the bathrooms was cleaned last week.
There is three outstanding photos on the shared album.
Each partner in the dance duo have veto rights over the routine.
The data from the pilot survey support the forecast.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "The number of" is singular: write "has fallen," not "have fallen."

Tip: "The number" is one count; keep the verb singular.

FALSE — Nearer subject "bathrooms" is plural, so the verb should be "were cleaned."

Tip: In neither…nor chains, only the last noun controls the verb.

FALSE — "Three outstanding photos" is plural, so you need "there are," not "there is."

Tip: Count what follows the verb in there-constructions.

FALSE — "Each partner" takes singular "has veto rights."

Tip: "Each" never takes a plural verb in standard formal English.

TRUE — In formal usage "data" is plural, so "support" is the agreed verb.

Tip: On formal exams, treat data as plural unless the prompt clearly marks informal style.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these sentences break agreement on purpose. Isolate the real subject — the number, the nearer nor-noun, the post-verbal noun after there, or each — and you will spot the mismatch quickly.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the referee nor the linesmen were briefed overnight.
The gardener, together with the volunteers, has approved the planting plan.
There are no further objections from the neighbours.
Every parcel above two kilos requires dual labelling.
A number of interns was assigned to the summer festival.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer subject "linesmen" is plural, so "were briefed" agrees.

Tip: Cover the first noun and read from "nor" onward.

TRUE — "Together with the volunteers" does not pluralise "The gardener"; singular "has" is correct.

Tip: Parenthetical with-phrases leave the head noun untouched.

TRUE — Plural "objections" correctly takes "there are."

Tip: "No" does not change number; match the noun that follows.

TRUE — "Every parcel" is singular, so "requires" is right.

Tip: Every/each + singular noun → singular verb.

FALSE — "A number of interns" needs plural "were assigned."

Tip: Swap in "several interns" — if that feels plural, keep the plural verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Most lines here are clean; the trap is the final "a number of" item that wrongly takes a singular verb. Use that contrast to cement the the-number / a-number distinction.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of open tickets is still above the club's service target.
Neither the solicitor nor the witnesses was available for the hearing.
There remain several chores that the housemates must finish.
The drama teacher, as well as the stage managers, are reviewing cues.
Each of the hiking clubs files its own risk assessment.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Singular "the number" correctly pairs with "is."

Tip: Focus on "number," not "tickets."

FALSE — Nearer subject "witnesses" is plural: use "were available."

Tip: Neither…nor proximity overrides the singular feel of "solicitor."

TRUE — Inverted "there remain" correctly agrees with plural "chores."

Tip: There-constructions can use verbs other than be; still match the following subject.

FALSE — "As well as the stage managers" is parenthetical; subject "drama teacher" needs "is reviewing."

Tip: Strip the as-well-as phrase before you choose the verb.

TRUE — "Each of the hiking clubs" takes singular "files."

Tip: "Of the hiking clubs" is a prepositional phrase, not the subject head.
tasks.solution_overview: Difficulty rises slightly with "there remain" and "as well as." Same method: identify the grammatical subject, ignore inserts, and match number.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of cyclists have demanded safer bike lanes.
Neither the understudy nor the chorus members were ready to rehearse.
The head gardener, along with her deputies, was copied on the schedule.
There is little room for another suitcase under the bunk.
The data on rainfall totals indicate a wetter spring.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Plural sense of "a number of" → "have demanded."

Tip: "A number of" almost always takes a plural verb in exam English.

TRUE — Nearer plural "chorus members" → "were ready."

Tip: Trust the last noun after nor.

TRUE — Head subject "head gardener" stays singular despite "along with her deputies."

Tip: Commas around the insert are a clue that it is not part of a compound subject.

TRUE — Uncountable "room" is singular, so "there is" fits.

Tip: After there is/are, uncountables take singular even when the idea feels broad.

TRUE — Formal plural "data" correctly takes "indicate."

Tip: Prefer plural agreement with data in formal writing.
tasks.solution_overview: All five sentences are grammatically sound. Use them as clean models of a number of, neither…nor, along with, there is with an uncountable, and formal plural data.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Every member of the book club has cast a vote.
The number of broken toys have doubled year on year.
Neither the tenant nor the landlords' agents is contesting the clause.
There are a clear timeline attached to the renovation steps.
The captain, together with the non-playing coaches, intends to resign if the bid fails.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Every member" → singular "has cast."

Tip: The of-phrase does not pluralise every/each.

FALSE — "The number of" needs singular "has doubled."

Tip: Do not agree with "toys."

FALSE — Nearer subject "agents" is plural: "are contesting," not "is."

Tip: Possessive markers on the nearer noun do not change its plural status.

FALSE — The real subject is singular "a clear timeline," so write "there is."

Tip: Articles and adjectives after there often hide a singular head.

TRUE — Singular captain remains the subject; "intends" is correct.

Tip: Together with never creates a plural compound subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed correct and incorrect lines force you to slow down on proximity after neither…nor and on singular heads after there. Name the subject aloud before you judge the verb.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of bakers was late with their sourdough orders.
Neither the guide nor the hikers was notified of the trail closure.
There is several pages missing from the scrapbook.
Each of the campsites have its own fire pit.
The data from last month's surveys show a narrower spread.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use plural "were late" after "a number of bakers."

Tip: If "their" later in the sentence feels natural, the verb is almost certainly plural.

FALSE — Nearer plural "hikers" needs "were notified."

Tip: Neither…nor: last noun wins.

FALSE — Plural "pages" requires "there are."

Tip: "Several" is a strong plural cue after there.

FALSE — "Each of" → singular "has its own fire pit."

Tip: "Its" already signals singular; keep the verb singular too.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "show."

Tip: Match data with plural verbs in exam answers unless told otherwise.
tasks.solution_overview: Four clear agreement errors surround one correct formal-data line. Scan for the usual suspects — a number, neither…nor, there is/are, each — before you mark true.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the secretary nor the volunteers have released the minutes.
The project lead, along with the helpers, has signed the rota.
There remain two conditions before we can start the trek.
Every one of the shortlisted bakers meets the hygiene checklist.
The number of active memberships are being reduced this quarter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer plural "volunteers" → "have released."

Tip: Read only from "nor" to the verb.

TRUE — Singular lead + along with… → "has signed."

Tip: Parenthetical helpers do not join the subject.

TRUE — Plural "conditions" correctly takes "remain."

Tip: Invert the sentence mentally: "two conditions remain."

TRUE — "Every one" is singular → "meets."

Tip: "Every one of" still points to a single unit for agreement.

FALSE — "The number of" is singular: "is being reduced."

Tip: Passive voice does not change the number of the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Mid-difficulty items combine inserts, every one of, and passive voice. Agreement still hinges on the same subject-finding habit — do not let the construction distract you.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the driver nor the passengers was listed on the boarding sheet.
A number of rules in the house agreement has been waived.
There is too many variables still open in the recipe.
The chair, as well as the committee secretaries, was delayed by the vote.
The data collected overnight do not yet justify a schedule change.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Nearer plural "passengers" → "were listed."

Tip: Long titles after nor still keep their plural number.

FALSE — "A number of rules" → plural "have been waived."

Tip: The of-phrase noun is plural; "a number of" takes that plurality.

FALSE — "Too many variables" is plural → "there are."

Tip: "Many" after there almost always signals a plural verb.

TRUE — Singular "chair" governs "was delayed"; secretaries are only an as-well-as insert.

Tip: Cross out the insert and re-read.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "do not yet justify."

Tip: Past participles after data ("collected") do not make the noun singular.
tasks.solution_overview: Here the distractors sit inside longer noun phrases. Peel the sentence to its skeleton subject before you accept or reject the verb.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Each monthly playlist submitted by the DJs goes to the host first.
Neither the landlord nor the tenants' solicitors have consented to the repair plan.
There appears to be several gaps in the packing checklist.
The podcast host, together with two editors, are pitching tomorrow.
The number of unsettled bookings has dropped below fifty.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Each monthly playlist" → singular "goes."

Tip: Long modifiers after each do not change singularity.

TRUE — Nearer plural "solicitors" → "have consented."

Tip: Possessive "tenants'" does not make the nearer noun singular.

FALSE — Although "appears" can introduce a clause, the logical subject "several gaps" is plural; prefer "there appear to be."

Tip: In there + appear/seem, still match the notional plural subject in careful exam English.

FALSE — Singular host + together with… → "is pitching."

Tip: Editors after together with are not co-subjects.

TRUE — "The number of" + singular "has dropped."

Tip: Keep agreeing with number, not bookings.
tasks.solution_overview: "There appears to be several" is a classic soft trap: the verb looks formal but still disagrees with a plural complement. Stay strict on number even in polished phrasing.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of regional coaches is attending the training weekend.
Neither the host nor the guests was willing to extend the stay.
There is only one schedule left to finalise before the show.
Every volunteer on the stall have signed the rota sheet.
The data in the appendix contradict the spoken summary.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "A number of regional coaches" → "are attending."

Tip: Replace with "several coaches" to hear the plural.

FALSE — Nearer plural "guests" → "were willing."

Tip: Do not let singular "host" pull the verb.

TRUE — Singular "one schedule" → "there is."

Tip: "Only one" is a reliable singular signal.

FALSE — "Every volunteer" → singular "has signed."

Tip: "On the stall" is only a locator phrase.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "contradict."

Tip: Plural verbs with data are expected in formal register.
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast the clean singular "there is only one" with the false singulars after a number of and every. Pattern recognition beats word-by-word guessing.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the buyer nor the sellers' lawyer has requested a delay.
The head chef, along with the sous-chefs, reviews the specials nightly.
There are still a few outstanding RSVPs from classmates.
Each of the flatshare partners retains a spare key.
The data underlying the fitness test suggest limited injury risk.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer singular "lawyer" → "has requested."

Tip: A singular nearer noun wins even when plural parties are nearby.

TRUE — Singular chef governs "reviews" despite along with.

Tip: Strip the insert; "the head chef reviews" must stand alone.

TRUE — Plural "RSVPs" → "there are."

Tip: "A few" marks plurality after there.

TRUE — "Each of" → singular "retains."

Tip: Partners in the of-phrase do not control the verb.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "suggest."

Tip: Participial modifiers ("underlying…") never change data's formal plurality.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are correct but denser. Treat them as benchmark sentences for proximity after neither…nor, along with, there are + a few, each of, and formal data.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of unresolved tickets are alarming the helpdesk.
Neither the sponsor nor the team captains was invited to the closed meeting.
There seems to be several inconsistencies between the two diaries.
The managing editor, as well as the reporters, have approved the feature.
A number of clauses in the lease survive completion.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "The number of" → singular "is alarming."

Tip: Continuous/progressive forms still follow the head subject's number.

FALSE — Nearer plural "team captains" → "were invited."

Tip: Long second nouns after nor are still plural when marked -s.

FALSE — Prefer "there seem to be several inconsistencies" to match the plural complement.

Tip: Seem/appear after there must still track the real subject's number in careful usage.

FALSE — Singular editor + as well as… → "has approved."

Tip: Reporters after as well as are not co-subjects.

TRUE — "A number of clauses" → plural "survive."

Tip: Present simple plural has no -s: survive, not survives.
tasks.solution_overview: Four failures and one clean "a number of" success. At this level, soft connectors like seems to be are designed to hide a plural complement — always check what follows.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the shop nor its branches is bound by the Sunday rule.
Every one of the contingent prizes has been disclosed in the notes.
There remain, after the rethink, three material open points.
The coach, together with the squad captains, was accountable for the overspend.
The data released this morning confirm the earlier forecast.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Nearer plural "branches" → "are bound."

Tip: Possessives ("its") before the nearer noun do not singularise it.

TRUE — "Every one of" → singular "has been disclosed."

Tip: Passive perfect still keeps singular agreement with every one.

TRUE — Plural "three material open points" → "remain," even with a mid-sentence insert.

Tip: Ignore the comma aside and match the postponed plural subject.

TRUE — Singular coach → "was accountable."

Tip: Together with never creates a plural subject.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "confirm."

Tip: Time adjuncts ("this morning") are irrelevant to number.
tasks.solution_overview: Inserted asides and passives raise the difficulty without changing the rules. Find the subject first; the verb will usually announce itself.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of practice drills was revised after the club meeting.
Neither the tutor nor the students' mentors has objected to the timetable.
There is, contrary to the notice, several unpaid bills still on the fridge.
Each branch that operates abroad file a local safety certificate.
The number of noise complaints has stabilised since the quiet hours.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "A number of … drills" → "were revised."

Tip: Long plural noun phrases after a number of still take plural verbs.

FALSE — Nearer plural "mentors" → "have objected."

Tip: Students' only marks possession; mentors remain plural.

FALSE — Plural "bills" → "there are," despite the interrupting phrase.

Tip: Cross out the contrary-to aside before choosing is/are.

FALSE — "Each branch" → singular "files."

Tip: Relative clauses after each do not licence a plural verb.

TRUE — "The number of" → singular "has stabilised."

Tip: Keep contrasting the number (singular) with a number (plural).
tasks.solution_overview: Interruptions and relative clauses are the main noise here. Mentally delete them, then apply the familiar agreement tests.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the parent club nor the satellite teams was named in the report.
The box office, along with the front-of-house stewards, approve large group bookings.
There appear to be a single bottleneck in the check-in workflow.
Every set of rehearsal notes for the cast is reviewed by the director.
The data on which the ranking rests are drawn from audited scores.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Nearer plural "teams" → "were named."

Tip: Extra adjectives before the nearer noun do not change its plural number.

FALSE — Singular "box office" + along with… → "approves."

Tip: Box office is a singular institutional subject here.

FALSE — The complement "a single bottleneck" is singular → "there appears to be."

Tip: Appear/seem after there must track a singular complement too — not only plurals.

TRUE — "Every set" is singular → "is reviewed."

Tip: "Set of notes" is one unit; every keeps it singular.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "are drawn," even inside a which-clause sandwich.

Tip: Relative clauses around data do not convert it to singular on formal papers.
highlights: There appear to be a single
tasks.solution_overview: Top band: reverse traps such as "there appear … a single" and institutional singulars like "box office." Read for the actual head noun, not the surrounding formality.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the organiser nor the registered helpers have accepted the revised timetable.
The general editor, together with outside advisers, has cleared the disclosure.
There remain, for the avoidance of doubt, two rules still in force.
Each of the house agreements provides for stepped fines.
The data furnished by the target school support a higher ranking.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer plural "helpers" → "have accepted."

Tip: Long nearer nouns after nor still obey proximity.

TRUE — Singular general editor governs "has cleared."

Tip: Together with outside advisers is parenthetical only.

TRUE — Plural "two rules" → "remain" despite the formal aside.

Tip: Padding between there and the subject changes nothing.

TRUE — "Each of" → singular "provides."

Tip: Agreements in the of-phrase stay out of the verb slot.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "support."

Tip: Past participles like "furnished" do not singularise data.
tasks.solution_overview: Five correct formal-register models. Internalise how inserts and dual adviser references still leave a single grammatical subject in charge of the verb.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of material safety clauses was triggered overnight.
Neither the organiser nor the other stewards in the group was prepared to waive the rule.
There is, when one examines the schedules carefully, more than two conflicting dates.
The lead reviewer, as well as the marking team, were responsible for the opinion.
The data that the model relies on have been restated twice this year.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "A number of … clauses" → "were triggered."

Tip: Dense noun phrases still follow the a-number-of plural rule.

FALSE — Nearer plural "stewards" → "were prepared."

Tip: Extra modifiers after the nearer noun ("in the group") do not make it singular.

FALSE — "More than two conflicting dates" is plural → "there are."

Tip: Quantity phrases greater than one take plural after there.

FALSE — Singular reviewer + as well as… → "was responsible."

Tip: Marking team after as well as is not a co-subject.

TRUE — Formal plural data correctly takes "have been restated."

Tip: Prefer plural agreement with data on formal exams unless the paper allows informal singular data.
tasks.solution_overview: Four agreement failures surround one clean formal-data line. Treat plural data as the safe exam default, and strip inserts before judging neither…nor, there is/are, and as well as.

tasks.title: Task 20
