tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the nominee captain nor the shadow captains have disclosed their interests.
The number of days between practices has improved after the fitness drive.
There appear to be fewer exceptions in this month's checklist.
Every parcel that exceeds the weight limit requires a second label.
The head teacher, along with the independent governors, have tabled a dissenting note.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer plural "shadow captains" → "have disclosed."

Tip: Doublets after nor still obey proximity.

TRUE — "The number of" → singular "has improved."

Tip: Of-phrases do not pluralise the number.

TRUE — Plural "fewer exceptions" → "there appear to be."

Tip: Fewer is a plural cue; match appear accordingly.

TRUE — "Every parcel" → singular "requires."

Tip: Relative clauses after every keep the verb singular.

FALSE — Singular head teacher + along with… → "has tabled."

Tip: Governors in the insert never join the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Close on a mixed set that recycles neither…nor, the number, there appear, every, and along with. One parenthetical plural distractor remains — strip it and the error is obvious.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Cyclists must wear a helmet on this coastal path.
The match might be cancelled beyond any possible doubt.
You need not bring a dish to the potluck if you are short on time.
We can must reserve a table before seven.
She ought to stretch before the morning run.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must" marks a hard rule here: helmets are required on the path.

Tip: For non-negotiable rules, use "must" + bare infinitive.

FALSE — "Might" only signals weak possibility, so "beyond any possible doubt" contradicts it.

Tip: Certainty language never sits with "might" or "could".

TRUE — "Need not" correctly removes obligation: the dish is optional.

Tip: "Need not" = no duty; "must not" = prohibition.

FALSE — Stacking "can" and "must" is ungrammatical; English allows only one modal before the main verb.

Tip: Choose ability or obligation — never both.

TRUE — "Ought to" + infinitive correctly advises a sensible warm-up.

Tip: "Ought" always needs "to": "ought to stretch", never "ought stretch".
tasks.solution_overview: This set mixes clear obligation, weak possibility, and a double-modal trap. Read each sentence for one job only: does the modal match the certainty or duty the rest of the sentence claims?

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Visitors must to leave wet umbrellas by the door.
You must not to feed the ducks near the jetty.
The delay may stem from a signal failure on the branch line.
They must have knew about the surprise party earlier.
The results could confirm the hypothesis in every scenario without exception.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Must" takes a bare infinitive: "must leave", not "must to leave".

Tip: Pure modals never take "to" before the main verb.

FALSE — After "must not", use the bare infinitive: "must not feed", not "must not to feed".

Tip: Only "ought" and patterns like "need to" bring "to".

TRUE — "May" hedges carefully: a signal failure is a possible cause, not a proven one.

Tip: Use "may" or "might" when evidence is incomplete.

FALSE — Modal perfect needs a past participle: "must have known", not "must have knew".

Tip: Pattern is modal + have + past participle for past deductions.

FALSE — "Could" expresses possibility, so it cannot guarantee an unconditional outcome "without exception".

Tip: Absolute certainty and a weak modal cannot share one claim.
tasks.solution_overview: Four traps crowd this set: illicit "to" after "must", another after "must not", a wrong past participle in modal perfect, and a weak modal that overclaims certainty. Only the cautious "may" sentence stands.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The post cannot have arrived yet — the box is still empty.
Neighbours might have overlooked the note on the gate.
We ought revise the packing list before we leave.
Guests may request an extra blanket at reception.
The ferry will likely be delayed for certain and without any doubt.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have arrived" is a solid modal-perfect deduction about a past event still unconfirmed by evidence.

Tip: Negative modal perfects deny a past possibility on logical grounds.

TRUE — "Might have overlooked" softens a past deduction — possible, not proven.

Tip: "Might have" + past participle = tentative past speculation.

FALSE — "Ought" requires "to": "ought to revise", not "ought revise".

Tip: Treat "ought to" as a fixed pair before the base verb.

TRUE — "May" here marks permission: guests are allowed to ask for a blanket.

Tip: In house rules, "may" often means "are allowed to".

FALSE — "Will likely" already hedges, so "for certain and without any doubt" clashes with that hedge.

Tip: Strip either the hedge or the certainty claim — they cannot both stand.
tasks.solution_overview: Modal perfects and permission "may" appear alongside one missing "to" after "ought" and one hedge-versus-certainty clash. Check structure first, then whether the strength of the modal fits the claim.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Swimmers must shower before entering the pool.
The forecast must show sunshine, though we have no evidence at all.
She could have posted the parcel before the cut-off.
You need not to renew the library card today.
The coach should reconsider the batting order.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must" correctly imposes a non-negotiable pool rule.

Tip: Safety and hygiene rules almost always take "must", not "might".

FALSE — Strong deduction "must" cannot coexist with "no evidence at all".

Tip: No evidence → use "may"/"might", not "must".

TRUE — "Could have posted" correctly frames a past possibility that remains open.

Tip: "Could have" + past participle = past possibility or missed opportunity.

FALSE — Modal "need not" takes a bare infinitive: "need not renew", not "need not to renew".

Tip: Contrast with main-verb "need to": "You need to renew" vs "You need not renew".

TRUE — "Should" appropriately advises a rethink of the line-up.

Tip: "Should" is the default for measured advice.
tasks.solution_overview: Obligation, deduction, and advice sit side by side. Flag any sentence where a strong modal ("must") is undercut by weak evidence, or where an extra "to" sneaks in after "need not".

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The nurse should have flagged the allergy sooner.
Campers may not light fires after dusk under site rules.
He must sign the consent form before the trial starts.
The clouds might suggest a short shower rather than a storm.
We could shorten the hike if we take the ridge path.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Should have flagged" correctly criticises a past missed duty with modal perfect.

Tip: "Should have" + past participle = past advice not followed / mild reproach.

TRUE — "May not" here denies permission under the rules — a standard reading.

Tip: Context decides: "may not" can mean prohibition or weak negative possibility.

TRUE — "Must sign" correctly imposes a hard pre-trial requirement with a bare infinitive.

Tip: Pure modals take the bare verb — no "to".

TRUE — "Might suggest" hedges an interpretation of the sky without overclaiming.

Tip: Soft epistemic modals protect you when signs admit more than one reading.

TRUE — "Could" correctly marks a feasible shorter route, not a guaranteed outcome.

Tip: Possibility "could" is fine when the sentence does not claim certainty.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound: past missed duty, rule-based "may not", hard obligation, hedged interpretation, and feasible optionality. Confirm that each modal’s strength matches the claim and that forms stay clean.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The museum might close early with absolute certainty.
Hosts ought to warn guests about the steep stairs.
They cannot have ignored the fire alarm in the hallway.
You should of updated the packing list after the forecast changed.
Volunteers need not bring their own tools to the park clean-up.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Might" and "absolute certainty" cancel each other out.

Tip: Match modal strength to the adverbial claim — weak modal, weak claim.

TRUE — "Ought to warn" correctly advises a prudent courtesy before guests arrive.

Tip: "Ought to" = strong advice, close to "should".

TRUE — "Cannot have ignored" is a firm negative deduction about a past event.

Tip: Loud evidence + "cannot have" = logical impossibility of the alternative.

FALSE — "Should of" is a spoken mishearing of "should have".

Tip: Always write "have", never "of", after a modal.

TRUE — "Need not bring" correctly lifts the obligation to supply tools.

Tip: Modal "need not" + bare infinitive removes duty without forbidding the action.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch for certainty clashes and the classic "should of" spelling trap. Clean advice, negative deduction, and waived obligation pass; overclaimed "might" and "of" for "have" fail.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Students must have finished the quiz by now — every desk is empty.
You may borrow my spare charger if yours is dead.
She might to join us after rehearsal.
Drivers should check tyre pressure before a long trip.
The cake need not be iced until tomorrow morning.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must have finished" is a strong past deduction backed by empty desks.

Tip: Evidence in the present often licenses "must have" about the recent past.

TRUE — "May borrow" correctly grants permission.

Tip: Offer/permission "may" + bare infinitive is standard.

FALSE — Drop the "to": "might join", not "might to join".

Tip: Pure modals never take "to" before the main verb.

TRUE — "Should check" is measured advice before travel.

Tip: "Should" softens obligation into recommendation.

TRUE — "Need not be iced" correctly says icing can wait — no present duty.

Tip: "Need not" + bare infinitive (passive or active) removes obligation.
tasks.solution_overview: Permission, advice, deduction, and waived duty are all fine here. The only failure is the stray "to" after "might" — strip it and the sentence works.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They could of left the keys under the flowerpot.
You mustn’t park across the neighbour’s drive.
The trail may become muddy after overnight rain.
We ought have booked tickets earlier.
She needn’t have cooked so much — half the trays went untouched.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Write "could have left", never "could of left".

Tip: "Of" after a modal is always wrong in standard writing.

TRUE — "Mustn’t park" correctly forbids the action.

Tip: "Must not / mustn’t" = prohibition, not "no need".

TRUE — "May become" hedges a weather-linked possibility.

Tip: Soft prediction after rain often takes "may" or "might".

FALSE — "Ought" needs "to": "ought to have booked".

Tip: Even in modal perfect, keep "ought to" intact: ought to + have + PP.

TRUE — "Needn’t have cooked" correctly means she cooked unnecessarily in the past.

Tip: "Needn’t have" + PP = past action done though it was not required.
tasks.solution_overview: Prohibition, weather hedge, and "needn’t have" for unnecessary past effort are clean. Failures are form-only: "of" for "have" and a missing "to" after "ought".

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The lights are on, so someone must be home.
He might have been waiting at the wrong platform.
You should must confirm the reservation by Friday.
Artists may exhibit in the foyer during festival week.
We need not to worry about tickets — the show is free.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present deduction "must be" fits strong evidence (lights on).

Tip: Present continuous evidence → "must" + bare infinitive for now-time certainty.

TRUE — "Might have been waiting" softens a past progressive speculation.

Tip: Modal + have been + -ing = tentative past continuous deduction.

FALSE — "Should must" stacks two obligation modals.

Tip: Use "should confirm" or "must confirm" — never both.

TRUE — "May exhibit" correctly allows participation during the festival.

Tip: Permission "may" works for temporary openings and invitations.

FALSE — Drop the "to": "need not worry", not "need not to worry".

Tip: Modal "need not" + bare verb; main-verb "need" takes "to".
tasks.solution_overview: Present and progressive past deductions are fine, as is festival permission. Reject stacked obligation and the illicit "to" after "need not".

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup must taste better once it has simmered a little longer.
She could have been practising piano when you called.
Players ought to arrive forty minutes before kick-off.
You may not take photographs inside the chapel.
They must have forgot the picnic basket in the boot.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must taste" here is a confident prediction based on cooking know-how, not a rule.

Tip: Epistemic "must" can project a near-certain outcome from experience.

TRUE — "Could have been practising" correctly frames an open past continuous possibility.

Tip: Progressive modal perfect softens what someone was doing at a past moment.

TRUE — "Ought to arrive" advises a sensible buffer before the match.

Tip: Keep "to" after "ought" even with time phrases.

TRUE — "May not take" denies permission inside the chapel.

Tip: In posted rules, "may not" often equals "are not allowed to".

FALSE — Past participle required: "must have forgotten", not "must have forgot".

Tip: Irregular verbs still need the participle after "have" in modal perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Four clean lines cover prediction, progressive past possibility, advice, and prohibition. Only the wrong past participle after "must have" fails.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bus might well be late in this fog.
You should have told me about the detour sooner.
He must to have left his scarf on the train.
We needn’t stay for the encore if you are tired.
The painting could be a later copy, though experts disagree.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Might well be" idiomatically strengthens a serious present possibility.

Tip: "Might well" ≈ "it is quite possible / rather likely".

TRUE — "Should have told" criticises a past missed courtesy.

Tip: "Should have" + PP = reproach about what did not happen.

FALSE — No "to" after "must": "must have left", not "must to have left".

Tip: Modal perfect is modal + have + PP — never insert "to".

TRUE — "Needn’t stay" correctly lifts the obligation to remain.

Tip: Contracted "needn’t" + bare infinitive is standard.

TRUE — "Could be" hedges an attribution without claiming proof.

Tip: Soft epistemic "could" fits scholarly disagreement.
tasks.solution_overview: Idiomatic "might well", past reproach, waived duty, and scholarly hedge are all valid. Reject only the illegal "to" inside a "must have" chain.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hikers must not leave litter on the ridge.
She may have been about to call when the signal dropped.
You ought to of packed a spare battery.
They couldn’t have finished the jigsaw already — half the pieces are still on the table.
We should water the seedlings every other morning.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must not leave" clearly prohibits littering.

Tip: "Must not" = do not do this; different from "need not".

TRUE — "May have been about to call" hedges an interrupted near-future-in-the-past plan.

Tip: "Be about to" can sit inside modal perfect for near-miss timing.

FALSE — Write "ought to have packed", never "ought to of packed".

Tip: "Have", not "of", even after "ought to".

TRUE — "Couldn’t have finished" denies a past completion on clear present evidence.

Tip: Visible leftover pieces license a firm negative past deduction.

TRUE — "Should water" advises a regular care routine.

Tip: Habitual advice often takes "should" + bare infinitive.
tasks.solution_overview: Prohibition, nested "about to", negative past deduction, and garden advice pass. The only failure is "of" standing in for "have" after "ought to".

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The choir must have been rehearsing for hours — their voices sound tired.
You may as well take the later train if the earlier one is packed.
She needn’t have to bring dessert; the host already baked two cakes.
They mightn’t have noticed the small print on the ticket.
We should have been leaving earlier to catch the opening act.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Progressive modal perfect "must have been rehearsing" fits present evidence of tired voices.

Tip: Tiredness now → strong deduction about continuous past effort.

TRUE — "May as well take" idiomatically recommends the practical option.

Tip: "May as well" + bare infinitive = "there is little reason not to".

FALSE — "Needn’t have to bring" double-marks absence of obligation; write "needn’t bring" or "doesn’t have to bring".

Tip: Pick one no-obligation marker — do not stack "need not" with "have to".

TRUE — "Mightn’t have noticed" softens a past negative deduction.

Tip: Contracted "mightn’t have" is acceptable in informal prose.

TRUE — "Should have been leaving" criticises a past progressive plan that started too late.

Tip: Progressive "should have been + -ing" = we ought to have been in the middle of leaving.
tasks.solution_overview: Progressive modal perfects and idioms like "may as well" are legitimate. Reject only the redundant "needn’t have to" pairing — one waived-duty marker is enough.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The battery must be dead — nothing lights up when I press the switch.
He could have been going to apologise before the argument flared again.
You mustn’t have borrowed my bike without asking — and the lock is still on it.
She ought to have been practising scales daily, not only before exams.
We may to have misread the trail markers in the dusk.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present "must be" is a strong deduction from immediate evidence.

Tip: Dead indicators + "must" = confident now-time conclusion.

TRUE — "Could have been going to apologise" hedges an aborted past intention.

Tip: "Be going to" can nest under modal perfects for plans that never landed.

TRUE — Here "mustn’t have borrowed" works with evidence that the lock is untouched, denying the past act.

Tip: Context matters: past "must not have" can deny an action that did not occur.

TRUE — "Ought to have been practising" criticises a past continuous habit that fell short.

Tip: Progressive past advisability: ought to + have been + -ing.

FALSE — "May to have" inserts an illegal "to" after the modal.

Tip: Pattern is "may have misread", never "may to have".
tasks.solution_overview: Nested "be going to", progressive "ought to have been", and evidenced "mustn’t have" are advanced but valid. Fail only the stray "to" after "may".

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The garden cannot but have suffered after three weeks without rain.
You should of been checking the oven timer more carefully.
They may well have taken the scenic route to avoid the motorway.
We needn’t have reserved seats — the hall was half empty.
She must can speak Spanish after a year in Madrid.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot but have suffered" is a formal idiom meaning "must inevitably have suffered".

Tip: "Cannot but" + bare infinitive / perfect signals inevitability.

FALSE — "Should of been" must be "should have been".

Tip: Same rule every time: "have", never "of".

TRUE — "May well have taken" strengthens a serious past possibility.

Tip: "May well have" = "it is quite possible that … did".

TRUE — "Needn’t have reserved" correctly means the past reservation was unnecessary.

Tip: Empty hall now proves the earlier booking was surplus.

FALSE — "Must can" stacks two modals; write "must be able to speak" or "can speak".

Tip: English forbids double pure modals — insert "be able to" if you need ability after "must".
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "cannot but" and "may well have" are acceptable advanced shapes. Reject "of" for "have" and the illegal double modal "must can".

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup should have been simmering gently, not boiling hard.
He might have left already, but we cannot be sure.
You need not have brought an umbrella — it never rained.
They mustn’t of crossed the frozen lake on foot.
We ought to update the shared shopping list before Friday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Should have been simmering" criticises the wrong past continuous cooking method.

Tip: Progressive modal perfect can target how something was being done.

TRUE — "Might have left" correctly softens an uncertain past deduction.

Tip: Pairing "might have" with "cannot be sure" is coherent hedging.

TRUE — "Need not have brought" correctly marks an unnecessary past action.

Tip: Dry weather after the fact proves the umbrella was surplus.

FALSE — Write "mustn’t have crossed", never "mustn’t of crossed".

Tip: Contractions do not license "of" for "have".

TRUE — "Ought to update" correctly advises a timely list refresh.

Tip: Present advice still needs "ought to" + bare infinitive.
tasks.solution_overview: Progressive past advice, soft deduction, and unnecessary past effort are clean. The single failure is another "of" standing in for "have" after "mustn’t".

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The archivist cannot have been other than delighted by the recovered letters.
You should must label the allergy on the lunchbox clearly.
We ought to have been watering the balcony plants daily in this heat.
He mightn’t have realised the path forked behind the barn.
She need not have to renew the membership until autumn.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have been other than delighted" is a formal double negation meaning she must have been delighted.

Tip: "Cannot have been other than …" = strong positive deduction in formal dress.

FALSE — "Should must" stacks two obligation modals.

Tip: Use "should label" or "must label" — never both.

TRUE — "Ought to have been watering" correctly criticises a past continuous habit that fell short.

Tip: Progressive past advisability: ought to + have been + -ing.

TRUE — "Mightn’t have realised" softens a past negative deduction about awareness.

Tip: Contracted "mightn’t have" fits informal narrative.

FALSE — "Need not have to renew" double-marks waived duty; write "need not renew" or "does not have to renew".

Tip: One no-obligation marker is enough.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal double-negative deduction and progressive "ought to have been" are legitimate. Reject stacked obligation ("should must") and the redundant "need not have to" pairing.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The ranger cannot but have noticed the abandoned campfire.
We should have had the boots resoled before the trek.
She may to have understated how steep the final climb was.
Flatmates mustn’t have taken cash from the jar overnight — and the note count proves they did not.
The guide might well have taken a shortcut through the orchard.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot but have noticed" means "must inevitably have noticed".

Tip: "Cannot but" + perfect is formal but grammatical for inevitability.

TRUE — "Should have had … resoled" correctly frames a past causative expectation.

Tip: Modal perfect can wrap causative "have + object + past participle".

FALSE — "May to have" inserts an illegal "to" after the modal.

Tip: Pattern is "may have understated", never "may to have".

TRUE — Here "mustn’t have taken" works as a past prohibition reading supported by evidence that the cash is untouched.

Tip: Context and corroboration matter with past "must not have".

TRUE — "Might well have taken" idiomatically strengthens a serious past suspicion.

Tip: "Might well have" = "it is quite possible that … did".
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced idioms ("cannot but", "might well have") and causative modal perfects are acceptable. Reject only the stray "to" after "may". Read past "mustn’t have" carefully against the evidence clause.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The chef must have been about to plate the dessert when the power cut hit.
You needn’t to have packed both jumpers and a heavy coat.
They could have been going to cycle the coastal path before the wind rose.
The map should not of omitted the footbridge over the creek.
We may as well have walked for all the good the crowded bus did.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must have been about to plate" correctly deduces an imminent past plan interrupted by the outage.

Tip: "Be about to" can sit inside a modal perfect for near-future-in-the-past deductions.

FALSE — Drop the "to": "needn’t have packed", not "needn’t to have packed".

Tip: Modal "need not/needn’t" never takes "to" before the verb chain.

TRUE — "Could have been going to cycle" hedges a past intention that never completed.

Tip: "Be going to" can nest under modal perfects for aborted plans.

FALSE — "Should not of omitted" must be "should not have omitted".

Tip: Same rule every time: "have", never "of".

TRUE — "May as well have walked" idiomatically means the bus achieved nothing useful.

Tip: "May as well have" + past participle = ironic "it would have made little difference".
tasks.solution_overview: Nested near-future and "be going to" inside modal perfects are advanced but valid. Failures are form-only: an extra "to" after "needn’t" and another "of" for "have". The ironic "may as well have" idiom is fine.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The volunteers cannot have been other than exhausted after the night shift at the shelter.
She should must escalate any safety concern to the site supervisor the same day.
We ought to have been updating the trail conditions continuously, not weekly.
He mightn’t have realised the ferry required advance booking in peak season.
The book club need not have to maintain two separate reading lists after the groups joined.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have been other than exhausted" means they must have been exhausted.

Tip: Formal "cannot have been other than …" = strong positive deduction.

FALSE — "Should must" stacks two obligation modals.

Tip: Use "should escalate" or "must escalate" — never both.

TRUE — "Ought to have been updating" correctly criticises a past continuous practice that fell short.

Tip: Progressive past advisability: ought to + have been + -ing.

TRUE — "Mightn’t have realised" softens a past negative deduction about awareness.

Tip: Contracted "mightn’t have" is acceptable in less formal prose.

FALSE — "Need not have to maintain" double-marks absence of obligation; write "need not maintain" or "do not have to maintain".

Tip: Pick one no-obligation marker — "need not" or negated "have to", not both stacked.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal double-negative deduction and progressive "ought to have been" are legitimate advanced shapes. Reject stacked obligation ("should must") and the redundant "need not have to" pairing — one marker of waived duty is enough.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbours painted the fence. → The fence was painted by the neighbours.
The cake was baked yesterday. → The chef baked the cake yesterday, and we know that for certain.
Several windows were broken by the storm.
The photograph was cropped before posting. → The photograph cropped itself before posting.
My sister watered the plants. → The plants were watered by my sister.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Object becomes subject, past simple becomes was + past participle, and the original agent stays in a by-phrase. Meaning is unchanged.

Tip: Keep the agent only when the active sentence actually names one.

FALSE — The passive names no agent, so the rewrite invents both a baker and certainty. A fair active would not claim you know who.

Tip: Agentless passives must stay agentless unless the source names the doer.

TRUE — Clear be + past participle with an explicit cause: were broken by the storm.

Tip: Plural subjects take were, not was, in past passive.

FALSE — Photographs do not crop themselves; the rewrite invents a reflexive agent and drops the implied human editor.

Tip: Never turn a missing agent into the patient acting on itself.

TRUE — Clean active→passive: watered → was watered, agent retained as by my sister.

Tip: Match tense: past simple active → past simple passive.
tasks.solution_overview: Treat each arrow as a meaning check, not a creative rewrite. Ask whether the second sentence keeps the same tense, the same participants, and the same certainty. If the first side hides the doer, the second side must not invent one.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The tickets were booked last Friday.
Mistakes were made during the rehearsal. → The rehearsal made mistakes deliberately.
The librarian shelved the returns. → The returns were shelved by the librarian.
The concert was cancelled yesterday. → Someone cancelled the concert yesterday, and we know exactly who.
The parcel been delivered by the courier this morning.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct past passive focusing on the tickets; no agent is required.

Tip: Agentless passive is fine when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

FALSE — Mistakes were made does not say the rehearsal caused them on purpose. The rewrite adds agency and intent that were never stated.

Tip: Do not smuggle deliberately into a neutral passive.

TRUE — Meaning-preserving transformation with agent kept: were shelved by the librarian.

Tip: Watch participle form: shelve → shelved.

FALSE — Knowing exactly who fabricates information the passive never supplied.

Tip: Someone… and we know exactly who is almost always a fake-agent trap.

FALSE — Missing was/has: need was delivered or has been delivered, not bare been delivered.

Tip: Passive always needs a form of be before the participle.
tasks.solution_overview: Start with form: is there a proper be + past participle? Then check meaning: any by-phrase or active rewrite must come from words already on the page, not from guesswork about who did it or why.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Volunteers designed the mural. → The mural was designed by volunteers.
The bridge was repaired in 2019.
Lost dogs are returned by the local shelter.
The groceries unpacked by my brother yesterday.
The coach cancelled practice. → Practice was cancelled by the coach.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Active object becomes passive subject; designed → was designed; agent retained.

Tip: Keep subject–verb number: the mural was, not were.

TRUE — Grammatical agentless past passive stating when the bridge was fixed.

Tip: Time phrases like in 2019 sit naturally with past passive.

TRUE — Present simple passive with a clear agent: are returned by…

Tip: Habitual processes often use present passive.

FALSE — Needs were unpacked (or have been unpacked). A lone past participle is not a finite passive clause.

Tip: If you can ask Were they unpacked?, you still need the were in the sentence.

TRUE — Cancelled → was cancelled; coach stays as by-agent.

Tip: Match the original tense when you flip voice.
highlights: are returned by the local shelter
tasks.solution_overview: Most items are form checks: past or present be + participle, with or without by. Spot the line that drops the auxiliary entirely — that is not a complete passive clause.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The playlist was shared online. → The playlist shared itself online.
No lessons can be scheduled this week. → This calendar prevents anyone from scheduling lessons deliberately.
The invitation was sent by the host. → We know the mayor personally sent the invitation.
The tent was damaged during the wind. → The wind damaged the tent.
The guests were notify of the delay on Monday.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Reflexive rewrite is nonsense; a playlist does not share itself.

Tip: Patient ≠ agent; do not force the subject to do the action to itself.

FALSE — Modal passive can be scheduled is neutral. The rewrite invents prevention and intent.

Tip: Modal passives must keep the same modality and force.

FALSE — by the host does not entail that the mayor did it personally.

Tip: Never upgrade a named agent into a different, more specific one.

TRUE — during the wind supplies the cause; The wind damaged the tent keeps that cause without inventing a human doer.

Tip: Event/cause subjects are allowed when the passive already situates the damage in that event.

FALSE — Wrong form: need were notified, not were notify.

Tip: After be, use the past participle, never the base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Four traps invent agents, intent, or wrong verb forms; only one pair keeps the same event. When you reverse passive→active, use only participants the original allows.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The suitcase is being weighed by airport staff.
The teacher has marked three essays. → Three essays have been marked by the teacher.
The photos will be printed after the trip.
The dog must be walked before dinner.
The attic was cleared by an old school friend.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present continuous passive: is being + past participle, agent retained.

Tip: Continuous passive needs being between be and the participle.

TRUE — Present perfect active → present perfect passive: have been marked by the teacher.

Tip: Perfect passive = have/has been + past participle.

TRUE — Future passive with will be + past participle; agent optional.

Tip: will be printed, not will printed.

TRUE — Modal passive: must be walked. Obligation sits on the walk, not on a named walker.

Tip: Modal + be + PP is the standard obligation passive.

TRUE — Past passive with agent: was cleared by an old school friend.

Tip: Cleared is the correct participle of clear.
highlights: have been marked by the teacher
was cleared by an old school friend
tasks.solution_overview: All five are well-formed passives across continuous, perfect, future, and modal patterns. Use them as clean templates: be (in the right tense) + past participle, then add by only when the agent is known.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The recipes are still being debated. → We know precisely which cousin is debating them.
Dad sent us the bus timetable. → We were sent the bus timetable by Dad.
The lamp crashed overnight. → The lamp was crashed overnight by itself intentionally.
New park rules have been posted by the city council.
The birthday banner design by Maya last week.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — are still being debated hides the agent; claiming we know precisely which cousin invents certainty.

Tip: Progressive agentless passives especially invite fake-agent traps.

TRUE — Double-object active allows We were sent the bus timetable by Dad (indirect object as subject).

Tip: With give/send/offer, either object can become the passive subject.

FALSE — Intransitive crash does not take this agentive passive, and by itself intentionally adds nonsense intent.

Tip: Many intransitive events resist a clean be + PP + by-agent rewrite.

TRUE — Present perfect passive with agent: have been posted by the city council.

Tip: Rules (plural) → have been, not has been.

FALSE — Incomplete: needs was designed / were designed, not a bare design by…

Tip: by alone does not create a passive; you still need be + participle.
highlights: have been posted by the city council
tasks.solution_overview: Watch three failure modes: inventing a discussant, forcing an intransitive into a reflexive intentional passive, and dropping be. The good lines keep agents that were already named.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The club is considering the proposal. → The proposal is being considered by the club.
All hikers must carry a map. → A map must be carried by all hikers.
The delay was occurred during the morning rush.
Mum postponed the picnic. → The picnic was postponed by Mum.
The pool filters are cleaned every Friday by the caretaker.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present continuous active → is being considered; agent retained.

Tip: Continuous passive = am/is/are being + PP.

TRUE — Modal obligation flips cleanly: must be carried by all hikers.

Tip: Keep must; do not weaken it to can or might.

FALSE — Occur is intransitive; was occurred is ungrammatical. Prefer The delay occurred… or The delay was caused…

Tip: Intransitives rarely form a true passive.

TRUE — Postponed → was postponed by Mum; meaning preserved.

Tip: Regular participle postponed matches the active verb.

TRUE — Present habitual passive with agent: are cleaned by the caretaker.

Tip: Habitual routines often use present passive.
highlights: is being considered by the club
must be carried by all hikers
tasks.solution_overview: Four transformations or stand-alone passives are sound. The odd one out forces an intransitive verb into was + past participle — a classic exam trap.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The deposit will be paid on 15 March.
IT locked the old tablets. → The old tablets were locked by IT.
The complaint has been escalate to the landlord.
The toast was delivered by a tired waiter.
The school awarded the prize to a Year 9 pupil. → The prize was awarded to a Year 9 pupil by the school.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Future passive will be paid; date adverbial is fine.

Tip: will be + PP, never will + PP alone.

TRUE — Past active → past passive with agent: were locked by IT.

Tip: Plural tablets → were, not was.

FALSE — Wrong participle form: has been escalated, not escalate.

Tip: Perfect passive = has/have been + past participle.

TRUE — Past passive with agent retained.

Tip: Delivered is the correct participle of deliver.

TRUE — Complex object pattern preserved: prize becomes subject; to a Year 9 pupil stays; by the school names the agent.

Tip: Keep prepositional complements when you flip voice.
highlights: was delivered by a tired waiter
was awarded to a Year 9 pupil by the school
tasks.solution_overview: Scan for the broken perfect passive (been + base verb). Everything else either is already a good passive or flips active→passive without changing who did what to whom.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rumour was confirmed this morning. → The class president confirmed the rumour this morning, so we know the speaker.
Staff uniforms are going to be washed next week.
The suitcase arrived damaged. → The suitcase was arrived damaged by the airline deliberately.
Nothing further can be done until the rain stops. → The groundskeeper is refusing to do anything further on purpose.
The posters were update last night by the art club.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — was confirmed does not name the class president; the rewrite fabricates the speaker.

Tip: so we know the speaker is a giveaway fake-agent claim.

TRUE — Going-to future passive: are going to be washed.

Tip: Insert be before the participle in going-to passives.

FALSE — Arrive is intransitive; was arrived is wrong, and deliberately invents intent.

Tip: Prefer The suitcase arrived damaged or The suitcase was damaged in transit.

FALSE — Neutral modal passive becomes an accusation of deliberate refusal — meaning not preserved.

Tip: can be done ≠ is refusing… on purpose.

FALSE — Need were updated, not were update.

Tip: Base verb after be is never enough for a passive.
tasks.solution_overview: Only one sentence is a clean future passive. The others either invent speakers and motives or break form with intransitive or base-verb passives.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The organisers had already finalised the seating. → The seating had already been finalised by the organisers.
Access to the gym is restricted to members.
The samples are currently taste by the judges.
Our cousins invited us to the barbecue. → We were invited to the barbecue by our cousins.
The mouldy bread was thrown away immediately.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past perfect active → past perfect passive: had been finalised by the organisers.

Tip: Perfect passive stacks been after had/has/have.

TRUE — Present passive stating a standing rule; agent optional.

Tip: is restricted to… keeps the limitation phrase.

FALSE — Need are currently being tasted (or are currently tasted), not are currently taste.

Tip: Progressive sense wants being + PP.

TRUE — Invite allows We were invited… by our cousins.

Tip: Keep the to-phrase when the original has one.

TRUE — Agentless past passive focusing on the bread.

Tip: Thrown is the correct irregular participle of throw.
tasks.solution_overview: Check the perfect and invitation passives against the originals, then catch the tasting line that uses a base verb where a participle (and often being) belongs.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The scores were announced by the process itself intentionally.
The guide will present the route on Tuesday. → The route will be presented by the guide on Tuesday.
Bikes should not be left in the hallway.
The vacancy was filled last month. → We know exactly which neighbour filled the vacancy.
The translation is being check by a native speaker.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A process cannot intentionally announce scores; agent and intent are both wrong.

Tip: by… itself intentionally is almost always false.

TRUE — Future active → will be presented by the guide; time phrase kept.

Tip: Move the object to subject position and keep will be.

TRUE — Modal passive prohibition: should not be left…

Tip: Negation sits with the modal: should not be + PP.

FALSE — Agentless was filled does not identify the neighbour.

Tip: Exactly which… claims knowledge the passive never gave.

FALSE — Need is being checked, not is being check.

Tip: After being, always use a past participle.
highlights: will be presented by the guide
tasks.solution_overview: Reject intentional process-agents and invented neighbours. Accept the future and modal passives that keep the original force, and fix continuous passives that use a base verb after being.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The passport application is being processed this week.
Security locked the gates at midnight. → The gates were locked at midnight by security.
Further tips can be found in the guidebook.
The internship offers have been accepted by both students.
The agenda was circulated to all attendees before noon.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present continuous passive without agent; focus on the application.

Tip: is being processed marks an action in progress.

TRUE — Meaning-preserving past passive with agent at the end.

Tip: Time adverbial can stay before or after the by-phrase.

TRUE — Modal passive can be found; typical of how-to notes.

Tip: Do not invent who finds the tips.

TRUE — Present perfect passive, plural agreement: have been accepted.

Tip: Both students stays as by-agent.

TRUE — Past passive with recipient phrase to all attendees.

Tip: Keep to-phrases when they carry essential meaning.
highlights: were locked at midnight by security
can be found in the guidebook
have been accepted by both students
tasks.solution_overview: A clean set of models: continuous, past with agent, modal, perfect, and recipient phrases. Use them as reference shapes when harder traps appear later.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It is said that the ferry service stopped overnight.
They gave the runners revised numbers. → Revised numbers were given to the runners.
The fridge crashed. → The fridge was crashed by the update script on purpose.
A decision has yet to be reached on the picnic date.
The costumes will have been fitted before the play opens.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Impersonal It is said that… is a standard reporting passive; no agent needed.

Tip: It is said/believed/expected that… hedges without naming a speaker.

TRUE — Direct object as subject: Revised numbers were given to the runners. Dropping vague they is allowed.

Tip: Omitting a vague they is fine; inventing a named VIP is not.

FALSE — Adds an agent and on purpose; the original intransitive crash states an event, not intentional causation.

Tip: Do not turn appliance failures into deliberate sabotage without evidence in the source.

TRUE — Perfect passive inside yet to be reached — formal and correct.

Tip: has yet to be + PP is a common hedge for unfinished decisions.

TRUE — Future perfect passive: will have been fitted before…

Tip: Future perfect passive = will have been + PP.
tasks.solution_overview: Impersonal reporting passives and future perfect passives are fair game. The crash rewrite fails because it invents both a culprit and intent the original never stated.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The scores were being finalised when the lights froze. → We know the junior scorer was finalising them alone.
Nobody can be blamed for the weather delay. → The bus driver is to blame for the weather delay.
The manuscript got published without peer review. → The manuscript published without peer review by itself.
Concerns have been raised about crowded platforms.
The tokens are expired by the security protocol every night intentionally by the tokens themselves.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — were being finalised does not identify a junior scorer working alone.

Tip: Continuous passives still hide agents unless a by-phrase appears.

FALSE — Nobody can be blamed contradicts naming the bus driver as blameworthy.

Tip: Respect negation: nobody ≠ a specific person.

FALSE — Even if get-passive is colloquially fine, by itself erases any external publisher and invents self-publication.

Tip: Get-passive still implies an external process, not the patient acting alone.

TRUE — Present perfect passive Concerns have been raised… — standard and agentless.

Tip: Raising concerns often stays agentless in everyday English.

FALSE — Garbled agent stack: protocol vs tokens themselves, plus intentionally — form and meaning both fail.

Tip: One clear by-agent is enough; reflexive intentional stacks are almost always wrong.
tasks.solution_overview: Four lines smuggle in named people, blame, or reflexive agents. Only the concerns sentence keeps a sober agentless perfect passive.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The roadblocks were lifted last week. → Last week saw the roadblocks lift themselves.
Fans expect a decision by Friday. → A decision is expected by Friday.
The wiring diagram should have been attached to the handbook.
The council owns the riverside path. → The riverside path is owned by the council.
The samples were being store in the cold room overnight.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Reflexive lift themselves is absurd; keep were lifted or name a real authority.

Tip: Roadblocks do not act on themselves.

TRUE — Expect → is expected; by Friday is a deadline, not a fake human agent.

Tip: by + time is not a by-agent; do not confuse the two.

TRUE — Modal perfect passive: should have been attached.

Tip: should have been + PP for past criticism or missed duty.

TRUE — Own passivises cleanly here: is owned by the council.

Tip: Ownership passives are common when describing who holds something.

FALSE — Need were being stored, not were being store.

Tip: being + past participle, never being + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate by-time from by-agent, accept modal perfect and ownership passives, and reject reflexive nonsense plus base verbs after being.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The shortlist will be announced tomorrow. → Tomorrow the panel chair will announce the shortlist, and that is certain.
Two seats have been reserved for the grandparents.
The bakery produces these loaves in Poland. → These loaves are produced in Poland.
The breach was reported anonymously. → A named neighbour reported the breach to take revenge.
The forms need signing before the trip. → The forms need to be signed before the trip.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — will be announced does not identify the panel chair or make that identity certain.

Tip: Certainty claims about a hidden agent fail the meaning test.

TRUE — Present perfect passive with a clear beneficiary for-phrase.

Tip: have been reserved, not has, with plural seats.

TRUE — Dropping the generic bakery subject is allowed when place remains; are produced in Poland keeps the core claim without inventing a new person.

Tip: Omitting a generic producer is fine; inventing a celebrity baker is not.

FALSE — Anonymously blocks naming a neighbour and inventing revenge motive.

Tip: Anonymous passives forbid named-agent actives.

TRUE — need signing and need to be signed are both acceptable obligation passives here; meaning aligns.

Tip: need signing ≈ need to be signed in formal British usage.
tasks.solution_overview: Dropping a generic producer is fine; naming a chair, neighbour, or revenge motive is not. Also accept the need to be signed paraphrase of need signing.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had the warning been heeded, the flood might have been avoided.
They are repairing the path now. → The path is repaired now by them as we speak.
The visitor was shown the garden before lunch.
It was agreed that bedtime would remain unchanged for six months.
The photos cannot be shared externally without permission.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past perfect passive in a conditional: had been heeded; might have been avoided is modal perfect passive.

Tip: Stacked passives in conditionals still need been + PP each time.

FALSE — Progressive active are repairing needs is being repaired, not is repaired, for an action in progress.

Tip: as we speak demands continuous passive, not simple passive.

TRUE — Double-object passive: The visitor was shown the garden…

Tip: Show/give/offer commonly allow recipient as passive subject.

TRUE — Impersonal It was agreed that… reports a decision without naming voters.

Tip: Do not invent which relative agreed.

TRUE — Modal passive prohibition cannot be shared… without permission.

Tip: Keep the without-phrase; it is part of the meaning.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced shapes: conditional perfect passives, impersonal it-passives, and recipient subjects. The weak line mismatches progressive meaning with a simple passive.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The motion was passed unanimously. → Every club member who opposed it still somehow passed it deliberately.
Little progress has been made on the kitchen renovation. → The landlord personally stalled the kitchen renovation on purpose.
The cookies were allowed to cool before icing. → The cookies allowed themselves to cool before icing.
The community centre based in Leeds oversees local youth clubs. → Local youth clubs are overseen by the community centre based in Leeds.
The password must changed every ninety days.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Unanimously already states the outcome; inventing opposing members who deliberately passed it contradicts the source.

Tip: Do not rewrite vote passives into paradoxical agent stories.

FALSE — Agentless little progress has been made does not name a landlord or allege purposeful stalling.

Tip: Progress passives especially attract fake-blame rewrites.

FALSE — were allowed to cool implies an external controller; allowed themselves invents reflexive agency.

Tip: Allow-passive ≠ self-action.

TRUE — Oversees → are overseen by; the same centre remains the agent, with the Leeds detail kept.

Tip: Carry modifiers of the agent into the by-phrase when they identify which centre.

FALSE — Missing be: must be changed, not must changed.

Tip: Modal passives always need be before the participle.
highlights: are overseen by the community centre
tasks.solution_overview: Only the community-centre oversight pair keeps the same agent under a clean voice flip. The rest invent blame, reflexive cool-downs, or drop be after a modal.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been briefed by the nurse, the parents approved the treatment. → The parents were briefed by the nurse and then approved the treatment.
The library books are to be returned within fourteen days.
What remains to be decided is the venue. → Someone has already decided the venue, and we know who.
The rare manuscript was being carefully restored when funding paused.
Under no circumstances should guest passwords be shared without encryption.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Perfect passive participle Having been briefed by the nurse unpacks fairly into were briefed by the nurse without inventing a new agent.

Tip: Participial passives still obey the no-fake-agent rule.

TRUE — be to + passive: are to be returned marks scheduled obligation.

Tip: are to be + PP is formal diary-style passive.

FALSE — remains to be decided means the venue is still open; claiming it is already decided by a known person reverses the meaning.

Tip: to be decided signals incompleteness, not a hidden finished decision.

TRUE — Past continuous passive was being carefully restored; agent optional.

Tip: Adverbs can sit between being and the participle.

TRUE — Modal passive after inversion still needs be: should… be shared.

Tip: Inversion does not remove the passive be.
tasks.solution_overview: Four advanced passives hold: participial, be-to, continuous, and inverted modal. The venue line fails because it turns an undecided state into a fabricated completed act.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No conclusions can be drawn from this data. → This data prevents anyone from drawing conclusions deliberately.
The school newsletter is expected to be published before the open day.
They had the boilers replaced overnight. → The boilers were replaced overnight.
It is believed the mix-up was caused by a booking error. → We know which clerk caused the mix-up and that the clerk acted deliberately.
Were the rules not to be enforced, the queue would lengthen. → If the rules were not enforced, the queue would lengthen.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Neutral modal passive becomes intentional prevention; meaning and force both change.

Tip: can be drawn does not accuse the data of deliberate obstruction.

TRUE — Nested passives: is expected + to be published — both layers are well formed.

Tip: Expect + to-infinitive passive is common in formal forecasts.

TRUE — Causative had… replaced pairs with a plain passive The boilers were replaced overnight without inventing who did the work.

Tip: Causative get/have + object + PP often aligns with a simple passive of the object.

FALSE — It is believed hedges; naming a clerk and alleging deliberate action fabricates agent and intent.

Tip: Belief passives especially forbid certainty-plus-motive rewrites.

TRUE — Inverted passive Were… not to be enforced paraphrases cleanly as If the rules were not enforced…

Tip: Formal inversion still encodes the same passive obligation/enforcement meaning.
highlights: prevents anyone from drawing conclusions deliberately
Were the rules not to be enforced
tasks.solution_overview: At the top band, watch nested passives and inverted conditionals that still keep meaning, and reject any rewrite that adds deliberate clerks, motives, or prevention the source never stated.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour who waters our plants is away this week.
The recipe which my aunt shared it needs less salt.
The library who opens on Sundays stays busy all day.
The bus that stops outside the school leaves at eight.
The park, that was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Who" correctly refers to a person in a restrictive clause that identifies which neighbour.

Tip: For people in defining clauses, "who" or "that" both work.

FALSE — Drop the leftover "it": the relative already fills the object slot — "which my aunt shared."

Tip: Never leave a second object pronoun after a relative that already stands for it.

FALSE — A library is a thing, so use "which" or "that," not "who."

Tip: Reserve "who" for people.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which bus; no commas needed.

Tip: No commas = the clause is essential to identify the noun.

FALSE — After commas (non-restrictive), use "which," not "that": "The park, which was closed…"

Tip: Commas signal extra information — and "that" is not welcome there.
tasks.solution_overview: Ask whether the clause names a person or a thing, and whether commas mark it as essential or extra. Then check that the relative itself carries the subject or object — no leftover "it."

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The chef whose soup won the contest teaches on Saturdays.
The cyclist who's helmet cracked bought a new one.
The concert, which sold out in an hour, starts at seven.
The students that organised the bake sale raised enough for the trip.
The garage, who stores our bikes, needs a new lock.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Whose" correctly shows possession: the soup belongs to the chef.

Tip: If you can rephrase as "X's Y," you almost always want "whose."

FALSE — You need possession, not "who is": write "whose helmet."

Tip: "Who's" = who is / who has; "whose" = of whom / of which.

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" with commas correctly adds non-essential detail about the concert.

Tip: Extra information between commas takes "which" for things, never "that."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" for people is acceptable in defining clauses.

Tip: In defining clauses about people, "who" sounds slightly more formal than "that."

FALSE — A garage is not a person; use "which": "The garage, which stores…"

Tip: Places and buildings take "which," not "who."
tasks.solution_overview: Separate "who's" (contraction) from "whose" (belonging), and keep "who" for people while "which" covers places, buildings, and events.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival, that locals love, fills the square each July.
The tutor whom we hired last autumn still helps on Fridays.
The kettle which boils too slowly needs replacing.
The friend who we invited yesterday cannot come after all.
The photos that Maya printed them are still on the table.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A comma-bound clause must use "which," not "that": "The festival, which locals love…"

Tip: Spot the commas first; they ban "that" in careful exam English.

TRUE — Formal "whom" correctly marks the object of "hired."

Tip: If the relative would be "him/her/them," "whom" is the careful choice.

TRUE — Restrictive "which" correctly defines which kettle; no commas required.

Tip: British formal writing often prefers "which" even in defining clauses about things.

TRUE — Informal object "who" is widely accepted here; the sentence is grammatical as written.

Tip: Exams may prefer "whom" after a preposition, but bare object "who" is usually fine.

FALSE — Remove the residual "them": "The photos that Maya printed are still…"

Tip: The relative already equals the object; a second object pronoun is always wrong.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch non-restrictive "that," object relatives (who/whom), and pronoun leftovers. If the clause already does the object’s job, nothing else should sit in that slot.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The runner who finished first still looked fresh.
The map that we borrowed shows every hiking trail.
The café whose windows face the river stays open late.
The singer who's opening the show arrives at six.
The film which the class watched last week was subtitled.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Restrictive "who" correctly identifies the runner.

Tip: No commas when the clause is needed to pick out which person.

TRUE — Defining "that" correctly restricts which map.

Tip: "That" is a safe default in restrictive clauses about things.

TRUE — "Whose" can mark possession for things as well as people.

Tip: "The café whose windows…" = "the café’s windows."

TRUE — "Who's" correctly expands to "who is" before "opening."

Tip: Try expanding the contraction; if "who is" fits, "who's" is right.

TRUE — Restrictive "which" correctly defines the film.

Tip: Either "which" or "that" works in defining clauses about things.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound models: people with "who," things with "that/which," possession with "whose," and a genuine "who's" = who is. Use them as clean reference patterns.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The cousin with whom we share a flat cooks on Sundays.
The playlist, that includes every song from the trip, is private.
Anyone who's keys are missing should check lost property.
The museum which we visited last month displays local pottery.
The coach that designed the drills will explain them tonight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Preposition + "whom" is the formal, correct pattern for a person as object.

Tip: After a preposition, prefer "whom" (people) or "which" (things), not "who" or "that."

FALSE — Non-restrictive needs "which": "The playlist, which includes…"

Tip: Commas + "that" is a classic exam fail.

FALSE — Possession requires "whose": "Anyone whose keys are missing…"

Tip: If "who is keys" sounds nonsense, you wanted "whose."

TRUE — Defining "which" correctly identifies the museum.

Tip: Object relatives can keep "which/that" or drop the pronoun in informal style.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" for a person is acceptable in defining clauses.

Tip: "Who" is often preferred for people, but "that" is not an error here.
tasks.solution_overview: Preposition + whom is the polished form; commas still forbid "that"; and "who's" vs "whose" remains a high-frequency trap. Expand every contraction before you mark true.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bakery from which we order bread raised its prices slightly.
The volunteer whom neighbours praised organised the litter pick.
The novel that Sam finished last night it still sits on the shelf.
Brighton, which hosts the festival, fills with visitors in May.
The friends who cake the party brought later left early.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "From which" correctly links a thing after a preposition.

Tip: Keep the preposition with "which/whom" in formal answers.

TRUE — "Whom" correctly marks the volunteer as the object of "praised."

Tip: If you can replace the relative with "him/her," "whom" is justified.

FALSE — Delete residual "it": "The novel that Sam finished last night still sits…"

Tip: One clause, one object slot — never both relative and "it."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Brighton.

Tip: Place names with commas almost always take "which," not "that."

FALSE — Word order collapses; write "The friends who brought the party cake later left early."

Tip: Keep the relative clause’s internal word order like a normal statement after the relative.
tasks.solution_overview: Preposition + which, object whom, and residual pronouns dominate here. If a leftover "it" remains, cut it; if word order inside the clause collapses, rebuild it as a normal statement.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour to whom the parcel was delivered signed for it.
The suitcase who's zip is broken stays in the loft.
Drivers whose licences have expired must renew them online.
The beach that we walked along at dusk was almost empty.
The headteacher, that announced the trip, answered questions calmly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "To whom" is the formal object pattern after a preposition.

Tip: Preposition + whom is almost always safe for people in exam English.

FALSE — A suitcase’s zip needs "whose," not "who's."

Tip: "Who's" never marks possession — expand it and the error is obvious.

TRUE — "Whose" correctly marks possession for people in a defining clause.

Tip: "Whose" works with plural noun heads just as with singular.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which beach.

Tip: Object "that/which" can often be omitted: "The beach we walked along…"

FALSE — Non-restrictive about a person needs "who": "The headteacher, who announced…"

Tip: Commas + person → "who"; commas + thing → "which"; never "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "to whom," possession with "whose," and the ban on "that" after commas are the three checks here. Expand every "who's" before you mark the sentence true.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The email which Jess sent yesterday still needs a reply.
The author of who the novel was written declined the interview.
The bridge that crosses the canal is closed for repairs.
Guests which arrive early may wait in the lobby.
The trainer whose tips improved my serve will join practice.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Defining "which" correctly identifies the email.

Tip: Subject or object relatives both allow "which/that" for things.

FALSE — After a preposition referring to a person, use "whom": "of whom the novel was written" (or better, rephrase).

Tip: "Of who" is almost never correct; "of whom" is the formal fix.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the bridge.

Tip: No commas when the clause picks out which bridge.

FALSE — Guests are people; use "who" or "that," not "which."

Tip: "Which" for people is a strong red flag in exam marking.

TRUE — "Whose tips" correctly shows possession.

Tip: "Whose + noun" is the clean possessive relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: People vs things and preposition + whom are the focus. Never use "which" for guests or classmates, and never leave "of who" after a preposition.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The notes, which the lecturer circulated, summarise the chapter.
The applicant whom the panel interviewed withdrew this morning.
Anyone who's still outside should come in before the rain.
The app that tracks sleep was updated overnight.
The room in which the rehearsal takes place is on the second floor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about known notes.

Tip: If removing the clause still leaves a clear noun, commas + "which" are right.

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly follows the panel as subject of "interviewed."

Tip: Swap in "him/her": if that fits, "whom" is justified.

TRUE — "Who's" = "who is" before "still outside."

Tip: Expand the contraction; if the sentence still works, keep "who's."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the app.

Tip: Everyday tech nouns follow the same who/which/that rules as any other thing.

TRUE — "In which" is the formal relative after a preposition for a place.

Tip: Formal writing prefers "in which" over a stranded preposition, though both can be grammatical.
tasks.solution_overview: These are clean mid-level models: non-restrictive "which," object "whom," a genuine "who's," defining "that," and formal "in which."

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The tent, that leaks in heavy rain, stays in the shed.
The clerk to who complaints should be sent sits at desk four.
Jars whose lids lack labels must be checked before use.
The witness who the lawyer called seemed unsure.
The recipe on which the cake depends needs soft butter.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "which" after commas: "The tent, which leaks in heavy rain…"

Tip: Everyday nouns follow the same comma rule as any other thing.

FALSE — After "to," use "whom": "to whom complaints should be sent."

Tip: Preposition + who is almost always wrong; make it "whom."

TRUE — "Whose" correctly marks possession for jars/lids.

Tip: "Whose" is fine for inanimate nouns in careful English.

TRUE — Object "who" is acceptable in modern usage for the person called.

Tip: Formal style may prefer "whom," but bare "who" as object is not marked wrong in most exams.

TRUE — "On which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Keep preposition + which together in formal answers.
tasks.solution_overview: Comma + "that," "to who," and possession for things are the main traps. Formal preposition + which/whom patterns earn easy true marks when you spot them.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The teammates with who we share a pitch signed the same form.
Edinburgh, which remains our favourite base, hosts the fringe each August.
The folder that Mia flagged contains old photos.
A classmate who's been seconded to the drama club still joins practice.
The prototype, which the lab tested last night, failed the heat check.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "whom" after "with": "with whom we share a pitch."

Tip: Any preposition before a person-relative wants "whom."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Edinburgh.

Tip: City names with commas take "which," not "that" or "who."

TRUE — Defining "that" correctly restricts which folder.

Tip: Ordinary nouns follow ordinary relative rules.

TRUE — "Who's been" = "who has been," a correct present-perfect relative.

Tip: "Who's" covers both "who is" and "who has."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds extra detail about the prototype.

Tip: If the noun is already identified, commas + "which" are the pair.
tasks.solution_overview: One clear "with who" error sits among solid non-restrictive and defining models. Confirm each true sentence’s person/thing choice and comma pattern before moving on.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide through whom we booked the tour confirmed the time.
Parcels that arrive damaged must be photographed immediately.
The gardener whose allotment we admired stays on until dusk.
The schedule for which we planned the weekend has changed.
Someone who's coat is still hanging here left early.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Through whom" correctly marks a person after a preposition.

Tip: Booking and arrangement phrases often need "through/with whom."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which parcels.

Tip: Everyday logistics nouns take the same defining "that/which" rules.

TRUE — "Whose allotment" correctly shows possession.

Tip: "Whose" works cleanly before a concrete noun.

TRUE — "For which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Prefer "for which" over informal stranded "which… for" in formal answers.

FALSE — Possession needs "whose": "Someone whose coat is still hanging…"

Tip: "Who's coat" expands to "who is coat" — never possession.
tasks.solution_overview: Four solid preposition and defining patterns frame one "who's + noun" trap. Expand the contraction and the false answer becomes obvious.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The dentist by whom the filling was done explained the aftercare.
Players which miss warm-up cannot start the match.
A rule whose wording is unclear should be rewritten.
The hall at which we rehearsed drew a large crowd.
Anyone who's locker number is faded should ask at reception.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "By whom" correctly marks the agent in a formal relative.

Tip: Passive-related "by whom" is formal but grammatical.

FALSE — People need "who/that": "Players who miss…"

Tip: Never use "which" for players, guests, or classmates.

TRUE — "Whose wording" correctly marks possession for a rule.

Tip: Documents and rules commonly take "whose" in exam English.

TRUE — "At which" correctly attaches the preposition to an event/place.

Tip: Prefer "at which / in which" in formal answers when asked.

FALSE — Use "whose": "Anyone whose locker number is faded…"

Tip: "Who's locker" = "who is locker," which never works.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "by whom" / "at which" sit beside people-"which" and "who's + noun" errors. Keep person/thing and contraction checks automatic at this level.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The friend in whom's flat we stayed later moved abroad.
Few of the tools on which the repair depends are in the box.
The baker that her sourdough won prizes has closed for a week.
Neighbours whom the council thanked stayed for photographs.
The shed where tools are kept, that flooded last spring, is locked.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Malformed possession; write "The friend in whose flat we stayed…"

Tip: Never stack "whom's"; use "whose" after the preposition.

TRUE — "On which" correctly links tools after a preposition.

Tip: "The X on which Y depends" is a high-value formal pattern.

FALSE — Replace "that her" with "whose": "The baker whose sourdough won prizes…"

Tip: "That + possessive" always signals a missing "whose."

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly refers to the neighbours thanked.

Tip: Subject of main clause + object relative "whom" is a clean formal structure.

FALSE — Mixing "where" with a second non-restrictive "that" is wrong; prefer "…, which flooded last spring,…"

Tip: A second relative after commas still cannot be "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Top-band items twist possession after prepositions and stack relatives. Reject "whom's" and "that her," keep "on which," and remember a second comma-bound clause still wants "which."

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The landlord to whose conditions we agreed released the keys.
Staff for whom flexitime was approved must log hours weekly.
The radio that the kids dismantled it cannot be put back together.
Lisbon, which we use as our summer base, hosts a street-food fair.
Anyone who's completed module three may sit the quiz.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "To whose conditions" correctly combines preposition and possession.

Tip: "To/with/under whose + noun" is advanced but correct.

TRUE — "For whom" correctly marks people after a preposition.

Tip: Approval/arrangement phrases often need "for whom."

FALSE — Remove "it": "The radio that the kids dismantled cannot be put back together."

Tip: Even in long sentences, residual objects are still errors.

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about Lisbon.

Tip: City names with commas take "which."

TRUE — "Who's completed" = "who has completed."

Tip: Present-perfect "who's" is possession’s innocent twin — expand to check.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "to whose" / "for whom" are trustworthy when the grammar fits; the leftover "it" is the only clear fail. Expand "who's" once more to confirm "who has."

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The mentor of whom we sought advice later joined another club.
A paragraph that its purpose is unclear should be cut.
Helpers who the organisers thanked now lead regional teams.
The portal via which parents upload forms went offline at noon.
The interim coach, that arrived in May, reorganised training.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Of whom" correctly marks the person after the preposition in a formal relative.

Tip: "Of whom we sought advice" is stiff but exam-correct.

FALSE — Use "whose": "A paragraph whose purpose is unclear…"

Tip: "That its" is the same broken pattern as "that her."

TRUE — Object "who" for people thanked is acceptable modern usage.

Tip: Formal alternatives use "whom"; both are usually accepted without a preceding preposition.

TRUE — "Via which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Tech/process nouns take "which" after prepositions, not "who."

FALSE — Non-restrictive about a person needs "who": "The interim coach, who arrived…"

Tip: Title + commas still bans "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "of whom" / "via which" contrast with "that its" and comma + "that" about a person. Diagnose possession failures and non-restrictive person clauses first.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The climbers with whom we shared a rope reached the ridge first.
Anyone whose rucksack holds food must hang it away from tents.
The rule under which the contest will be judged is printed on page two.
A volunteer who's already briefed the stewards need not attend the dry run.
The criteria against which entries are scored were agreed last autumn.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "With whom" correctly marks people after a preposition in a defining clause.

Tip: Shared-activity language often uses "with whom we shared…"

TRUE — "Whose rucksack" correctly shows possession.

Tip: Outdoor and everyday policies love "anyone whose + noun" constructions.

TRUE — "Under which" correctly links the governing framework.
