Tip: Contest and club English frequently uses "under which."

TRUE — "Who's already briefed" = "who has already briefed."

Tip: Final check: expand "who's"; if "who has" fits, the sentence can stand.

TRUE — "Against which" correctly marks the standard of comparison.

Tip: "The X against which Y is scored" is a polished relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean advanced set: preposition + whom/which, possessive "whose," and "who's" = who has. Use these as your checklist for person, thing, possession, and contraction.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The shelf on whose edge the vase sat collapsed overnight.
Children for who the workshop was designed must be under twelve.
The camera that its battery died mid-shoot still needs charging.
The island off which we camped has no mobile signal.
Someone who's waiting by the gate should come inside now.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "On whose edge" correctly combines preposition and possession for a thing.

Tip: "On/in/at whose + noun" works for inanimate heads too.

FALSE — After "for," use "whom": "Children for whom the workshop was designed…"

Tip: Preposition + who is almost always wrong for people.

FALSE — Replace "that its" with "whose": "The camera whose battery died…"

Tip: "That its" is a possession failure in disguise.

TRUE — "Off which" correctly attaches the preposition to a place.

Tip: Geography often uses "off/near/beside which" in formal relatives.

TRUE — "Who's waiting" = "who is waiting."

Tip: Expand once; if "who is" fits, keep "who's."
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced possession after prepositions mixes with "for who" and "that its" traps. Fix person-preposition forms and replace broken "that + possessive" with "whose."

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The path along which we walked ends at the lighthouse.
A neighbour who's dog barks at dawn has apologised twice.
The committee members whom the mayor praised stayed for tea.
The oven, that overheats on the fan setting, needs a service.
Few of the routes by which hikers reach the summit stay open in winter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Along which" correctly links a place after a preposition.

Tip: Path/road/route phrases love "along/by which."

FALSE — Possession needs "whose": "A neighbour whose dog barks…"

Tip: "Who's dog" = "who is dog" — expand and reject.

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly refers to the members praised.

Tip: Subject of the relative clause + object "whom" is a clean formal structure.

FALSE — Non-restrictive needs "which": "The oven, which overheats…"

Tip: Commas still ban "that," even for household nouns.

TRUE — "By which" correctly marks the means/route.

Tip: "The X by which Y happens" is a polished relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal path relatives contrast with "who's + noun" and comma + "that." Expand contractions and check commas before you trust a late-set true.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The potter from whom we bought the bowls still runs Saturday classes.
Anyone whose laptop battery dies mid-flight should carry a spare charger.
The chapter after which the quiz begins covers relative pronouns.
A neighbour who's lived here since March already knows every shortcut.
The tune to which the choir rehearsed was written last winter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "From whom" correctly marks a person after a preposition.

Tip: Buying/learning phrases often use "from whom we bought/learned…"

TRUE — "Whose laptop battery" correctly shows possession.

Tip: Travel reminders love "anyone whose + noun."

TRUE — "After which" correctly links sequence for a thing.

Tip: Chapter/section English frequently uses "after which / before which."

TRUE — "Who's lived" = "who has lived."

Tip: Final check: expand "who's"; if "who has" fits, the sentence can stand.

TRUE — "To which" correctly attaches the preposition to a tune/thing.

Tip: Music and ceremony phrases often need "to which" in formal relatives.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean capstone of advanced but correct relatives: preposition + whom/which, possessive "whose," and "who's" = who has. Use these as your final checklist for person, thing, possession, and contraction.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Mia avoids talking on the phone while she cycles through traffic.
The twins enjoy to bake cinnamon rolls on rainy Sundays.
After the match, the coach decided postponing the next training session.
Noah refused to share his notes before the chemistry quiz.
Lara promised delivering the costumes for the school play by Thursday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid takes a gerund, so "avoids talking" is the natural pattern.

Tip: Memorise avoid + -ing; an infinitive after avoid is almost always wrong.

FALSE — Enjoy needs a gerund, not an infinitive: "enjoy baking," not "enjoy to bake."

Tip: Like, love, and enjoy prefer -ing when the object is an activity.

FALSE — Decide takes a to-infinitive: "decided to postpone," not a gerund.

Tip: Decide / refuse / promise / plan / hope / expect pattern with to + base verb.

TRUE — Refuse correctly takes a to-infinitive: "refuse to share."

Tip: If the meaning is "will not do X," expect refuse + to-infinitive.

FALSE — Promise takes a to-infinitive: "promised to deliver," not a gerund.

Tip: Promise patterns like decide and refuse — to + verb, not -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: This set drills the core split: avoid and enjoy need -ing, while decide, refuse, and promise need to + verb. Check each verb's fixed pattern before you judge the sentence.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hiking club is considering organising a dawn walk next month.
Sofia enjoys reading graphic novels on the train.
The family decided to camp beside the lake this weekend.
The barista refused accepting tips during the charity day.
Jamal promised to text when his flight landed.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Consider takes a gerund: "considering organising" is correct.

Tip: Consider / avoid / enjoy / finish / suggest all take -ing when followed by a verb.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is the standard pattern: "enjoy reading."

Tip: If enjoy is followed by an activity, use -ing, not to.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to camp."

Tip: Decision verbs (decide, agree, refuse, promise) lean toward to + base verb.

FALSE — Refuse needs a to-infinitive: "refused to accept," not a gerund.

Tip: Swap -ing for to + verb after refuse and the sentence usually repairs itself.

TRUE — Promise correctly takes a to-infinitive: "promised to text."

Tip: Promise + to-infinitive expresses a future commitment.
tasks.solution_overview: Four verbs here follow their textbook patterns correctly; only refuse is broken. Treat refuse like decide and promise — always to + verb.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The librarian avoided to mention the overdue fines in front of the class.
Trainee chefs enjoy to practise knife skills on quiet mornings.
Management is considering to outsource the school canteen.
The band decided expanding their tour into two neighbouring towns.
The driver refused to open the boot without seeing ID.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Avoid needs -ing: "avoided mentioning," not "avoided to mention."

Tip: Avoid + gerund is fixed; do not borrow the to-infinitive from decide/promise.

FALSE — Enjoy takes a gerund: "enjoy practising."

Tip: Enjoy / avoid / consider share the -ing pattern.

FALSE — Consider takes -ing: "considering outsourcing."

Tip: If you can swap in "the idea of …ing," you want a gerund after consider.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to expand."

Tip: Decide never takes a bare gerund as its complement.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to open."

Tip: Refusal language almost always pairs with to + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Four classic wrong-pattern lines and one clean refuse + to. Flip every avoid/enjoy/consider error to -ing and every decide error to to + verb.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We stopped to buy ice cream when we reached the pier.
Please stop to chew gum during the recital.
On the motorway they stopped talking and listened to the news.
She stopped to smoking after her doctor warned her.
He stopped typing when the fire alarm sounded.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive means pause in order to do something else: they interrupted the journey to buy ice cream.

Tip: Stop to = interrupt activity A so you can do activity B.

FALSE — Here you want quit the habit: "stop chewing," not "stop to chew."

Tip: Stop -ing = quit / no longer do that activity.

TRUE — Stop + gerund means they quit talking.

Tip: If the meaning is "no longer do X," use stop + -ing.

FALSE — Habit quitting needs the gerund: "stopped smoking," not "stopped to smoking."

Tip: Never mix to and -ing after stop in the same slot.

TRUE — Stop + gerund correctly means he quit typing when the alarm rang.

Tip: Sudden interruption of the same action → stop + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Stop changes meaning with form: stop to = pause in order to; stop -ing = quit the activity. Ask which sense the sentence needs before you mark it.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Athletes often avoid eating heavy meals right before a race.
My grandparents enjoy gardening in the late afternoon.
Have you considered joining the community choir?
Elena decided studying abroad for one semester.
The museum promised to reopen the sculpture wing in May.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid eating."

Tip: Health and habit advice often uses avoid + -ing.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund names a liked activity: "enjoy gardening."

Tip: Enjoy almost never takes to + verb in standard English.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considered joining."

Tip: Consider = think about doing → -ing.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to study."

Tip: Decide / choose / refuse / promise → to-infinitive.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to reopen."

Tip: Commitments after promise use to + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Clean models for avoid, enjoy, consider, and promise sit beside one decide error. Keep the -ing trio separate from the to-infinitive trio.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tourists should avoid to swim near the rocks after dark.
Kids usually enjoy building sandcastles at low tide.
We are considering to rent bikes for the coastal path.
The jury refused to discuss the case outside the room.
Dad promised calling us as soon as the ferry docked.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Avoid takes -ing: "avoid swimming."

Tip: Warnings with avoid always want the gerund.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoy building."

Tip: Enjoy + activity = -ing every time.

FALSE — Consider takes -ing: "considering renting."

Tip: Consider to + verb is a frequent exam trap — reject it.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to discuss."

Tip: Refuse patterns with decide and promise.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to call."

Tip: Promise + -ing is not standard for future commitments.
tasks.solution_overview: Two clean lines (enjoy, refuse) and three pattern flips. Watch especially avoid/consider + to and promise + -ing.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Runners stopped to stretch at the water station.
Please stop shouting; the neighbours can hear you.
We stopped for buying tickets at the kiosk.
She stopped to check the map because the path forked.
He stopped to listen music and missed the announcement.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop to stretch = pause the run in order to stretch.

Tip: Purpose after an interruption → stop + to-infinitive.

TRUE — Stop shouting = quit the noisy behaviour.

Tip: Quit an ongoing action → stop + -ing.

FALSE — After stop, use to + verb for purpose, not for + -ing: "stopped to buy tickets."

Tip: For + -ing after stop is not the purpose pattern you want here.

TRUE — Stop to check = interrupt travel in order to check the map.

Tip: Reason/purpose after pause → to-infinitive.

FALSE — Listen needs to: "stopped listening to music" (quit) or "stopped to listen to music" (pause in order to). As written, both form and preposition fail.

Tip: After stop, choose to or -ing by meaning — and keep listen to intact.
tasks.solution_overview: Deepen the stop contrast and catch side traps like for + -ing and missing to after listen. Meaning still decides between to and -ing.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I avoid checking social media before breakfast.
They enjoy to watch documentaries about deep-sea life.
Have you considered changing your route to avoid the roadworks?
The committee decided to cancel the outdoor picnic.
She refused helping with the dishes until her homework was done.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid checking."

Tip: Avoid + -ing for habits you try not to do.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoy watching."

Tip: Enjoy to + verb is almost never right.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considered changing."

Tip: Consider = weigh an option → -ing.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to cancel."

Tip: Decisions about future actions take to + verb.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to help."

Tip: Refuse + -ing is a classic false friend with avoid/enjoy.
tasks.solution_overview: Mix of clean avoid/consider/decide lines and two flips (enjoy to, refuse -ing). Group the verbs by pattern before scoring.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: After years of late nights, he finally stopped drinking energy drinks.
We stopped to ask a local which tram went to the museum.
They stopped to arguing when the teacher walked in.
She never enjoys waiting in long airport queues.
The cast promised rehearsing every evening until opening night.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund = quit the habit of drinking energy drinks.

Tip: Habit change → stop + -ing.

TRUE — Stop to ask = pause the journey in order to ask.

Tip: Purpose after a pause → stop + to.

FALSE — Quit arguing needs the gerund alone: "stopped arguing," not "stopped to arguing."

Tip: Do not glue to onto a gerund after stop.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct (here negated): "enjoys waiting."

Tip: Negation does not change the enjoy + -ing pattern.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to rehearse."

Tip: Promise + -ing fails the commitment pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Stop meaning splits again, plus a hybrid "to arguing" error and a promise trap. Keep purpose (to) versus cessation (-ing) sharply separate.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Passengers should avoid blocking the aisle with large suitcases.
Would you consider to volunteer at the food bank this winter?
The captain decided to turn back because of the fog.
My brother refuses admitting he lost the house keys.
Aunt Priya enjoys knitting scarves for the whole family.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid blocking."

Tip: Public notices often use avoid + -ing.

FALSE — Consider takes -ing: "consider volunteering."

Tip: Consider to is a frequent trap — rewrite with -ing.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to turn."

Tip: Sudden decisions still take to + verb.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refuses to admit."

Tip: Refuse + -ing mimics avoid wrongly — flip it.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoys knitting."

Tip: Hobby verbs after enjoy always take -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Three solid models and two crossed patterns (consider to, refuse -ing). Sort each verb into the -ing list or the to list before you answer.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We decided not to climb the ridge after the weather warning.
She avoids not to sit near the speakers at concerts.
They refused not to apologise, even though everyone expected it.
He promised not to spoil the ending of the film.
I enjoy not waking up to an alarm on Sundays.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Decide + not + to-infinitive is the correct negation: "decided not to climb."

Tip: Negate the infinitive with not before to, not with a gerund.

FALSE — Avoid already means "not do"; use "avoids sitting," not "avoids not to sit."

Tip: Avoid + -ing; do not stack an extra not + to.

FALSE — The intended sense is almost always "refused to apologise" (would not apologise). "Refused not to apologise" is a double negative mess.

Tip: Refuse + to + verb; put not only when you truly mean "refuse to not do X."

TRUE — Promise + not + to-infinitive is correct: "promised not to spoil."

Tip: Negation sits before to in the infinitive pattern.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund works with negation inside the activity: "enjoy not waking."

Tip: Enjoy still wants -ing even when the activity is a negative state.
tasks.solution_overview: Negation tests the same fixed patterns: not to after decide/promise, plain -ing after avoid/enjoy, and careful handling of refuse.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Midway through the hike we stopped drinking from the stream and switched to bottled water.
Midway through the hike we stopped to drink from our bottles.
The guide stopped us from approaching the cliff edge.
Please stop to interrupting the speaker with side comments.
They stopped singing as soon as the conductor raised her hand.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund = quit the activity of drinking from the stream.

Tip: Same action ends → stop + -ing.

TRUE — Stop to drink = pause walking in order to drink.

Tip: Purpose of the pause → stop + to.

TRUE — Stop someone from + -ing is a related but valid pattern: prevent them from doing X.

Tip: Stop + object + from + -ing = prevent.

FALSE — Quit interrupting needs "stop interrupting," not "stop to interrupting."

Tip: Never attach to directly to an -ing form after stop.

TRUE — Stop + gerund = they quit singing on cue.

Tip: Instant cessation of the same action → -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Pair stop to / stop -ing with the prevent pattern stop someone from -ing, and reject the hybrid "to interrupting."

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having considered moving house, they decided to stay another year.
She enjoys to be the first to arrive at rehearsals.
We avoided discussing politics at the family dinner.
He refused being photographed without his consent.
The mayor promised to fund the new skate park next spring.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Consider + gerund and decide + to-infinitive both follow their fixed patterns in one sentence.

Tip: Different verbs in the same sentence can still keep their own complements.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoys being."

Tip: Enjoy + being / doing, never enjoy to be in this sense.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided discussing."

Tip: Sensitive topics often pair with avoid + -ing.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to be photographed."

Tip: Passive infinitives still follow refuse + to.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to fund."

Tip: Public commitments use promise + to.
tasks.solution_overview: Stacked verbs, a passive after refuse, and an enjoy trap. Track each verb's complement independently.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I never stop to wonder how the magician hid the coin.
I never stop wondering how the magician hid the coin.
Doctors advised him to stop to smoke immediately.
They decided against postponing the wedding.
She is considering whether to accept the internship offer.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The intended idiom is continuous curiosity: "never stop wondering" (gerund), not pause-in-order-to wonder.

Tip: Never stop + -ing = keep doing something all the time.

TRUE — Never stop + gerund correctly means the wondering continues.

Tip: Idiomatic "can't/never stop -ing" always wants the gerund.

FALSE — Quit smoking needs "stop smoking"; "stop to smoke" would mean pause something else in order to smoke.

Tip: Medical advice to quit → stop + -ing.

TRUE — Decide against + gerund is a valid related pattern: "decided against postponing."

Tip: Decide to + verb OR decide against + -ing.

TRUE — Consider whether + to-infinitive is grammatical when whether introduces the option.

Tip: Bare consider + verb → -ing; consider whether → to is fine.
tasks.solution_overview: Idioms and near-neighbours: never stop -ing, stop smoking vs stop to smoke, decide against -ing, and consider whether to.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Rather than argue, they decided to sleep on the problem.
She avoids to be seen wearing the same outfit twice.
We enjoy being invited to their rooftop barbecues.
He refused to let the puppy sleep on the sofa.
The club promised arranging free coaching for beginners.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to sleep."

Tip: Rather than does not change decide's to-pattern.

FALSE — Avoid needs -ing: "avoids being seen."

Tip: Passive gerunds still follow avoid + -ing.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund (passive) is correct: "enjoy being invited."

Tip: Enjoy + being + past participle is a common natural pattern.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to let."

Tip: Refuse to let / refuse to allow keep the to.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to arrange."

Tip: Promise + -ing is still wrong even with a kind offer.
tasks.solution_overview: Passive gerunds after avoid/enjoy and a promise error. Form (active/passive) does not rewrite the verb's complement rule.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: What made them stop to check the tyre pressure was a strange vibration.
What made them stop checking their phones was the no-device rule.
Investors are considering selling a small stake in the start-up.
She decided that postponing the trip would be wiser.
He enjoys when friends drop by without calling first.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop to check = pause driving in order to check the tyres.

Tip: Cleft "what made them…" still keeps stop's meaning split.

TRUE — Stop checking = quit the phone-checking habit.

Tip: Same cleft frame, opposite stop pattern — meaning decides.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct (one rare finance-tinged line): "considering selling."

Tip: Even in money contexts, consider still wants -ing.

TRUE — Decide that + clause is grammatical; the gerund postponing is the subject of the that-clause, not decide's complement.

Tip: Decide to + verb OR decide that + clause — both work.

TRUE — Enjoy can take a when-clause as its object; no verb-complement conflict arises.

Tip: Enjoy + noun/gerund/clause — but not enjoy to + verb.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound once you separate stop's two meanings and allow decide that / enjoy when as alternative structures.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Far from avoiding to answer, she volunteered the awkward detail first.
They kept promising finishing the mural before the festival.
Only after refusing to compromise did the two sides walk out.
Having enjoyed to sail as children, they booked a dinghy again.
Stop to pretend you did not hear the question.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Avoid still needs -ing: "avoiding answering."

Tip: Far from + -ing does not license avoid + to.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promising to finish."

Tip: Keep / start do not change promise's to-pattern.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct inside the inversion: "refusing to compromise."

Tip: Inversion and emphasis leave the refuse + to pattern intact.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoyed sailing."

Tip: Perfect participle having enjoyed still takes -ing.

FALSE — Quit pretending needs "stop pretending," not "stop to pretend" (which would mean pause in order to pretend).

Tip: Commands to quit an act → stop + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Hard wrappers (far from, keep -ing, inversion, having -ed) still cannot rewrite avoid/enjoy/promise/stop. Only refuse to survives cleanly.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She stopped to mean that she was leaving; she simply paused for breath.
If you stop meaning what you say, people stop trusting you.
We are still considering how to phrase the apology.
He decided on renting the attic flat above the bakery.
They refused their friends' offer of driving them home.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Nonsense meaning: stop to mean is not English for "intend." Use "She did not mean…" or similar.

Tip: Stop to only works when the infinitive is a real purpose action.

TRUE — Stop + gerund twice: quit meaning X / quit trusting Y.

Tip: Parallel stop + -ing structures keep the "cease" sense.

TRUE — Consider + how + to-infinitive is fine when how introduces the method.

Tip: Consider + -ing OR consider + wh-word + to.

TRUE — Decide on + gerund/noun is a valid alternative to decide to + verb.

Tip: Decide to go OR decide on going — both grammatical.

TRUE — Refuse can take a noun object ("refused their friends' offer"); the of + -ing belongs to offer, not to refuse.

Tip: Refuse + noun and refuse + to + verb are both correct.
tasks.solution_overview: Edge grammar: impossible stop to mean, parallel stop -ing, consider how to, decide on -ing, and refuse + noun. Look past the first verb when the complement sits elsewhere.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided interrupting the poet mid-line.
Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided to interrupt the poet mid-line.
They promised that they would water the plants while we were away.
He enjoys that his sister always remembers his birthday.
We stopped short of promising to host the entire reunion.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided interrupting."

Tip: Fronted participle clauses do not change avoid's -ing rule.

FALSE — Same sentence with the wrong complement: avoid needs -ing, not to.

Tip: Compare the pair; only the gerund version works.

TRUE — Promise that + clause is a valid alternative to promise to + verb.

Tip: Promise to water OR promise that we will water.

TRUE — Enjoy that + clause is acceptable; the that-clause is the object.

Tip: Enjoy + -ing for activities; enjoy that for facts/situations.

TRUE — Stop short of + -ing is an idiom meaning "almost but not quite"; promising keeps its own to.

Tip: Idioms can nest: stop short of + gerund, and inside it promise + to.
tasks.solution_overview: Minimal pairs, that-clause alternatives, and the idiom stop short of -ing. Confirm which structure is actually complementing which verb.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had they considered postponing, they might have decided to wait for clearer skies.
She cannot help enjoying to win, even in friendly matches.
Whatever they refuse to discuss in public, they still avoid lying to each other.
To stop to worry is not the same as to stop worrying.
Only those who promise delivering results on time keep their places on the team.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Consider + gerund and decide + to-infinitive both correct inside a conditional.

Tip: Complex syntax still respects each verb's fixed complement.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoying winning" (and cannot help + -ing is itself a gerund pattern).

Tip: Nested -ing does not license enjoy to.

TRUE — Refuse + to and avoid + -ing both correct in parallel clauses.

Tip: Different verbs, different complements — both can be right at once.

TRUE — The contrast is precisely the teaching point: stop to worry ≠ stop worrying.

Tip: Infinitive subjects can showcase the stop meaning split cleanly.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promise to deliver."

Tip: Relative clauses do not unlock promise + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Final stress test: stacked patterns, cannot help + enjoy, parallel refuse/avoid, the stop meaning contrast as subject, and a last promise trap.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The match starts at seven." → "She said the match started at seven."
Direct: "Where is the bus stop?" → "He asked where was the bus stop."
Direct: "We will bake bread tomorrow." → "They said they will bake bread tomorrow."
Direct: "Did you lock the bike?" → "She asked if I had locked the bike."
Direct: "I finished the essay yesterday." → "He said he had finished the essay yesterday."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After a past reporting verb, present simple backshifts to past simple: "starts" becomes "started."

Tip: Past said/asked usually pulls the reported verb one step back in time.

FALSE — Embedded wh-questions keep statement order: subject before the verb. "Where was the bus stop?" is still direct-question order.

Tip: Use "where the bus stop was," not "where was…"

FALSE — "Will" normally backshifts to "would," and "tomorrow" usually becomes "the next day."

Tip: "They said they would bake bread the next day."

TRUE — Yes/no questions take if/whether plus statement order, and past simple often becomes past perfect.

Tip: "asked if/whether + subject + had + past participle."

FALSE — Time markers shift with the tense: "yesterday" becomes "the day before" (or "the previous day").

Tip: Pair backshift with deictic shifts: yesterday → the day before; tomorrow → the next day.
tasks.solution_overview: This set drills the core trio: tense backshift after said/asked, statement word order in embedded questions, and shifting time markers like yesterday. Mark each line as a legal report of the given direct speech — or not.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I can swim across the lake." → "She said she can swim across the lake."
Direct: "When does the museum open?" → "He asked when the museum opened."
Direct: "We must pack today." → "She said they had to pack that day."
Direct: "I have watered the plants." → "He said he had watered the plants."
Direct: "Are the tickets ready?" → "She asked are the tickets ready."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Ability "can" typically backshifts to "could" after a past reporting verb.

Tip: "She said she could swim across the lake."

TRUE — Wh-word stays, tense backshifts, and the clause keeps subject–verb statement order.

Tip: "asked when + subject + past verb," never "when does/did…"

TRUE — Obligation "must" often becomes "had to," and "today" shifts to "that day."

Tip: Present obligation markers (must/today) usually reshape in past reports.

TRUE — Present perfect backshifts cleanly to past perfect after said.

Tip: have/has + past participle → had + past participle.

FALSE — Reported yes/no questions need if/whether and statement order, not inverted "are the tickets…"

Tip: "She asked whether the tickets were ready."
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on modal backshift (can → could, must → had to), present perfect → past perfect, and the if/whether pattern for yes/no reports. Embedded wh-questions should already feel like statements.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The choir rehearses here tomorrow." → "He said the choir rehearsed here tomorrow."
Direct: "Why did the neighbour leave?" → "She asked why did the neighbour leave."
Direct: "I am reading the novel now." → "He said he was reading the novel then."
Direct: "Do not feed the stray cats." → "She told me do not feed the stray cats."
Direct: "We may hike next weekend." → "They said they may hike next weekend."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Place and time markers usually shift: "here" → "there," "tomorrow" → "the next day" / "the following day."

Tip: "He said the choir rehearsed there the following day."

FALSE — Embedded why-questions need statement order and usually past-perfect backshift: not "why did the neighbour…"

Tip: "She asked why the neighbour had left."

TRUE — Present continuous backshifts to past continuous, and "now" becomes "then."

Tip: am/is/are + -ing → was/were + -ing; now → then.

FALSE — Negative commands in reports use told/asked + object + not + to-infinitive.

Tip: "She told me not to feed the stray cats."

FALSE — "May" for possibility often becomes "might," and "next weekend" should become "the following weekend."

Tip: "They said they might hike the following weekend."
tasks.solution_overview: Four traps stack deictics, leftover do-support, unshifted may/next, and a bare negative command. Only the continuous now→then line is clean.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Please text me the address." → "He asked me to text him the address."
Direct: "Who watered the garden?" → "She asked who had watered the garden."
Direct: "I will have finished by Friday." → "He said he would have finished by Friday."
Direct: "This recipe needs more salt." → "She said that recipe needed more salt."
Direct: "Have you seen my keys?" → "He asked had I seen his keys."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Polite requests report as asked + object + to-infinitive.

Tip: Direct "Please…" → "asked someone to…"

TRUE — Subject questions keep who as subject; the tense still backshifts.

Tip: "asked who had watered…" is statement-like and correctly shifted.

TRUE — Future perfect "will have finished" backshifts to "would have finished."

Tip: will → would even inside perfect constructions.

TRUE — "This" often becomes "that" after a past report, with present → past.

Tip: Demonstratives move with the reporting frame.

FALSE — Yes/no perfect questions need if/whether + statement order, not "had I…" inversion.

Tip: "He asked whether I had seen his keys."
tasks.solution_overview: Four solid reports cover requests, subject questions, future perfect backshift, and this→that. The trap is leftover question inversion after asked.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The soup is too salty." → "Mia told that the soup was too salty."
Direct: "How long have you lived here?" → "She asked how long I had lived there."
Direct: "We shall meet at noon." → "He said they should meet at noon."
Direct: "I saw the fox last night." → "She said she had seen the fox the night before."
Direct: "Can you join the hike?" → "He asked could I join the hike."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Tell" needs a personal object: tell someone that…; without an object, use "said that…"

Tip: said that / told us that — never bare "told that."

TRUE — Present perfect → past perfect, "here" → "there," and statement order after how long.

Tip: Bundle tense, place, and order shifts together.

TRUE — Formal "shall" for future often reports as "should" (or "would") after past said.

Tip: Treat shall like will when backshifting future meaning.

TRUE — Past simple → past perfect and "last night" → "the night before."

Tip: Relative past time phrases shift just like yesterday/tomorrow.

FALSE — Modal yes/no reports need if/whether + subject + could, not "could I…" inversion.

Tip: "He asked if I could join the hike."
tasks.solution_overview: Say versus tell joins the usual backshift package. Watch for missing objects after tell and for inverted modals after asked.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Bring a spare towel." → "She told us to bring a spare towel."
Direct: "I may be late." → "He said he might be late."
Direct: "Where have they put the map?" → "She asked where they had put the map."
Direct: "We were discussing the film." → "He said they had been discussing the film."
Direct: "I leave for Lisbon tonight." → "She said she was leaving for Lisbon that night."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Imperatives report as tell/ask + object + to-infinitive.

Tip: Command verb drops; to + base verb carries the instruction.

TRUE — Possibility "may" commonly becomes "might" in past reports.

Tip: may → might is the safe exam backshift.

TRUE — Wh-word + statement order + present perfect → past perfect.

Tip: "asked where they had put…" — no auxiliary before the subject.

TRUE — Past continuous often becomes past perfect continuous after a past reporting verb.

Tip: was/were + -ing → had been + -ing when sequence needs a further step back.

TRUE — Present simple for a near arrangement can report as past continuous, with "tonight" → "that night."

Tip: Timetabled or arranged futures often surface as was/were + -ing in reports.
tasks.solution_overview: All five lines are clean reports: commands with to-infinitive, modal may→might, embedded perfect questions, past continuous deepening, and arranged-future reporting.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I must have left my scarf at the café." → "He said he must have left his scarf at the café."
Direct: "Will the library renew the card?" → "She asked would the library renew the card."
Direct: "These clouds are gathering." → "He said those clouds were gathering."
Direct: "I used to cycle to school." → "She said she used to cycle to school."
Direct: "Don't forget the tickets." → "He reminded me not to forget the tickets."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Deduction "must have" often stays unchanged because it already refers to a past conclusion.

Tip: Logical deduction with must have need not backshift further.

FALSE — Yes/no with will needs if/whether + would + subject, not "would the library…" inversion.

Tip: "She asked whether the library would renew the card."

TRUE — "These" → "those" and present continuous → past continuous.

Tip: Demonstratives shift with the reporting viewpoint.

TRUE — "Used to" already marks past habit and normally stays as used to after said.

Tip: No further backshift is required for used to.

TRUE — Negative reminders use not + to-infinitive after remind/tell.

Tip: "reminded me not to forget…" mirrors "told me not to…"
tasks.solution_overview: Some forms resist further shift (must have, used to); others still demand if/whether and statement order. Separate "leave alone" cases from order traps.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Why are you delaying the trip?" → "She asked why were we delaying the trip."
Direct: "I ought to call my sister." → "He said he ought to call his sister."
Direct: "We arrived two days ago." → "They said they had arrived two days ago."
Direct: "Is this the final draft?" → "He asked if that was the final draft."
Direct: "I will phone you later today." → "She said she would phone me later that day."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Keep statement order: "why we were delaying," not "why were we…"

Tip: After asked, never reinvert the auxiliary before the subject.

TRUE — "Ought to" typically remains ought to in reported speech.

Tip: Ought to is already modal-like and usually does not change form.

FALSE — "Ago" normally becomes "before" / "earlier" in past reports; keeping "ago" clashes with the shifted frame.

Tip: "They said they had arrived two days before."

TRUE — Yes/no with if, this→that, and present→past all apply together.

Tip: Bundle if + demonstrative shift + tense shift.

TRUE — will→would and today→that day after past said.

Tip: Future markers and same-day time words both move.
tasks.solution_overview: The hard spots are inverted wh-clauses and leftover "ago." Ought to and clean if/that/will shifts show the correct pattern.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "We need not renew the membership yet." → "She said they need not renew the membership yet."
Direct: "What time does the ferry leave?" → "He asked what time the ferry left."
Direct: "I have been waiting since Monday." → "She said she had been waiting since Monday."
Direct: "Come back the day after tomorrow." → "They told us to come back in two days' time."
Direct: "I can't approve this design." → "He said he couldn't approve that design."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Need not" for lack of obligation often stays need not (or becomes did not need to).

Tip: Either unchanged need not or did not need to is acceptable; bare "needed not" is wrong.

TRUE — Wh-clause with statement order and present→past.

Tip: "asked what time + subject + past verb."

TRUE — Present perfect continuous backshifts to past perfect continuous.

Tip: have/has been + -ing → had been + -ing.

TRUE — "The day after tomorrow" can paraphrase as "in two days' time" / "two days later."

Tip: Distant relative time phrases are often reworded, not left literal.

TRUE — can→could and this→that in one tidy report.

Tip: Modal ability and demonstratives usually shift together after past said.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are acceptable advanced reports: need not, embedded timetable questions, perfect continuous backshift, reworded far-future time, and can/this shifts.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Who did you invite?" → "She asked who did I invite."
Direct: "The cherries ripened last year." → "He said the cherries had ripened the year before."
Direct: "Shall I postpone the picnic?" → "She asked if she should postpone the picnic."
Direct: "We are going to plant lavender." → "They said they were going to plant lavender."
Direct: "I won't leave until Friday." → "He said he won't leave until Friday."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Object questions drop do-support and use statement order: "who I had invited."

Tip: After asked, no "did" before the subject.

TRUE — Past simple → past perfect and "last year" → "the year before."

Tip: Calendar "last…" phrases become "the … before / previous …"

TRUE — Offer/suggestion shall I… reports as if/whether + should.

Tip: "asked if she should…" is the standard mapping.

TRUE — "Be going to" backshifts was/were going to after past said.

Tip: Treat going-to futures like other present forms that shift one step.

FALSE — "Won't" should become "wouldn't" after a past reporting verb.

Tip: will/won't → would/wouldn't in standard backshift.
tasks.solution_overview: Object-question do-support and unshifted won't are the failures. Going-to futures, shall→should offers, and last-year time shifts are the models.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide said, "Water freezes at zero," and later reported that water freezes at zero.
Direct: "Could you pass the salt?" → "She asked me if I could pass the salt."
Direct: "I was cooking when the power failed." → "He said he had been cooking when the power had failed."
Direct: "Whose umbrella is this?" → "He asked whose umbrella was this."
Direct: "We needn't have brought extra chairs." → "She said they needn't have brought extra chairs."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — When the situation is still true, some writers keep present tense after a past report; it is acceptable for ongoing facts.

Tip: Backshift is usual but not compulsory for permanently or still-valid truths.

TRUE — Polite could you… can report as asked + if + could + statement order.

Tip: Ability/request could often stays could inside if-clauses.

FALSE — Over-shifting both verbs to past perfect can distort simultaneous past events; keep the time-clause past simple if it marks the interrupting moment.

Tip: Prefer "had been cooking when the power failed."

FALSE — Statement order needed: "whose umbrella this was," not "whose umbrella was this."

Tip: Possessive wh-questions still lose inversion in reports.

TRUE — "Needn't have" for unnecessary past action commonly remains needn't have.

Tip: Perfect modal forms for past comments often stay put.
tasks.solution_overview: Optional non-backshift for still-true facts sits beside over-shifted time clauses and inverted whose-questions. Perfect need not and polite could-if reports are fine.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Let's postpone the rehearsal." → "She suggested postponing the rehearsal."
Direct: "I wish I knew the answer." → "He said he wished he knew the answer."
Direct: "Had you finished before the storm?" → "She asked whether I had finished before the storm."
Direct: "We thrived here last spring." → "They said they had thrived there the previous spring."
Direct: "You had better rest." → "He said I had better rest."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Let's…" suggestions often report as suggested + gerund (or suggested that…).

Tip: Suggest takes a gerund or a that-clause, not bare to-infinitive without that.

TRUE — Wish-clauses already sit in a past-like form; reporting them usually keeps wished + past form.

Tip: Do not force a further unnatural backshift inside wish.

TRUE — Past perfect yes/no questions report with if/whether + had + past participle and statement order.

Tip: Inversion from the direct Had you… disappears after asked.

TRUE — Past simple → past perfect plus here→there and last→previous.

Tip: Stack place and calendar shifts with the tense change.

TRUE — "Had better" for advice typically remains had better after said.

Tip: Had better does not become would better.
tasks.solution_overview: Every line is a valid report: let's→suggest + -ing, wish retention, whether + past perfect, stacked deictics, and unchanged had better.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I would rather stay indoors." → "She said she would rather stayed indoors."
Direct: "When will you publish the photos?" → "He asked when we would publish the photos."
Direct: "I might have misread the map." → "He said he might have misread the map."
Direct: "Stay where you are." → "Security told us to stay where we were."
Direct: "Did the nurse call you yesterday?" → "She asked if the nurse had called me yesterday."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — After would rather, keep the base verb: "would rather stay," not "stayed."

Tip: Would rather + bare infinitive survives reporting.

TRUE — will→would inside a wh-clause with statement order.

Tip: "asked when + subject + would + verb."

TRUE — "Might have" for past possibility usually stays might have.

Tip: Perfect modals of speculation rarely need further change.

TRUE — Imperative plus embedded where-clause: to-infinitive outside, backshift inside the where-clause.

Tip: "to stay where we were" — both layers handled.

FALSE — "Yesterday" should become "the day before" once the reporting verb is past.

Tip: "…had called me the day before."
tasks.solution_overview: Would rather keeps a base verb; yesterday still must shift. Wh-future reports, might have, and nested where-clauses show controlled backshift.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I insist that the lyrics be rewritten." → "She insisted that the lyrics be rewritten."
Direct: "How much did the festival cost?" → "He asked how much the festival had cost."
Direct: "We will be launching next Monday." → "They said they would be launching the following Monday."
Direct: "I never said that." → "She claimed she had never said that."
Direct: "Are you being serious?" → "He asked if I was being serious."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Formal mandative subjunctive after insist often stays be + past participle in the report.

Tip: Reporting insist that… can preserve the base-form subjunctive.

TRUE — Object how-much questions drop did and backshift to past perfect with statement order.

Tip: "asked how much + subject + had + past participle."

TRUE — Future continuous will be + -ing → would be + -ing, and next → the following.

Tip: Progressive futures backshift the will piece only.

TRUE — Past simple negation becomes past perfect in a past report when the earlier speech act is prior.

Tip: "had never said" places the denial further back.

TRUE — Present continuous being → past continuous being after if.

Tip: "asked if I was being…" — statement order, tense shifted.
highlights: how much the festival had cost
tasks.solution_overview: All five succeed: preserved mandative be, cleaned object questions, future continuous backshift, prior-speech past perfect, and continuous being after if.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I would have called if I had known." → "She said she would have called if she had known."
Direct: "Which shelf holds the spices?" → "He asked which shelf did hold the spices."
Direct: "The offer expires the day after tomorrow." → "They said the offer expired two days later."
Direct: "Must we disclose the allergy?" → "She asked if they had to disclose the allergy."
Direct: "I am to present at nine." → "He said he was to present at nine."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Conditional perfect forms already sit far back and typically stay would have / had + past participle when reported.

Tip: Do not invent an extra layer beyond would have + past perfect.

FALSE — No do-support in the embedded clause: "which shelf held the spices."

Tip: Wh-determiners keep statement order without did.

TRUE — "The day after tomorrow" → "two days later" / "in two days" is a natural time rewrite.

Tip: Far deixis is often paraphrased in polished reports.

TRUE — Obligation must in questions often becomes had to after asked if.

Tip: "asked if they had to…" is the usual mapping.

TRUE — Formal "be to" for scheduled duty backshifts was/were to.

Tip: am/is/are to → was/were to after past said.
tasks.solution_overview: One illegal did in a which-clause breaks the set. Elsewhere, remote conditionals, time paraphrase, must→had to, and be-to schedules report cleanly.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "You needn't worry about the weather." → "He told me I didn't need to worry about the weather."
Direct: "Whereabouts is the camping stove?" → "She asked whereabouts was the camping stove."
Direct: "I have got to leave now." → "He said he had got to leave then."
Direct: "We shall have completed the mural by June." → "They said they would have completed the mural by June."
Direct: "Why must the window stay open?" → "She asked why the window had to stay open."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Needn't" can report as didn't need to / needn't after a past frame.

Tip: Personal object after told plus shifted lack-of-obligation form.

FALSE — Even with whereabouts, keep statement order: "whereabouts the camping stove was."

Tip: Any wh-word still bans auxiliary-before-subject after asked.

TRUE — "Have got to" obligation backshifts to had got to, and now→then.

Tip: Treat have got to like must for backshift purposes.

TRUE — shall have + past participle (future perfect) → would have + past participle.

Tip: Future perfect always yields would have in standard past reports.

TRUE — why + must → why + had to with statement order.

Tip: Obligation questions lose must inversion and often become had to.
tasks.solution_overview: Whereabouts inversion is the sole fault. Needn't→didn't need to, have got to, future perfect, and why-must→had to are sound.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Were the paths cleared last winter?" → "She asked whether the paths had been cleared the previous winter."
Direct: "I would prefer you not to spoil this yet." → "She said she would prefer us not to spoil that yet."
Direct: "Dare I ask for a refund?" → "He asked if he dared ask for a refund."
Direct: "The team will have been rehearsing for six hours by then." → "She said the team would have been rehearsing for six hours by then."
Direct: "What if we delay the concert?" → "He asked what if we delayed the concert."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Passive past yes/no → whether + past perfect passive + last→previous.

Tip: Voice stays passive; only tense and time words move.

TRUE — Would prefer + object + not to stays structurally; pronouns and this→that adjust.

Tip: Preference patterns largely keep their skeleton under reporting.

TRUE — Rare dare questions can report as if + dared + bare infinitive.

Tip: Modal-like dare often becomes a past lexical dare in reports.

TRUE — Future perfect continuous will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing.

Tip: Only will becomes would; the rest of the stack stays.

TRUE — "What if…" hypotheticals often keep what if and simply backshift the following verb.

Tip: "asked what if we delayed…" is natural exam English.
highlights: had been cleared the previous winter
tasks.solution_overview: A clean advanced sweep: passive perfect reports, prefer + not to, dare, future perfect continuous, and what-if backshift — all grammatical.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Seldom have we seen such fog." → "She said seldom had they seen such fog."
Direct: "I was to have signed before noon." → "He said he was to have signed before noon."
Direct: "Who should we notify first?" → "She asked who should we notify first."
Direct: "The bread will still be warm tomorrow morning." → "He said the bread would still be warm the next morning."
Direct: "Might the shop extend its hours?" → "They asked might the shop extend its hours."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negative inversion can survive inside the reported clause after said, with pronoun and tense already matching.

Tip: Reporting rare inverted rhetoric may keep the inverted shape.

TRUE — "Was to have + past participle" (unfulfilled plan) typically remains was to have…

Tip: This past-scheduled perfect form needs no further shift.

FALSE — Embedded object questions need statement order: "who we should notify first."

Tip: Modal should still follows the subject after asked.

TRUE — Future will → would, and tomorrow morning → the next morning.

Tip: Will and time words move together after past said.

FALSE — Yes/no might needs if/whether + subject + might, not "might the shop…"

Tip: "They asked whether the shop might extend…"
tasks.solution_overview: Inverted who-should and bare might-yes/no fail. Surviving rhetorical inversion, was-to-have, and would + next-morning time shifts are acceptable.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I'd rather you didn't spoil this." → "She said she'd rather I didn't spoil that."
Direct: "How come the cake collapsed?" → "He asked how come the cake had collapsed."
Direct: "We used not to skip breakfast." → "They said they used not to skip breakfast."
Direct: "Will you have finished by the time I call?" → "She asked if I would have finished by the time she called."
Direct: "Suppose we freeze the leftovers." → "He suggested that we freeze the leftovers."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Would rather + past clause for preference about someone else keeps that past shape; this→that adjusts.

Tip: Preferential rather-clauses are not forced into past perfect.

TRUE — Informal how come reports with statement order and optional past perfect for a prior failure.

Tip: "asked how come + subject + (had) + past participle."

TRUE — "Used not to" (or didn't use to) for past habit can remain used not to.

Tip: Habitual used to patterns are already past-oriented.

TRUE — Future perfect in a yes/no question → if + would have, and the time-clause present→past.

Tip: Both the main future perfect and the by-the-time clause shift.

TRUE — Suppose-ideas often become suggested that + base or past form in formal reports.

Tip: Mandative or tentative freeze after suggested that is exam-friendly.
highlights: how come the cake had collapsed
tasks.solution_overview: All five are advanced but valid: rather + past clause, how come, used not to, nested would-have with by-the-time, and suggested that.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Not only is the path steep, but the wind is fierce." → "She said not only was the path steep, but the wind was fierce."
Direct: "I needn't have packed every jumper." → "He said he needn't have packed every jumper."
Direct: "Where should the chairs sit?" → "She asked where should the chairs sit."
Direct: "By next March we will have been leasing the studio for a decade." → "They said that by the following March they would have been leasing the studio for a decade."
Direct: "Was anyone monitoring the feed then?" → "She asked was anyone monitoring the feed then."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correlative not only…but also can keep inversion after said while tenses sit in the past.

Tip: Reporting flashy inversion is optional but grammatical if pronouns and tenses align.

TRUE — Needn't have for unnecessary past action stays needn't have.

Tip: Perfect absence-of-need does not become hadn't need.

FALSE — Statement order required: "where the chairs should sit."

Tip: Modal should follows the subject in embedded wh-questions.

TRUE — next→the following and will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing.

Tip: Long future-perfect-continuous stacks only change will→would.

FALSE — Yes/no past continuous needs if/whether + statement order: "whether anyone was monitoring…"

Tip: Never leave bare "was anyone…" after asked.
tasks.solution_overview: Two order failures remain: should after where, and bare was-anyone after asked. Inverted not only, needn't have, and future perfect continuous reports are fine.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She packed a apple in her lunchbox for the hike.
He bought an umbrella before the outdoor concert.
We need an new bicycle for the weekend trip.
The coach approved an plan for the relay team.
Please send me an email with the rehearsal times.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Apple" begins with a vowel sound, so English needs "an apple," not "a apple."

Tip: Match a/an to the sound that follows, not just the first letter on the page.

TRUE — "Umbrella" starts with a vowel sound, so "an umbrella" is the correct first-mention form.

Tip: First mention of one countable thing usually takes a/an — but only the matching form.

FALSE — "New" begins with a consonant sound (/n/), so English needs "a new bicycle," not "an new bicycle."

Tip: Adjectives do not change the a/an rule — listen to the sound right after a/an.

FALSE — "Plan" begins with a consonant sound, so use "a plan," not "an plan."

Tip: The rest of the sentence can stay; only the form before plan is wrong.

TRUE — "Email" begins with a vowel sound (/iː/), so "an email" is correct.

Tip: Say the next word aloud; if it starts with a vowel sound, use an.
tasks.solution_overview: This set is about choosing a versus an before a singular countable noun. Listen for vowel versus consonant sounds right after the determiner, including when an adjective comes first.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide asked for an honest answer about the trail conditions.
They hired a European tutor for their French exchange.
She completed a MBA while volunteering at the library.
We reserved an hotel near the festival grounds.
He is an university student in biology.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Honest" starts with a silent h, so the spoken form begins with a vowel sound and takes "an."

Tip: Silent letters still decide a/an by sound, not spelling.

TRUE — "European" begins with a /j/ sound (like "you"), which counts as a consonant sound, so "a European" is correct.

Tip: Eu- and u- words often take a when they sound like they start with "y."

FALSE — "MBA" is normally read letter by letter, starting with /em/, a vowel sound, so it needs "an MBA."

Tip: With abbreviations, base a/an on how you pronounce the first letter.

FALSE — In standard modern pronunciation, "hotel" keeps the /h/, so "a hotel" is the usual form, not "an hotel."

Tip: Prefer a before clearly sounded h- words in contemporary English.

FALSE — "University" starts with a /j/ sound, so the correct form is "a university student."

Tip: If you can hear a "y" glide at the start, choose a.
tasks.solution_overview: These sentences turn on sound, not spelling. Silent h, letter names in abbreviations, and the "y" glide in words like European and university are the traps to watch.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I read a novel yesterday; the novel kept me awake until dawn.
Please close a window; it is freezing in here.
She joined the choir as a junior soprano in 2022.
Could you pass me a salt from the tray?
They opened an café on the corner last spring.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — First mention uses "a novel"; the second mention switches to "the novel" because the same book is now identified.

Tip: a/an introduces; the points back to something already specified.

FALSE — In this situation the window is a specific one in the room, so English expects "the window," not "a window."

Tip: When both speakers can identify the thing, prefer the.

TRUE — Roles after "as" commonly take a/an for one role among many: "as a junior soprano."

Tip: Occupations and roles usually need a/an in this pattern.

FALSE — At the table, "salt" is a specific shared item, so "the salt" is the natural choice.

Tip: Shared, obvious objects in the immediate setting take the.

FALSE — "Café" begins with a consonant sound (/k/), so use "a café," not "an café."

Tip: Spelling with a vowel letter does not override a consonant sound.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on whether the noun is newly introduced or already clear to both speakers. First mention and shared, obvious objects follow different patterns.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The sun was still low when the runners started.
Moon looks unusually bright tonight over the harbour.
She is only person who finished the crossword.
This is same recipe we used last winter.
He is the tallest player on the school team.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Unique celestial bodies take "the": "the sun." The runners are also definite in context.

Tip: One-of-a-kind referents almost always need the.

FALSE — "Moon" in this sense needs "the moon"; leaving it bare is not standard.

Tip: Pair the with unique natural landmarks and celestial objects.

FALSE — "Only" before a singular noun requires "the only person."

Tip: Patterns with only, same, next, and last usually need the.

FALSE — The fixed pattern is "the same recipe," not bare "same recipe."

Tip: "Same" almost never stands without the in this use.

TRUE — Superlative forms take "the": "the tallest player."

Tip: If you see -est or most + adjective for a unique ranking, expect the.
tasks.solution_overview: Unique things, superlatives, and words like only and same strongly prefer the. Check whether the noun points to one identifiable item in the world or in the set.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hikers received useful advice from the ranger.
She gave me an advice about packing for cold weather.
We still need more informations before we choose a route.
The lab ordered new equipment for the science fair.
They bought an furniture for the guest room.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Advice" is uncountable, so it appears with zero article here and is modified by "useful," not by a/an.

Tip: Uncountable abstract nouns often take zero article when used in a general sense.

FALSE — "Advice" cannot take "an"; say "some advice" or "a piece of advice."

Tip: If you need a countable unit, use a piece/bit/item of + uncountable noun.

FALSE — "Information" has no plural form in standard English; use "more information," not "informations."

Tip: Watch for false plurals on uncountable nouns.

TRUE — "Equipment" is uncountable and correctly appears without a/an; "new" simply describes the mass noun.

Tip: Zero article + adjective + uncountable noun is a common correct pattern.

FALSE — "Furniture" is uncountable, so "an furniture" is impossible; use "furniture" or "a piece of furniture."

Tip: Do not place a/an directly before classic uncountables like furniture, equipment, or advice.
tasks.solution_overview: Uncountable nouns reject a/an and usually reject plural -s. Prefer zero article for general reference, or a quantifying phrase such as a piece of when you need a unit.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Progress on the mural has been slower than expected.
The news were surprising for the whole neighbourhood.
Research shows that morning light can improve mood.
We lack an evidence to support that claim.
Traffic was heavy on the way to the airport.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Progress" is uncountable and correctly used with zero article for a general process underway.

Tip: Zero article is normal with progress, research, and similar abstracts.

FALSE — "News" is uncountable and takes a singular verb: "The news was surprising." The determiner "the" can stay; the verb must agree.

Tip: "News" looks plural but behaves as singular.

TRUE — General research findings use zero article: "Research shows…"

Tip: When you mean research as a field or body of work in general, omit a/the.

FALSE — "Evidence" is uncountable, so "an evidence" is wrong; use "evidence" or "a piece of evidence."

Tip: Specificity does not make evidence countable with a/an.

TRUE — "Traffic" is uncountable and takes zero article in this general statement about conditions.

Tip: Mass nouns for weather, traffic, and similar conditions usually need no a/an.
tasks.solution_overview: Several everyday nouns are uncountable even when they end in -s or feel countable. Keep zero article for general reference and avoid a/an before evidence, progress, and traffic.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Children need clear routines at home.
The neighbours expect quieter evenings during exam week.
Water is still scarce after the long drought.
She drinks the coffee every morning before class.
Teachers should explain key ideas carefully.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Plural nouns in a general sense take zero article: "Children need…"

Tip: General plurals usually omit the.

TRUE — Here "the neighbours" can refer to the known people next door, so the is acceptable and natural.

Tip: The + plural is fine when the group is definite in context.

TRUE — Uncountable "water" used generically takes zero article.

Tip: Materials and substances in general statements often need no determiner.

FALSE — Habitual general coffee-drinking uses zero article: "She drinks coffee every morning," not "the coffee," unless a specific coffee is meant.

Tip: Do not force the onto uncountables used in a general habitual sense.

TRUE — Plural "Teachers" in a general professional statement correctly takes zero article.

Tip: Job-title plurals meaning "teachers in general" stay bare.
tasks.solution_overview: General plurals and general uncountables prefer zero article. Use the only when the group or substance is already limited to a known set.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He goes to work by bus on most weekdays.
She travelled to Lisbon by a train last Friday.
They sent the parcels by courier overnight.
I usually go to the home after the evening class.
We went to school together in the same district.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Fixed patterns "go to work" and "by bus" both use zero article.

Tip: Memorise by + transport and go to work/school/bed as zero-article chunks.

FALSE — The transport pattern is "by train," not "by a train."

Tip: After by for means of transport, do not insert a/an.

TRUE — "By courier" follows the same zero-article transport/delivery pattern.

Tip: By + service/means is typically bare.

FALSE — The fixed expression is "go home," never "go to the home" in this meaning.

Tip: Home after go/arrive/get normally takes no to and no the.

TRUE — "Go to school" with zero article means attendance as a student, which fits this sentence.

Tip: Purpose-of-institution uses often drop the.
tasks.solution_overview: Several high-frequency chunks freeze the determiner choice: by bus/train, go to work/school, and go home. Treat them as fixed patterns rather than building them word by word.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Her brother is still in hospital after the operation.
We drove past the hospital on our way to the lake.
Three activists are in the prison for peaceful protest.
The prison on the hill dates from the nineteenth century.
She stayed in bed until noon because of a migraine.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — British English uses zero article in "in hospital" when the person is there as a patient.

Tip: Purpose (patient/prisoner/student) often means zero article with the institution.

TRUE — When the building itself is meant as a location landmark, "the hospital" is correct.

Tip: Switch to the when you mean the building, not the institutional purpose.

FALSE — As inmates, the natural British pattern is "in prison," not "in the prison."

Tip: Purpose reading → zero; building reading → the.

TRUE — Referring to a specific building as a landmark correctly takes "the prison."

Tip: Physical description and location cues usually signal the building reading.

TRUE — "In bed" for resting/sleeping takes zero article in the standard idiom.

Tip: In bed / in church / in hospital follow the same purpose logic.
tasks.solution_overview: Institution nouns flip between zero article (purpose: patient, prisoner) and the (the building as a place). Read the sentence for purpose versus physical location.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She plays the piano at family gatherings.
He plays the football for the local amateur side.
They listen to the radio during the morning walk.
I watched a television until midnight after the film.
She is learning the violin with a private tutor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Musical instruments take "the" in this general ability/habit pattern: "play the piano."

Tip: play + the + instrument is the default.

FALSE — Sports use zero article: "play football," not "play the football."

Tip: Contrast instruments (the) with sports and games (zero).

TRUE — "Listen to the radio" is the standard pattern for the medium.

Tip: the radio / the news are common fixed media patterns.

FALSE — Habitual or general TV watching is "watch television," not "watch a television," unless you mean one physical set.

Tip: Medium versus device: medium often takes zero; a specific device can take a/the.

TRUE — "Learn the violin" follows the same instrument rule as play the piano.

Tip: Keep the with named instruments after play/learn.
tasks.solution_overview: Instruments prefer the; sports prefer zero. Media words like radio and television also have preferred patterns—do not invent a/an forms where the medium itself is meant.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Most students supported the later start time.
The most of guests opposed the outdoor seating plan.
Half of the cake has already been eaten.
Both finalists gave a strong closing speech.
All of luggage must be labelled before check-in.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Most" + plural noun takes zero article when speaking generally about the majority: "Most students…"

Tip: most + noun (no the) for general majorities.

FALSE — Do not say "the most of guests"; use "most of the guests" or "most guests."

Tip: After most of, you normally need the + definite noun phrase.

TRUE — "Half of the cake" correctly combines the quantifier with a definite noun phrase.

Tip: half/most/some of + the + specific noun is a safe pattern.

TRUE — "Both finalists" needs no article before both; "a strong closing speech" correctly introduces one speech each.

Tip: both/all/each have their own determiner rules—do not stack the before both.

FALSE — "All of luggage" is incomplete; write "all of the luggage" or "all luggage."

Tip: all of must be followed by a determined noun phrase (often with the).
tasks.solution_overview: Quantifier patterns interact with determiners: most + noun, most of the + noun, half of the +, and all of the +. Avoid blending those frames.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She is studying economics at a well-known university.
He majored in the history before joining the museum.
They offer a course in photography this term.
The mathematics in this puzzle is unexpectedly elegant.
She teaches the English at a private college.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Academic subjects usually take zero article: "studying economics."

Tip: Subject names in general study contexts stay bare.

FALSE — As a field of study, use "history," not "the history," unless a specific history is meant.

Tip: Zero article for subjects; the only when the noun is narrowed (the history of X).

TRUE — "Photography" as a course subject correctly appears without a/the before the subject name; "a course" is the countable shell.

Tip: Count the course, not the subject noun itself.

TRUE — Here "the mathematics" refers to the specific maths in this puzzle, so the is justified.

Tip: The + subject is fine when limited by a postmodifier or clear context.

FALSE — Language subjects in general take zero article: "teaches English," not "teaches the English."

Tip: Language names as school subjects are usually bare.
tasks.solution_overview: Subject and language names are bare in general academic use, but the appears when the noun is limited to a specific body of material. Separate the countable "course" from the subject label.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The Netherlands remains a popular cycling destination.
She moved to United Kingdom after finishing her degree.
Their hostel is just outside Hague, near the sea.
We spent two weeks in Brazil last summer.
The Amazon is vital to several rainforest ecosystems.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Country names that are plural or include a common noun often take "the": "the Netherlands."

Tip: the with Netherlands, United Kingdom, United States, Philippines, etc.

FALSE — The standard form is "the United Kingdom," not bare "United Kingdom" after to.

Tip: Full political names with Kingdom/States/Republic usually need the.

FALSE — The city is "The Hague," so the sentence needs "outside The Hague."

Tip: A few place names include The as part of the name.

TRUE — Most single-name countries take zero article: "in Brazil."

Tip: Default for country and city names is zero unless the name belongs to a the-group.

TRUE — Famous rivers take "the": "the Amazon."

Tip: the with rivers, seas, oceans, and canal names.
tasks.solution_overview: Geography has compact rules: most countries and cities are bare, but plural/political names and many waterways take the. A handful of names include The as part of the proper noun.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Lake Victoria appears in several geography textbooks.
They sailed across Atlantic on a freighter.
Mount Everest still attracts extreme hikers.
We spent a week in Alps after the festival.
The Sahara stretches across much of North Africa.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Individual lakes usually take zero article: "Lake Victoria."

Tip: Lake + name → typically zero; the Great Lakes is an exception as a group.

FALSE — Oceans and seas need "the": "the Atlantic."

Tip: the Atlantic / the Pacific / the Mediterranean.

TRUE — Mountains named with Mount take zero article: "Mount Everest."

Tip: Mount/Mt + name = zero; mountain ranges take the.

FALSE — Mountain ranges take "the": "the Alps."

Tip: Ranges and island groups usually need the.

TRUE — Deserts take "the": "the Sahara."

Tip: the Sahara / the Gobi follow the desert pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Natural features split cleanly: lakes and Mount-names are often bare; oceans, ranges, deserts, and many seas take the. Learn the groups rather than guessing per word.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Poverty remains a serious challenge in many regions.
The life is unpredictable for freelance artists.
Society must balance growth with environmental limits.
She values the honesty above everything else in friendships.
Curiosity drives long-term learning in this field.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Abstract nouns used in a general sense take zero article: "Poverty remains…"

Tip: General abstracts (poverty, society, curiosity) are usually bare.

FALSE — General "life" does not take the: "Life is unpredictable…"

Tip: Use the life only when limited (the life of an artist, the life she wanted).

TRUE — "Society" in a broad general claim correctly appears without a/the.

Tip: Zero article signals the concept as a whole.

FALSE — As a general virtue, prefer "honesty," not "the honesty," unless a specific instance is meant.

Tip: Abstract virtues in general statements stay bare.

TRUE — "Curiosity" as a general driver of learning takes zero article.

Tip: If no postmodifier narrows the abstract, omit the.
tasks.solution_overview: General abstract nouns prefer zero article. Add the only when a of-phrase or clear context turns the abstract into a specific instance.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The advice she received from her coach was unusually clear.
Equipment that arrived yesterday is still in the hallway.
