An information in the appendix contradicts the summary.
The research published last week challenges our assumptions.
We need a progress before the next rehearsal.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Uncountable "advice" can take "the" when a relative clause identifies a specific body of advice.

Tip: Uncountable + the is fine once the noun is made specific.

TRUE — "Equipment" remains uncountable; zero article works even with a defining relative clause when the noun is used as a mass.

Tip: You may also say "the equipment that arrived…" — both can be acceptable; bare is not wrong here.

FALSE — "Information" cannot take "an"; use "information" or "a piece of information."

Tip: Specificity does not magically make an uncountable noun countable with a/an.

TRUE — "The research published last week" correctly uses the because the postmodifier identifies a particular study set.

Tip: Postmodifiers often licence the with otherwise general uncountables.

FALSE — "Progress" is uncountable, so "a progress" is wrong; say "progress" or "some progress."

Tip: Never place a/an directly before progress.
tasks.solution_overview: Uncountables can take the when narrowed by context, but they still reject a/an. Specificity changes zero versus the, not countability itself.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She was appointed the captain of the rowing club.
He became a head of the drama department after the reshuffle.
They elected her treasurer of the local book club.
She is a only photographer who stayed until closing.
He remains the unique finalist still active in round three.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After appoint/elect/name, English often uses "the" + unique role: "appointed the captain."

Tip: Unique office titles after appoint/elect frequently take the.

FALSE — Prefer "the head of the drama department" for a unique post, or rephrase; "a head of…" sounds like one of several equal heads.

Tip: Unique organisational roles usually take the, not a.

TRUE — Zero article is also possible after elect/appoint when the title follows directly: "elected her treasurer."

Tip: Both "elected her treasurer" and "elected her the treasurer" appear; bare title after the object is standard.

FALSE — "Only" requires "the only photographer," not "a only." Also, "only" begins with a vowel sound, so a would be wrong even without that rule.

Tip: the only is a fixed determiner pattern.

FALSE — Native wording prefers "the only finalist" (or "the sole finalist"); "the unique finalist" is awkward in this ranking sense.

Tip: For exclusivity in a set, only/sole beats unique with the.
tasks.solution_overview: Titles and unique roles have special determiner habits after appoint/elect and with only. Aim for the with unique posts, and keep the only as a locked chunk.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of neighbours have requested clearer recycling rules.
The number of open tickets fell after the software update.
She has a knowledge of Portuguese that helps on trips.
He has knowledge of Portuguese from years in Lisbon.
We saw a rise in visitors after the gallery redesign.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "A number of" means "several" and correctly pairs with a plural noun; the determiner pattern itself is standard.

Tip: a number of + plural is a fixed quantifying frame.

TRUE — "The number of" correctly refers to a specific total; here the noun phrase is fully determined and grammatical.

Tip: Contrast a number of (several) with the number of (the total count).

TRUE — "A knowledge of" is an accepted pattern when knowledge is limited to a field: "a knowledge of Portuguese."

Tip: Some abstracts allow a when followed by of + field.

TRUE — Zero-article "knowledge of" is equally natural for the same idea.

Tip: Both a knowledge of and knowledge of can be correct; meaning stays general-competence.

TRUE — Countable "rise" correctly takes "a" for a newly mentioned increase: "a rise in visitors."

Tip: Singular countable nouns need a determiner in this slot.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch fixed frames such as a number of versus the number of, and notice when abstracts optionally take a before of-phrases. Singular countables like rise still need a determiner.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Next week we will finalise the festival programme.
The next week we will finalise the festival programme.
In 1990s many families still relied on paper maps.
In the 1990s many families still relied on paper maps.
On Monday morning the team packs for the match.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Time expressions like "next week," "last year," and "this morning" take zero article in standard adverbial use.

Tip: next/last/this + time unit → usually zero.

FALSE — "The next week" is wrong in this future-plan adverbial; keep bare "next week."

Tip: Save the next for sequenced items inside a known series (the next slide), not for calendar next week.

FALSE — Decades need "the": "in the 1990s."

Tip: the + decade/century is the normal historical pattern.

TRUE — "In the 1990s" correctly includes the.

Tip: Same pattern for the 1800s, the twentieth century, etc.

TRUE — Days and parts of days used adverbially are often bare: "On Monday morning…"

Tip: on Monday / in summer / at night frequently take zero article.
tasks.solution_overview: Time phrases are highly patterned: next/last week stay bare, while decades and centuries take the. Do not import the into calendar adverbials where English expects zero.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She is in charge of costumes for the school play.
He was hit on head during the basketball practice.
They shook hands after settling the argument.
Please write the essay from beginning to the end carefully.
We need to keep the garden under control this summer.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "In charge of costumes" uses zero article before the functional area in this common pattern.

Tip: Many be/in + noun phrases freeze without a/the (in charge, in debt, in trouble).

FALSE — Body-contact idioms take possessive or the: "on the head" / "on his head," not bare "on head."

Tip: on the + body part is the usual set phrase after verbs like hit/pat.

TRUE — "Shake hands" is a fixed zero-article idiom.

Tip: Learn hands/arms/legs idioms as chunks; do not insert the automatically.

FALSE — The paired idiom is "from beginning to end" (both bare) or "from the beginning to the end"; mixing bare beginning with "the end" is inconsistent.

Tip: Keep both sides of a fixed pair parallel in determiner choice.

TRUE — "Under control" is a zero-article prepositional idiom.

Tip: under control / in progress / on schedule are typically bare.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced accuracy often means recognising idioms where determiner choice is frozen. Prefer the set phrase over building articles logically word by word.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Many hikers reached the ridge before sunset.
There is much enthusiasm for the weekend pottery class.
Much tourists queued outside the museum.
Few of the recipes needed special equipment.
We received little praise after the choir rehearsal.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Many" correctly quantifies the plural countable noun "hikers".

Tip: many + countable plural (hikers, tickets, songs).

TRUE — "Much" correctly quantifies the uncountable noun "enthusiasm".

Tip: much + uncountable (enthusiasm, praise, progress).

FALSE — "Tourists" is countable plural, so "much" is wrong; use "many tourists".

Tip: never pair much with a bare plural countable.

TRUE — "Few of" + plural countable is grammatical (here: few of the recipes).

Tip: few/a few work with countables; little/a little with uncountables.

TRUE — "Little" correctly quantifies uncountable "praise".

Tip: little = not much (uncountable); few = not many (countable).
tasks.solution_overview: This opener drills the core split: many/few with countables, much/little with uncountables. Scan each noun first—if it can take -s as a plural, avoid much and little.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The amount of litter on the beach has fallen since spring.
The number of cyclists has risen sharply.
The amount of cyclists has decreased this month.
A large number of neighbours joined the street clean-up.
There was a large amount of fog over the harbour.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Amount of" pairs correctly with uncountable "litter".

Tip: amount of + uncountable mass nouns.

TRUE — "Number of" pairs correctly with countable "cyclists" and takes singular "has".

Tip: the number of + plural noun → singular verb.

FALSE — "Cyclists" is countable; prefer "the number of cyclists," not "amount of".

Tip: amount → uncountable; number → countable.

TRUE — "A large number of" correctly introduces plural countable "neighbours".

Tip: a number of + plural usually takes a plural verb.

TRUE — "Amount of" correctly quantifies uncountable "fog".

Tip: fog, traffic, advice, and news are typically uncountable.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on amount versus number. If you can count the units (cyclists, neighbours), use number; if you measure a mass (litter, fog), use amount.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: All of the equipment is new.
The equipments in the lab need updating.
We bought three new pieces of equipment.
There are many evidences against the claim.
The evidence supports the detective's conclusion.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Uncountable "equipment" takes a singular verb ("is").

Tip: equipment never takes a plural -s in standard English.

FALSE — "Equipment" is uncountable; do not write "equipments".

Tip: use "pieces of equipment" when you need a count.

TRUE — "Pieces of equipment" is the correct count expression.

Tip: piece/item of + uncountable lets you count units.

FALSE — "Evidence" is uncountable; avoid "evidences" and "many evidences".

Tip: say "much evidence" or "several pieces of evidence".

TRUE — Uncountable "evidence" correctly takes a singular verb.

Tip: evidence, information, and research behave as singular masses.
tasks.solution_overview: Classic exam traps: equipment and evidence are uncountable. Count them only with piece/item of, and keep the verb singular when the noun is the subject.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Less information was available than we expected.
Fewer matches were cancelled this week.
Less noise was reported after the new windows arrived.
There is little doubt about the team's formation.
There is little doubt about the festival schedule.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Less" correctly pairs with uncountable "information".

Tip: less + uncountable; fewer + countable plural.

TRUE — "Fewer" correctly pairs with countable "matches".

Tip: if the noun is plural and countable, prefer fewer.

TRUE — "Noise" is uncountable, so "less noise" is the right pair.

Tip: less + mass nouns (noise, traffic, waste).

TRUE — "Little doubt" is the correct uncountable pattern with singular "is".

Tip: there is little + uncountable.

TRUE — Same pattern again: uncountable "doubt" with singular "is" and "little".

Tip: there is/are must match whether the noun is countable plural.
tasks.solution_overview: All five sentences are correct here: less/little with uncountables (information, noise, doubt) and fewer with countable matches. Use this set as a clean baseline before the later traps.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We still need much more data before we publish the survey.
How many volunteers attended the beach clean-up?
How much volunteers attended the beach clean-up?
Only a few bakers entered the pie contest.
Only a little bakers entered the pie contest.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Much" correctly quantifies uncountable "data" in careful exam English.

Tip: in exams, treat data as uncountable with much/little.

TRUE — "How many" correctly asks about countable people (volunteers).

Tip: how many + countable; how much + uncountable.

FALSE — "Volunteers" are people you can count; use "how many," not "how much".

Tip: if you could answer with a number of people, use many.

TRUE — "A few" correctly quantifies plural countable "bakers".

Tip: a few = some (positive); few = not many (negative tone).

FALSE — "Bakers" is countable plural; "a little" is reserved for uncountables.

Tip: a little flour / a few bakers.
tasks.solution_overview: Questions with how much/how many and the a few/a little contrast show up constantly. Decide whether the noun is a countable set of people/items or a mass quantity.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Much of the novel was unfinished.
Much of the novels was unfinished.
Many of the novels were unfinished.
Several of the chapters were cut.
A great deal of research has been published on sleep.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Much of" + singular unit ("the novel") is fine with singular "was".

Tip: much of the + singular noun ≈ a large part of it.

FALSE — With plural "novels," prefer "many of the novels were," not "much of … was".

Tip: much of + singular/mass; many of + plural.

TRUE — "Many of the novels were" correctly matches plural countable + plural verb.

Tip: of-phrases still need verb agreement with the counted noun.

TRUE — "Several" quantifies plural countable "chapters" with plural "were".

Tip: several always implies more than two countables.

TRUE — "A great deal of" pairs with uncountable "research" and singular "has".

Tip: a great deal of ≈ much; use with uncountables.
tasks.solution_overview: Of-phrases (much of / many of / several of) force you to look at the noun after of. Match the quantifier and the verb to that noun's countability and number.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She gave me some useful advice on the audition.
She gave me some useful advices on the audition.
We need more detailed information from the guide.
We need more detailed informations from the guide.
The news was announced after the match ended.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Advice" is uncountable; "some useful advice" is correct.

Tip: one piece of advice / some advice—never advices.

FALSE — Do not pluralise "advice" as "advices" in standard English.

Tip: count advice with piece(s) of advice.

TRUE — "Information" is uncountable and correctly used without -s.

Tip: information never takes a plural -s in exam English.

FALSE — "Informations" is ungrammatical; keep "information" uncountable.

Tip: bits/pieces of information if you need a count.

TRUE — "News" looks plural but is uncountable and takes singular "was".

Tip: the news is … (not are).
tasks.solution_overview: Advice, information, and news are high-frequency uncountables that learners over-pluralise. Keep them singular and use piece/bit of when you must count.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There is too much homework in this module.
There are too many homeworks in this module.
We have made little progress on the mural.
We have made few progress on the mural.
Only a little time remains before the concert starts.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Homework" is uncountable, so "too much" + singular "is" is correct.

Tip: much/little with mass nouns like homework and progress.

FALSE — "Homeworks" is not standard; keep "homework" uncountable.

Tip: if it feels like a pile of study work, treat it as a mass noun.

TRUE — "Little progress" correctly uses little with uncountable "progress".

Tip: progress is never "progresses" in this sense.

FALSE — "Progress" is uncountable, so "few" is wrong; use "little progress".

Tip: few needs a plural countable noun.

TRUE — "A little time" correctly quantifies uncountable "time".

Tip: a little = some (positive); little = not much (negative).
tasks.solution_overview: Mass nouns from everyday study and hobbies—homework, progress, time—take much/little, not many/few. Watch the positive "a little" versus the negative bare "little".

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Fewer runners than expected finished the half marathon.
Less runners than expected finished the half marathon.
The café used less sugar in the lemonade this summer.
The café used fewer sugar in the lemonade this summer.
There were fewer typos in the revised draft.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Runners" is countable plural, so "fewer" is the precise choice.

Tip: fewer people / fewer typos / fewer days.

FALSE — Prefer "fewer runners"; "less" with plural people is a common trap.

Tip: exams still reward fewer + countable plural.

TRUE — "Sugar" is uncountable here, so "less sugar" is correct.

Tip: less + sugar/time/space; fewer + spoons/hours/rooms when counted.

FALSE — "Sugar" as a mass noun takes "less," not "fewer".

Tip: fewer only works if the noun is plural and countable.

TRUE — "Typos" is countable plural, so "fewer typos" is correct.

Tip: if you can put a number in front, use fewer.
tasks.solution_overview: Less vs fewer is a classic trap. Count the noun: plural countables want fewer; mass quantities like sugar want less.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A large amount of evidence was presented in court.
A large number of evidence was presented in court.
Several pieces of evidence were disclosed yesterday.
The equipment have already been installed.
Most of the furniture was damaged in transit.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Amount of evidence" correctly treats evidence as uncountable with singular "was".

Tip: amount of + evidence/equipment/furniture.

FALSE — "Evidence" is not a countable plural; do not use "number of evidence".

Tip: number of + plural countables only.

TRUE — "Pieces of evidence" is the correct countable paraphrase with plural "were".

Tip: piece of unlocks counting for uncountables.

FALSE — "Equipment" is uncountable and needs singular "has," not "have".

Tip: all the equipment is … / has been …

TRUE — "Furniture" is uncountable and correctly takes singular "was".

Tip: furniture, luggage, and equipment share this pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Evidence, equipment, and furniture stay uncountable even when you mean several items. Use amount/pieces of, and keep agreement singular unless you count with piece/item.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There is not much time left to revise the essay.
There are not many times left to revise the essay.
We have plenty of chances to reschedule the picnic.
We have plenty of chancs to reschedule the picnic.
Hardly any of the guests supported the playlist change.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Uncountable "time" (duration) correctly pairs with "much" and singular "is".

Tip: not much time = little time remaining.

FALSE — "Times" changes the meaning awkwardly; for remaining duration use "much time," not "many times".

Tip: many times = frequency; much time = duration.

TRUE — "Plenty of" works with plural countable "chances".

Tip: plenty of works with both countables and uncountables.

FALSE — Spelling/count error: the plural is "chances," not "chancs".

Tip: watch irregular -y → -ies and silent-e plurals on countables.

TRUE — "Hardly any of" + plural countable is a natural negative quantifier pattern.

Tip: hardly any ≈ almost no/none.
tasks.solution_overview: Time as duration is uncountable (much time), while chances are countable. Negative quantifiers like hardly any still require the right noun type underneath.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A few of the students raised lighting concerns.
Few of the students raised lighting concerns, which surprised the tutor.
Little of the flour remains for the final batch.
A little of the flour remains for the final batch.
Few of the flour remains for the final batch.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "A few of" + plural countable correctly signals a small but real number.

Tip: a few = some (neutral/positive).

TRUE — Bare "few of" is grammatical and stresses scarcity (negative tone).

Tip: few vs a few is tone, not grammar—both need countables.

TRUE — "Little of" + uncountable "flour" correctly stresses almost none remains.

Tip: little of the + uncountable.

TRUE — "A little of" + uncountable is also grammatical and more positive (some remains).

Tip: a little = some; little = not much.

FALSE — "Flour" is uncountable here; "few of the flour" mixes few (countable) with a mass noun.

Tip: few of the bags/cups; little of the flour/milk.
tasks.solution_overview: A few/few and a little/little are all grammatical in the right environments—the trap is swapping them across the countable/uncountable line, especially with mass food nouns like flour.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of remote learners is increasing every year.
The number of remote learners are increasing every year.
A number of remote learners are requesting evening classes.
A number of remote learners is requesting evening classes.
The amount of remote learners is increasing every year.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "The number of" is a singular subject, so "is" is correct.

Tip: the number of + plural noun → singular verb.

FALSE — Do not use plural "are" after "the number of".

Tip: lock the verb to number (singular), not to learners.

TRUE — "A number of" means several and normally takes a plural verb.

Tip: a number of ≈ some/several → plural verb.

FALSE — With "a number of learners," prefer plural "are," not singular "is".

Tip: contrast the number (singular) vs a number (plural).

FALSE — "Learners" are countable people; use "number of," not "amount of".

Tip: amount of work; number of learners.
highlights: A number of remote learners are
A number of remote learners is
tasks.solution_overview: This task stacks two traps: the number vs a number (verb agreement) and amount vs number (countability). Read the determiner before "number," then check whether people should be counted with number at all.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Much of what the coach recommended has already been tried.
Many of what the coach recommended has already been tried.
None of the evidence points to intentional foul play.
None of the evidences point to intentional foul play.
Both of the equipment need replacing before the trip.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Much of what…" treats the content as an uncountable mass and takes singular "has".

Tip: much of what / much of the advice → singular.

FALSE — "What the coach recommended" is not a plural countable set; "many of what" is unnatural.

Tip: many of those drills / many of the tips.

TRUE — "None of the evidence" with uncountable evidence commonly takes singular "points".

Tip: none of + uncountable → singular verb in careful formal English.

FALSE — "Evidences" is wrong; keep evidence uncountable.

Tip: none of the evidence / none of the pieces of evidence.

FALSE — "Equipment" is uncountable, so "both of the equipment" fails; say "both pieces of equipment".

Tip: both needs two countable units.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced of-phrases: much of what…, none of the evidence, and both… only work when the noun after of can be counted the way the quantifier requires.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We have received a great deal of positive feedback.
We have received a great number of positive feedback.
There was a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.
There were a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.
Only a small proportion of listeners chose the jazz option.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "A great deal of" correctly quantifies uncountable "feedback".

Tip: a great deal of ≈ much.

FALSE — "Feedback" is uncountable; "a great number of feedback" is wrong.

Tip: a great number of comments/emails; a great deal of feedback.

TRUE — "Quantity of" with a mass noun and singular "was" is correct.

Tip: quantity/amount often take singular agreement with mass nouns.

FALSE — Singular "quantity" as subject takes "was," not "were".

Tip: there was a large quantity of …

TRUE — "Proportion of" + plural countable "listeners" is a standard survey quantifier.

Tip: proportion/percentage of + plural noun is common in reports.
tasks.solution_overview: Deal/number/quantity/proportion look similar but select different noun types and verb forms. Match the head noun's countability, then agree the verb with the quantifier phrase.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Research shows that morning light can improve alertness.
Researches show that morning light can improve alertness.
Several researches have confirmed the same pattern.
Several studies have confirmed the same pattern.
A piece of research published last year challenged the consensus.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Uncountable "research" correctly takes singular "shows".

Tip: research is / research shows …

FALSE — Do not pluralise academic "research" as "researches" in this sense.

Tip: use studies/projects when you need a plural countable.

FALSE — "Several researches" is unidiomatic; prefer "several studies" or "several research projects".

Tip: several needs a countable plural.

TRUE — "Studies" is the countable counterpart you need after "several".

Tip: research (mass) vs studies (count).

TRUE — "A piece of research" is an acceptable count expression for one study.

Tip: piece of research / item of research in formal prose.
tasks.solution_overview: Research behaves like evidence: keep it uncountable, switch to studies when you need several, or use a piece of research for a single unit.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Far fewer runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.
Far less runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.
Considerably less clutter is left after the spring clean.
Considerably fewer clutter is left after the spring clean.
There has been far too much gossip and far too few facts.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Far fewer" intensifies fewer with countable "runners".

Tip: far/much/considerably can modify fewer/less.

FALSE — Plural countable "runners" needs "fewer," not "less".

Tip: far fewer people; far less interest.

TRUE — "Considerably less clutter" correctly uses less with uncountable clutter.

Tip: intensifiers do not change the countable rule.

FALSE — "Clutter" is uncountable, so "fewer clutter" is wrong.

Tip: fewer boxes; less clutter.

TRUE — Parallel contrast: much + uncountable gossip; few + countable facts.

Tip: mixed quantifiers in one sentence still obey each noun's type.
tasks.solution_overview: Intensifiers (far, considerably, too) dress up the same less/fewer and much/few choices. Strip the adverb and decide from the noun alone.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Each item of equipment must be labelled before the hike.
Each equipment must be labelled before the hike.
No further evidence is required at this stage.
No further evidences are required at this stage.
A substantial amount of sunlight has already flooded the atrium.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Item of equipment" correctly creates a countable unit after "each".

Tip: each needs a singular countable noun.

FALSE — "Each equipment" fails because equipment is uncountable.

Tip: each piece/item of equipment.

TRUE — "Evidence" stays uncountable with singular "is".

Tip: no further evidence is …

FALSE — Avoid plural "evidences" and the plural verb that follows it.

Tip: further pieces of evidence if you insist on counting.

TRUE — "Amount of sunlight" treats sunlight as an uncountable mass with singular "has".

Tip: sunlight, rainwater, and fog often behave as uncountables.
tasks.solution_overview: Determiners like each and no further expose uncountable nouns quickly. If the determiner demands a countable unit, insert piece/item of before equipment or evidence.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Scarcely any of the luggage was recovered after the delay.
Scarcely any of the luggages were recovered after the delay.
A surprising number of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.
A surprising amount of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.
Too little attention has been paid to hydration on long walks.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Luggage" is uncountable; "scarcely any of the luggage was" is correct.

Tip: luggage/baggage like furniture: no plural -s.

FALSE — "Luggages" is non-standard; keep luggage uncountable with singular agreement.

Tip: pieces of luggage if you need a count.

TRUE — "Criteria" is plural; "a surprising number of the criteria were" matches countability and plural verb.

Tip: criterion (singular) / criteria (plural).

FALSE — Prefer "number of the criteria"; amount is for mass nouns, not plural criteria.

Tip: amount of inconsistency; number of criteria.

TRUE — "Too little attention" correctly uses little with uncountable attention.

Tip: little attention / much attention; few comments.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixes luggage (uncountable) with criteria (plural countable) and attention (uncountable). Identify each head noun's class before choosing any/number/amount/little.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The jury found insufficient evidence to convict.
The jury found insufficient evidences to convict.
There remains a large number of unresolved questions in the chapter.
There remains a large amount of unresolved questions in the chapter.
Fewer than ten percent of the equipment have been calibrated.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Insufficient evidence" correctly keeps evidence uncountable.

Tip: sufficient/insufficient + uncountable evidence/information.

FALSE — "Evidences" is wrong in this legal/academic sense.

Tip: insufficient pieces of evidence if counting is required.

FALSE — "A large number of unresolved questions" is plural in sense, so prefer "there remain," not singular "remains".

Tip: there remain + plural; there remains + singular/mass.

FALSE — "Questions" are countable, so "amount of unresolved questions" is off, and singular "remains" still clashes.

Tip: number of questions remain; amount of uncertainty remains.

FALSE — Double error: equipment is uncountable (not "fewer than ten percent of the equipment have"); prefer "less than ten percent of the equipment has been calibrated" or "fewer than ten pieces of equipment have…".

Tip: percent of + uncountable → singular; fewer needs countable units.
tasks.solution_overview: The hardest set combines evidence, number vs amount, there remain(s), and percent-of agreement with equipment. Resolve countability first, then force verb agreement to follow.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.
My sister's flat is larger than mine.
Of the three trails, this path is the worse.
The new bus stop is closer than the old one.
She sings more better than she did at the school concert.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Heavier" already marks the comparative, so "more heavier" doubles the form. Write "heavier" alone.

Tip: Drop "more" when the adjective already ends in -er.

TRUE — One-syllable "large" correctly takes -er: "larger than".

Tip: Short adjectives usually add -er, not "more."

FALSE — Ranking among three trails needs the superlative "worst," not the comparative "worse."

Tip: Of three or more → -est / worst / best; of two → -er / worse / better.

TRUE — One-syllable "close" correctly forms "closer than" for a two-item comparison.

Tip: Two things → comparative; a whole group → superlative.

FALSE — "Better" is already comparative; "more better" is a double mark. Use "better" alone.

Tip: Never stack "more" with an irregular comparative.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan each sentence for how comparison is marked. Watch for double forms (more + -er) and check whether you need a comparative (two items) or a superlative (a group). Irregulars like better/worse already carry the meaning — do not add "more."

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Among the five bakeries on the high street, Miller's has the freshest bread.
That soup tastes gooder than the one from yesterday.
The evening train was quieter than the morning service.
This novel is more interesting than the film adaptation.
It was the most coldest winter walk we have ever taken.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Freshest" correctly ranks one bakery among five.

Tip: Use -est / most when ranking inside a group of three or more.

FALSE — The irregular comparative of "good" is "better," not "gooder."

Tip: Memorise good → better → best; never invent -er on irregulars.

TRUE — Two-syllable "quiet" correctly takes -er: "quieter."

Tip: Many short adjectives use -er / -est rather than more / most.

TRUE — Multi-syllable "interesting" correctly takes "more … than."

Tip: Longer adjectives prefer more/most, not -er/-est.

FALSE — "Coldest" is already a superlative; "most coldest" doubles it. Use "the coldest."

Tip: Never pair "most" with an -est form.
tasks.solution_overview: Check whether the adjective needs -er/-est or more/most, and whether any irregular (good/better/best) is mangled. Double superlatives like "most coldest" are always wrong.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is more taller than his twin brother.
Of all the desserts, this tart is the less sweet.
Her explanation was clearer than the textbook chapter.
The weekend weather turned more worser after noon.
My laptop runs gooder after the software update.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Taller" already includes the comparative; delete "more."

Tip: more + -er is never needed.

FALSE — Ranking among all desserts needs "the least sweet," not "the less sweet."

Tip: less = comparative (two); least = superlative (a group).

TRUE — Two-syllable "clear" commonly takes -er: "clearer than."

Tip: Many clear-type adjectives accept -er as well as more.

FALSE — "Worse" is already comparative; "more worser" piles two errors. Use "worse."

Tip: bad → worse → worst; never add more or -er.

FALSE — Replace "gooder" with "better."

Tip: good / better / best is fixed — no homemade forms.
tasks.solution_overview: This set stacks the beginner traps: double marking, less vs least, and broken irregulars. Fix the comparison word first, then check whether the sentence compares two things or ranks a whole set.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Today's quiz was easier than Monday's.
She chose the most cheap ticket available online.
Our garden is smaller than the neighbour's.
This playlist is the best of the three we built.
The museum was more farther from the hotel than we expected.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Easy" correctly becomes "easier" (y → i + -er).

Tip: Consonant + y adjectives change y to i before -er/-est.

FALSE — One-syllable "cheap" takes "cheapest," not "most cheap."

Tip: Prefer -est on short adjectives unless the form sounds awkward.

TRUE — "Smaller than" is the standard comparative for "small."

Tip: Double the final consonant when needed (big → bigger), but "small" simply adds -er.

TRUE — "The best of the three" correctly uses the irregular superlative for a set of three.

Tip: good → better → best.

FALSE — "Farther/further" is already comparative; do not add "more." Use "farther/further … than."

Tip: Irregulars never take an extra "more."
tasks.solution_overview: Confirm spelling of -er forms, avoid "most" on short adjectives that want -est, and leave irregulars like best and farther alone — they do not need "more."

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This curry is spicier than the mild version on the menu.
Between the two coats, the wool one is the warmest.
She felt worse after skipping breakfast.
Of the four rooms, the attic is the more quiet.
His second attempt was better than the first.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Spicy" correctly forms "spicier" for a two-item food comparison.

Tip: -y adjectives → -ier / -iest.

FALSE — With only two coats, use the comparative "warmer," not the superlative "warmest."

Tip: Between two → comparative; among many → superlative.

TRUE — "Worse" is the correct irregular comparative of "bad/ill."

Tip: bad/ill → worse → worst.

FALSE — Ranking four rooms needs "the quietest" (or "the most quiet"), not "the more quiet."

Tip: Superlative for a group of three or more.

TRUE — "Better than" correctly compares two attempts.

Tip: Two items → better; a whole group → best.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on the two-versus-many rule. "Between the two" almost always wants a comparative, while "of the four" wants a superlative. Keep irregular worse/better clean.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The kitchen looked tidier after we cleared the counter.
This café is more popular than the one by the river.
My phone battery lasts longer than yours.
She bought the least expensive bike in the shop.
He runs more faster in the evenings than in the mornings.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Tidy" correctly becomes "tidier" after a clear-up.

Tip: consonant + y → -ier.

TRUE — Multi-syllable "popular" correctly takes "more … than."

Tip: Three-syllable adjectives almost always use more/most.

TRUE — "Longer than" correctly compares battery life for two phones.

Tip: Duration often uses long / longer / longest.

TRUE — "The least expensive" correctly ranks cost among many bikes.

Tip: least + adjective = superlative of inferiority.

FALSE — "Faster" already marks the comparative; delete "more."

Tip: Adverbs formed with -er also reject an extra "more."
tasks.solution_overview: Most sentences here are clean models. The one clear fault is stacking "more" on an -er adverb. Treat least + adjective as the standard way to rank "smallest amount of" a quality.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The river is deeper here than near the bridge.
Of the two recipes, this one is the simplest.
Their dog is friendlier than ours.
She felt more happier after the phone call.
This is the worst film I have seen all year.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Deeper than" correctly compares two stretches of the river.

Tip: One-syllable adjectives take -er for two-item contrasts.

FALSE — Only two recipes → use "simpler," not the superlative "the simplest."

Tip: Of/between two → comparative.

TRUE — "Friendly" correctly forms "friendlier" ("more friendly" is also acceptable).

Tip: -y adjectives commonly take -ier.

FALSE — "Happier" already includes the comparative; remove "more."

Tip: happy → happier → happiest.

TRUE — "The worst" is the correct irregular superlative.

Tip: bad → worse → worst.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch "of the two" — that phrase almost always blocks a superlative. Keep -ier spelling tidy and leave irregular worst alone.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The second episode was less exciting than the pilot.
He is the elder of the two cousins.
This rucksack is bigest than I need for a day hike.
Among her hobbies, pottery is the most relaxing.
We walked further than planned before turning back.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Less exciting than" correctly compares two episodes with a longer adjective.

Tip: less + adjective + than = comparative of inferiority.

TRUE — "Elder" is a traditional comparative used for people in a family pair; "the elder of the two" is fine.

Tip: elder/eldest mainly for family; older/oldest for general age.

FALSE — Spelling and form fail: write "bigger than," not "bigest than."

Tip: big → bigger → biggest (double g); and use comparative with than.

TRUE — "The most relaxing" correctly ranks one hobby among several.

Tip: -ing adjectives of three syllables take most.

TRUE — "Further than" is a standard irregular comparative of distance/extent.

Tip: farther/further both work for physical distance in modern English.
tasks.solution_overview: This set adds less + adjective, family elder, and the spelling trap big → bigger. Read than-clauses carefully: they want a comparative, not a mangled superlative spelling.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This tea is as strong as the one from the market stall.
Her handwriting is as neat than her brother's.
The park feels as peaceful as it did in spring.
He is not as tall as his older sister.
The sequel was as good than the original.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Equality uses "as + adjective + as."

Tip: as … as compares sameness, not ranking.

FALSE — After "as neat" you need "as," not "than": "as neat as."

Tip: than belongs with comparatives; as … as marks equality.

TRUE — "As peaceful as" correctly states equal calm.

Tip: Keep both as-markers; dropping the second one breaks the pattern.

TRUE — "Not as tall as" is the standard negative equality pattern.

Tip: not as … as ≈ less … than in everyday meaning.

FALSE — Replace "than" with "as": "as good as the original."

Tip: Never mix as … than.
tasks.solution_overview: Equality comparisons live in the as … as frame. If you see than after as + adjective, the sentence is wrong — swap than for the second as.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She drives much more carefully than she did last year.
This bag is far heavier than it looks.
The climb was a lot more harder than the map suggested.
He speaks English better than I expected.
They arrived slightly earlier than the others.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Intensifier "much" correctly strengthens "more carefully."

Tip: much / far / a lot can boost comparatives.

TRUE — "Far heavier" correctly intensifies a short comparative.

Tip: far + -er is natural and strong.

FALSE — "A lot more harder" doubles the comparative. Use "a lot harder" or "much harder."

Tip: Intensifiers sit before one comparative form, not two.

TRUE — "Better than" correctly compares performance; "I expected" is a fine clause after than.

Tip: Irregular better needs no "more."

TRUE — "Slightly earlier" correctly softens the comparative of "early."

Tip: slightly / a bit / rather can modify comparatives.
tasks.solution_overview: Intensifiers (much, far, a lot, slightly) are fine before a single comparative. They become wrong the moment they sit beside a second comparative marker such as more + -er.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Prague is one of the most beautiful cities I have visited.
She is one of the smarter students in the class.
This is one of the best meals we have cooked at home.
He is one of the tallest player on the team.
That was one of the funnier jokes in the show.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "One of the most + adjective + plural noun" is the correct pattern.

Tip: one of the + superlative + plural.

FALSE — After "one of the" you need a superlative: "one of the smartest students."

Tip: one of the blocks ordinary comparatives.

TRUE — "One of the best meals" correctly pairs irregular superlative with plural.

Tip: best / worst fit the same frame.

FALSE — "One of" requires a plural noun: "one of the tallest players."

Tip: one of + plural always.

FALSE — Use the superlative: "one of the funniest jokes."

Tip: Comparative -er forms do not follow "one of the."
highlights: one of the most beautiful cities
tasks.solution_overview: Remember the fixed frame: one of the + superlative + plural noun. Comparatives and singular nouns after "one of" are the usual exam traps.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The more she practised, the more confident she became.
The harder he trained, the better his times got.
More she waited, more anxious she felt.
The less we argued, the happier the evening felt.
The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "The more …, the more …" correctly links two parallel comparatives.

Tip: Keep "the" before each comparative in this pattern.

TRUE — Mixed forms work: "the harder …, the better …"

Tip: -er and irregular comparatives both fit the frame.

FALSE — Restore the articles: "The more she waited, the more anxious she felt."

Tip: Dropping "the" breaks the correlative comparative.

TRUE — "The less …, the happier …" is a valid inferiority pair.

Tip: less / fewer can lead the first half.

TRUE — "The sooner …, the cheaper …" is a classic fixed double comparative.

Tip: Time and cost often appear in this pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Correlative comparatives need "the + comparative" in both halves. If either "the" disappears, rebuild the sentence before you mark it true.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She paints more skilfully than anyone else in the club.
He finished the puzzle quicker than I did.
Please speak more slow so I can follow the recipe.
The choir sang better last night than at the rehearsal.
They danced more graceful than the other couple.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "More skilfully" correctly forms the comparative of a -ly adverb.

Tip: Long adverbs take more/most, not -er.

TRUE — "Quicker" (or "more quickly") is acceptable in modern usage for manner here.

Tip: Short adverb comparatives often allow -er in everyday English.

FALSE — Use "more slowly," not "more slow," when modifying the verb speak.

Tip: Adjective slow ≠ adverb slowly.

TRUE — "Better" correctly compares how they sang on two occasions.

Tip: well → better → best (adverb).

FALSE — Manner needs "more gracefully," not the adjective "graceful."

Tip: After danced/spoke/sang, prefer adverb forms.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate adjective and adverb comparison. When the word modifies a verb (speak, dance, sing), you usually need an adverb comparative — more slowly / more gracefully / better — not a bare adjective.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This jacket is superior than the one I bought last winter.
Her design is inferior to the earlier sketch.
Fresh pasta is preferable to the dried kind for this sauce.
The coastal path is preferable than the inland route.
His answer was different from mine.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Latinate "superior" pairs with "to," not "than": "superior to."

Tip: superior / inferior / preferable → to.

TRUE — "Inferior to" is the correct fixed comparative-like pattern.

Tip: Do not rewrite these with -er forms.

TRUE — "Preferable to" correctly states a preference between two options.

Tip: preferable to = better as a choice than.

FALSE — Replace "than" with "to": "preferable to the inland route."

Tip: Preferable never takes than.

TRUE — "Different from" is the standard British exam form.

Tip: Treat different from as safe in exams.
tasks.solution_overview: Some comparison words never take than. Superior, inferior, and preferable lock to "to." Learn those fixed prepositions separately from ordinary -er / more patterns.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There were fewer people at the market than on Saturday.
We had less time than we needed to catch the ferry.
She made less mistakes on the second draft.
He drinks less coffee than he used to.
There is fewer traffic on this road after nine.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Fewer people" correctly uses fewer with a countable plural.

Tip: fewer + countable; less + uncountable.

TRUE — "Less time" correctly pairs with uncountable time.

Tip: time, money, traffic, and advice usually take less.

FALSE — "Mistakes" is countable; write "fewer mistakes."

Tip: If you can count them, prefer fewer in careful English.

TRUE — "Less coffee" correctly treats coffee as an uncountable amount.

Tip: less + mass noun.

FALSE — "Traffic" is uncountable; use "less traffic," not "fewer traffic."

Tip: fewer needs a plural countable noun.
tasks.solution_overview: Less and fewer are comparative quantity words. Decide first whether the noun is countable plural or an uncountable mass, then pick fewer or less.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: My week got busier and busier as the festival approached.
The music grew more and more louder near the stage.
The waves became higher and higher before the storm.
She felt worse and worse during the long flight.
The puzzle grew increasingly more difficult toward the end.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Busier and busier" correctly shows gradual increase with a repeated comparative.

Tip: Adj-er and adj-er = steadily more.

FALSE — "More and more louder" doubles the marking. Use "louder and louder" or "more and more loud."

Tip: Pick one comparative system and stick to it.

TRUE — "Higher and higher" correctly intensifies a short comparative.

Tip: Repeat the -er form for gradual change.

TRUE — "Worse and worse" correctly repeats the irregular comparative.

Tip: Irregulars can double the same way: better and better, worse and worse.

FALSE — "Increasingly" already means "more and more," so "increasingly more difficult" is redundant. Prefer "increasingly difficult" or "more and more difficult."

Tip: Do not stack increasingly with more.
tasks.solution_overview: Gradual-change patterns either repeat one comparative (louder and louder) or use more and more + base adjective. Mixing systems — or adding increasingly to more — creates double marking.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No other beach on the island is as clean as this one.
This hostel is cheaper than any other place we checked.
She is taller than any girl in her class.
This route is the shortest of any other path to the lake.
He plays the piano better than anyone else in the family.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "No other … as … as" correctly sets up a unique equality comparison.

Tip: no other + as … as ≈ this is the cleanest.

TRUE — "Cheaper than any other" correctly excludes the rest of the set.

Tip: any other keeps the compared item outside the group.

FALSE — Include herself out of the group: "taller than any other girl" (or "anyone else").

Tip: Without other/else, the sentence oddly includes her in "any girl."

FALSE — Do not mix "the shortest" with "of any other." Prefer "the shortest path" or "shorter than any other path."

Tip: Superlative and "any other" usually fight each other.

TRUE — "Better than anyone else" correctly uses else to exclude him.

Tip: else / other prevents logical self-comparison.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced comparison often hinges on exclusion words: other and else. Without them, a person can be compared with a group that still includes that person — a classic logic trap.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I prefer walking to cycling when the weather is mild.
She prefers tea than coffee in the morning.
They would rather stay in than go out tonight.
He would rather to leave early than miss the last train.
We prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Prefer A to B" is the standard comparative preference pattern.

Tip: prefer + noun/gerund + to + noun/gerund.

FALSE — Prefer takes "to," not "than": "prefers tea to coffee."

Tip: prefer … than is almost always wrong.

TRUE — "Would rather … than …" correctly contrasts two base-verb options.

Tip: would rather + bare infinitive + than + bare infinitive.

FALSE — After "would rather" use the bare infinitive: "would rather leave," not "would rather to leave."

Tip: Delete to after would rather.

TRUE — "Prefer … rather than …" is an accepted alternative to prefer … to … with parallel -ing forms.

Tip: Keep the two sides parallel (cooking / ordering).
tasks.solution_overview: Preference structures are cousins of comparatives: prefer A to B, and would rather A than B. Watch the preposition (to, not than) and the bare infinitive after would rather.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The new café is nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be.
This trail is not nearly as steep than the guidebook claimed.
Her second cake was twice as large as the first.
The second half was half as long than the opening act.
Today feels slightly less humid than yesterday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Nowhere near as … as" correctly intensifies a negative equality comparison.

Tip: nowhere near as / not nearly as + adjective + as.

FALSE — Keep the as … as frame: "not nearly as steep as …," not "than."

Tip: Intensifiers do not change the need for a second as.

TRUE — "Twice as large as" correctly multiplies an equality comparison.

Tip: twice / three times + as + adjective + as.

FALSE — Write "half as long as," not "half as long than."

Tip: Multipliers still need as … as.

TRUE — "Slightly less humid than" correctly softens a comparative of inferiority.

Tip: less + adjective + than remains available beside as … as patterns.
tasks.solution_overview: Scaled equality (twice as, half as, not nearly as, nowhere near as) still needs a closing as. Than only returns when you switch to a true comparative such as less … than.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit.
She is by far the most organised person in our flatshare.
This crossword is much the harder I have tried this month.
He is easily the funniest host on the late-night shows.
That was by far a better concert than the one in March.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Of all … the freshest" correctly pairs a group phrase with a superlative.

Tip: of all / among all → superlative.

TRUE — "By far the most organised" correctly intensifies a superlative.

Tip: by far / easily / much the + superlative.

FALSE — With "much the," use a superlative: "much the hardest," not "much the harder."

Tip: much the + -est / most …

TRUE — "Easily the funniest" correctly strengthens a superlative ranking.

Tip: easily the + superlative is common in speech and exams.

TRUE — "By far a better … than" can intensify a comparative when two concerts are compared.

Tip: by far works with both superlatives and clear two-item comparatives.
tasks.solution_overview: Final polish: intensifiers like by far, easily, and much the usually lock onto superlatives. If the sentence clearly compares only two items, a comparative after by far can still work — but "much the harder" is the wrong grade of comparison.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Despite the heavy rain, we finished the outdoor photography session.
Despite of the heavy rain, we finished the outdoor photography session.
Although the heavy rain, we finished the outdoor photography session.
Because the delay, the museum tour started twenty minutes late.
The picnic was cancelled owing a sudden thunderstorm.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Despite" takes a noun phrase directly, so "Despite the heavy rain" is well formed before the main clause.

Tip: If you can replace the linker with "in spite of," you almost always want a noun, not a full clause.

FALSE — Never write "despite of." Use "despite the heavy rain" or "in spite of the heavy rain."

Tip: "Despite of" is one of the most common exam traps — delete "of" on sight.

FALSE — "Although" needs a clause with a verb: "Although it rained heavily," not a bare noun phrase.

Tip: Ask "is there a finite verb after although?" If not, switch to despite / in spite of.

FALSE — "Because" introduces a clause; for a noun use "because of the delay" (or "Because there was a delay").

Tip: "Because" + noun is almost always wrong — insert "of" or rebuild as a full clause.

FALSE — The fixed pattern is "owing to" + noun: "owing to a sudden thunderstorm."

Tip: Treat "owing to" as one unit; if "to" is missing, the sentence fails.
tasks.solution_overview: This set checks whether you pick the right linker shape: noun after despite / because of / owing to, and a full clause after although / because. Read each connector and ask what kind of material follows it before you mark true or false.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of the crowded platform, Maya found a seat on the morning train.
Although the crowded platform, Maya found a seat on the morning train.
The trail was icy; however, the hikers still reached the summit café.
The trail was icy, however the hikers still reached the summit café without stronger punctuation.
The concert started late owing technical problems with the sound desk.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "In spite of" + noun phrase is the correct concessive pattern here.

Tip: "In spite of" and "despite" are interchangeable before a noun; neither takes a bare clause.

FALSE — "Although" needs a clause with a verb: "Although the platform was crowded…"

Tip: A noun after although is almost always a despite transplant — rewrite or switch linker.

TRUE — As a conjunctive adverb, "however" sits well after a semicolon (or full stop) between two independent clauses.

Tip: Semicolon / period + however + comma is the clean formal pattern.

FALSE — A bare comma before conjunctive "however" is weak or wrong in formal writing; prefer a semicolon or a new sentence.

Tip: If however could start a new sentence, do not glue it with only a comma.

FALSE — Restore the full linker: "owing to technical problems."

Tip: "Owing" without "to" is never complete in this pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast linkers come in two families: despite / in spite of (noun) versus although (clause), plus however between full sentences. Check punctuation around however and whether owing to is complete.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because of the closed bridge, cyclists took the riverside path instead.
Because the bridge was closed, cyclists took the riverside path instead.
Even though the recipe looked complicated, Leo baked the cake successfully.
Even though the complicated recipe, Leo baked the cake successfully.
Whereas the first half was quiet, the second half of the match was frantic.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Because of" + noun phrase correctly gives the reason.

Tip: Use because of before nouns; reserve bare because for clauses.

TRUE — "Because" + full clause is the other correct reason pattern.

Tip: If you already have subject + verb after because, do not add "of."

TRUE — "Even though" takes a clause, and "the recipe looked complicated" supplies one.

Tip: Even though ≈ although: both want finite clauses.

FALSE — "Even though" cannot take a noun phrase alone; write "even though the recipe looked complicated."

Tip: Swap even though → despite when only a noun follows.

TRUE — "Whereas" contrasts two full clauses cleanly.

Tip: Whereas needs clause + clause; "whereas a quiet first half" without a verb is wrong.
tasks.solution_overview: Cause and concession each have a clause form and a noun form. Match because / even though / whereas to clauses, and because of to nouns — that single check resolves most of these items.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Despite of repeated reminders, Nina forgot to water the balcony plants.
In spite the repeated reminders, Nina forgot to water the balcony plants.
Although Nina forgot to water the plants, they somehow survived the weekend.
The library was quiet because of a school holiday in the neighbourhood.
Tickets sold out early; however, a few returns appeared at the box office.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Drop "of": "Despite repeated reminders…"

Tip: Despite never partners with of; in spite always needs of.

FALSE — The full phrase is "in spite of," not "in spite" alone.

Tip: Remember the trio: despite / in spite of / although — learn the prepositions as fixed spelling.

TRUE — Although + clause correctly sets up the contrast with the main clause.

Tip: When the concessive idea has its own verb, although is usually safer than despite.

TRUE — Because of + noun phrase is the right causal linker here.

Tip: A school holiday is a noun phrase, so because of (not bare because) is required.

TRUE — Semicolon + however correctly joins two contrasting independent clauses.

Tip: Read however as a sentence adverb: it likes strong punctuation before it.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch the spelling pairs: despite (no of) versus in spite of (of required). Then confirm although and however are doing clause-level work with proper punctuation.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Owing to thick fog, the ferry crossing was postponed until noon.
Because of thick fog, the ferry crossing was postponed until noon.
Despite the fog lingering all morning, several walkers still set out.
Although the fog lingered all morning, several walkers still set out.
However, the coastal path remained closed for safety checks.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Owing to" + noun phrase correctly states the cause.

Tip: Formal notices often prefer owing to / because of before abstract nouns like fog.

TRUE — "Because of" + noun phrase is an equally correct causal pattern here.

Tip: Because of and owing to are near-interchangeable before nouns.

TRUE — Despite can take a gerund noun phrase ("the fog lingering all morning").

Tip: Despite + -ing phrase is fine; despite + finite clause usually is not.

TRUE — Although + finite clause ("lingered") is the clean concessive form.

Tip: If you can hear a tensed verb after although, the clause test usually passes.

TRUE — Sentence-initial "However," with a following comma correctly opens a contrast.

Tip: Starting with However is fine; just do not leave it mid-sentence with only a weak comma before it.
tasks.solution_overview: Here the traps sit in small words: the missing to after owing, and the wrong follow-on after although versus despite. Read the material after each linker as carefully as the linker itself.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rehearsal stopped because of a broken stage light.
The rehearsal stopped because a stage light was broken.
The rehearsal stopped because of a stage light was broken.
In spite of the broken light, the cast finished Act Two.
Whereas the lighting failed, the orchestra kept perfect timing.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Because of + noun phrase correctly explains the stoppage.

Tip: A broken stage light is a noun — because of fits.

TRUE — Because + clause is equally correct when you spell out subject + verb.

Tip: Both because and because of can be right; the grammar after them decides.

FALSE — Do not stack "because of" onto a full clause; drop "of" or rewrite the clause as a noun.

Tip: "Because of + subject + verb" is almost always a false hybrid.

TRUE — In spite of + noun phrase is the right concessive frame.

Tip: The broken light is a noun idea — in spite of / despite both work.

TRUE — Whereas contrasts two complete clauses about lighting versus the orchestra.

Tip: Use whereas for side-by-side contrasts, not for simple cause.
highlights: because of a stage light was
tasks.solution_overview: Cause linkers are easy until someone glues because of onto a whole clause. Check that after because of you only have a noun idea, and after because / whereas you have a real clause.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Despite the fact that the kitchen was tiny, they hosted a lively dinner.
Despite that the kitchen was tiny, they hosted a lively dinner.
Although the kitchen was tiny, they hosted a lively dinner.
The kitchen was tiny. However, the dinner still felt generous.
Space was limited however the hosts somehow seated twelve guests comfortably.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Despite the fact that" + clause is an accepted formal workaround when you need a clause after despite.

Tip: Prefer plain although when you can; despite the fact that is wordy but grammatical.

FALSE — "Despite that" + clause is non-standard in careful exam English; use although or despite the fact that.

Tip: If you want a clause, switch to although rather than forcing despite.

TRUE — Although + clause is the cleanest concessive choice here.

Tip: When both options work, although is usually shorter and safer than despite the fact that.

TRUE — A full stop before However correctly separates the contrasting sentences.

Tip: Period + However + comma is as strong as semicolon + however.

FALSE — Running however between clauses with no strong punctuation is incorrect in formal writing.

Tip: Never leave however floating between clauses with zero commas or stops.
tasks.solution_overview: Despite wants nouns; although wants clauses; however wants sentence-level punctuation. These five lines test those three habits in a dinner-party story.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Owing to a power cut, the cinema switched to an earlier screening.
Because of a power cut, the cinema switched to an earlier screening.
Although the power cut, the cinema switched to an earlier screening.
In spite of the power cut, the audience stayed in their seats.
Whereas the power cut, the audience stayed in their seats.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Owing to + noun correctly marks the cause of the schedule change.

Tip: Owing to and because of are near twins before nouns.

TRUE — Because of + noun is equally correct in the same slot.

Tip: Either linker works; do not mix them with although’s clause rule.

FALSE — Although needs "Although there was a power cut" or similar, not a bare noun.

Tip: Power cut is a noun — feed it to despite / because of / owing to instead.

TRUE — In spite of + noun correctly frames the concession.

Tip: Staying seated despite a power cut is a classic despite / in spite of pattern.

FALSE — Whereas requires a full clause, not a noun phrase.

Tip: Rewrite as "Whereas the power failed…" or switch to despite.
tasks.solution_overview: Same noun idea — the power cut — can follow owing to, because of, or in spite of, but not although or whereas. Let the linker dictate the grammar of what follows.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The experiment succeeded despite early doubts from the lab team.
The experiment succeeded in spite of early doubts from the lab team.
The experiment succeeded although early doubts from the lab team.
Early doubts were widespread; however, the results still matched the prediction.
Early doubts were widespread, the results however still matched the prediction with no change in word order.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Despite + noun phrase correctly expresses concession after the main clause.

Tip: Mid- or end-sentence despite is fine when a noun follows.

TRUE — In spite of mirrors despite before the same noun phrase.

Tip: Prefer one style consistently in a report; both are grammatical.

FALSE — Although cannot take "early doubts…" without a verb.

Tip: "Although the team had doubts" would repair it.

TRUE — Semicolon + however correctly contrasts doubts with the successful results.

Tip: Keep a comma after however in this pattern.

FALSE — Dropping however into the middle without proper clause punctuation makes the sentence clumsy and formally wrong here.

Tip: Put however at the clause edge with a semicolon or period, not as a loose insert.
tasks.solution_overview: Concession after a success statement usually wants despite / in spite of + noun. Although needs a clause, and however needs clear sentence boundaries — do not bury it mid-clause.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because of rising pollen levels, many runners skipped the morning jog.
Because pollen levels were rising, many runners skipped the morning jog.
Because of pollen levels were rising, many runners skipped the morning jog.
Even though pollen levels were high, a few athletes still trained outdoors.
Even though high pollen levels, a few athletes still trained outdoors.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Because of + noun phrase correctly states the reason.

Tip: Rising pollen levels behaves as a noun idea after because of.

TRUE — Because + finite clause is the matching clause form.

Tip: Keep because of and because as a clean pair: noun versus clause.

FALSE — Because of must not introduce a full clause with were.

Tip: If you see a tensed verb after because of, rewrite immediately.

TRUE — Even though + clause correctly marks concession.

Tip: Even though and although share the same clause requirement.

FALSE — Even though cannot take a bare noun phrase.

Tip: Switch to despite high pollen levels, or add a verb after even though.
tasks.solution_overview: Cause and concession swap partners easily: because of / despite take nouns; because / even though take clauses. Spot the hybrid "because of + were" and the bare noun after even though.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She kept painting, although her wrist ached after every session.
She kept painting despite her wrist ached after every session.
She kept painting in spite of her aching wrist.
Her wrist ached; she continued, however, with shorter sessions.
Her wrist ached, however she continued with shorter sessions using only a comma.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Although + finite clause correctly softens the contrast.

Tip: Pain + continued activity is a natural although pattern.

FALSE — Despite cannot take the finite clause "her wrist ached."

Tip: Use although, or "despite her aching wrist."

TRUE — In spite of + noun phrase is the correct concessive noun form.

Tip: Convert the clause idea into a noun (aching wrist) for in spite of / despite.

TRUE — Parenthetical however between commas correctly contrasts ache with persistence.

Tip: Mid-clause however with commas on both sides is allowed.

FALSE — However joining two clauses with only a preceding comma is a classic splice error.

Tip: Semicolon or period before however when it links full clauses.
tasks.solution_overview: This set contrasts clause linkers with noun linkers around the same idea, then checks two however patterns: legal parenthetical commas versus an illegal comma splice.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Owing to roadworks on the ring road, the coach arrived forty minutes late.
Owing roadworks on the ring road, the coach arrived forty minutes late.
Despite roadworks slowing traffic, several passengers still made their connections.
Although roadworks slowing traffic, several passengers still made their connections.
Whereas the outbound coach was late, the return journey ran on time.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Owing to + noun correctly explains the late arrival.

Tip: Travel notices often open with owing to + cause.

FALSE — Missing to: write "owing to roadworks."

Tip: Scan for orphan "owing" without "to."

TRUE — Despite + -ing phrase ("roadworks slowing traffic") is grammatical.

Tip: Despite + noun/-ing ≈ although + clause.

FALSE — Although needs a finite verb: "Although roadworks slowed traffic…"

Tip: "Although + -ing" without a clear subject is a frequent transfer error.

TRUE — Whereas contrasts two complete clauses about outbound versus return.

Tip: Whereas likes balanced clause pairs, not noun fragments.
tasks.solution_overview: Check owing to completeness, then decide whether an -ing phrase belongs after despite (yes) or after although (usually no). Whereas still demands two full clauses.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The choir performed well despite having had only two rehearsals that week.
The choir performed well although having had only two rehearsals that week.
Because of having only two rehearsals, the conductor shortened the programme.
Because having only two rehearsals, the conductor shortened the programme.
Having had only two rehearsals; however, the choir still sounded confident.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Despite + perfect gerund phrase correctly marks concession.

Tip: Despite + having (had) … is a polished formal pattern.

FALSE — Although needs a finite clause: "Although the choir had had only two rehearsals…"

Tip: Do not transplant a despite -ing phrase under although.

TRUE — Because of + gerund noun phrase correctly states the cause.

Tip: Because of can take -ing phrases that act like nouns.

FALSE — Bare because needs subject + verb, not a hanging -ing phrase.

Tip: Add of, or rewrite: "Because they had only two rehearsals…"

FALSE — A dangling -ing opener cannot be glued to however with only a semicolon in this broken shape; rebuild as two full clauses.

Tip: However still needs a proper independent clause before and after it.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced concession and cause often use -ing phrases. They fit after despite / because of, but not after bare although / because, and they cannot rescue a malformed however pair.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of what the guidebook claimed, the gallery was still closed on Mondays.
Despite what the guidebook claimed, the gallery was still closed on Mondays.
Although what the guidebook claimed, the gallery was still closed on Mondays.
The guidebook was outdated; the gallery, however, posted clear opening hours online.
The guidebook was outdated however the gallery posted clear opening hours online.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — In spite of + free relative ("what…") works because the what-clause acts as a noun.

Tip: What/how clauses can follow in spite of / despite / because of.

TRUE — Despite + the same what-clause is equally correct.

Tip: Despite and in spite of share this noun-like object pattern.

FALSE — Although needs an ordinary clause, not "although what…" without a verb frame.

Tip: Prefer "Although the guidebook claimed otherwise…"

TRUE — Parenthetical however between commas correctly contrasts outdated print with online hours.

Tip: Commas both sides signal parenthetical however, not a splice.

FALSE — No strong punctuation before however between two clauses.

Tip: Insert a semicolon or start a new sentence.
tasks.solution_overview: Wh-clauses behave like nouns after despite / in spite of, but although still wants a normal subject–verb clause. Pair that with a careful however punctuation check.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whereas most guests preferred the terrace, a few stayed indoors near the fireplace.
Despite most guests preferred the terrace, a few stayed indoors near the fireplace.
In spite of most guests preferring the terrace, a few stayed indoors near the fireplace.
Because of most guests preferring the terrace, the hosts moved the buffet outside.
Although most guests preferring the terrace, the hosts moved the buffet outside.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whereas + finite clause correctly opens a balanced contrast.

Tip: Whereas needs a tensed verb in each half of the contrast.

FALSE — Despite cannot take "most guests preferred…" as a finite clause.

Tip: Switch to although, or to "despite most guests preferring…"

TRUE — In spite of + -ing phrase correctly compresses the same idea.

Tip: Preferring turns the clause into a noun-like object for in spite of.

TRUE — Because of + -ing phrase correctly marks cause.

Tip: The same -ing phrase can serve cause (because of) or concession (in spite of).

FALSE — Although still needs "Although most guests preferred…" with a finite verb.

Tip: Final check on every although: find the tensed verb or mark false.
highlights: In spite of most guests preferring
tasks.solution_overview: One party detail — terrace versus indoors — is reshaped under five linkers. Name the linker, name what follows it, and the true/false call becomes mechanical.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of having little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.
Despite of having little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.
Although having little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.
Although he had little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.
Free time was scarce; however, the club rides still felt restorative.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — In spite of + having… correctly frames concession with a gerund.

Tip: Having + noun after in spite of / despite is a reliable pattern.

FALSE — Remove of: "Despite having little free time…"

Tip: Despite + -ing is fine; despite of + -ing is not.

FALSE — Although does not take a bare -ing phrase in careful formal English; add a subject + finite verb.

Tip: "Although having…" is a common L2 transfer error from despite.

TRUE — Although + full clause repairs the previous pattern.

Tip: Insert a clear subject (he / Sam) after although when in doubt.

TRUE — Semicolon + however correctly contrasts scarce time with the value of the rides.

Tip: Keep however’s comma after the linker.
tasks.solution_overview: Gerund concessions after in spite of / despite are elegant, but although still wants a full clause. Watch the fake "despite of" and the fake "although -ing" twins.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
