statements: The match resumed, owing to a brief break in the storm clouds.
The match resumed owing a brief break in the storm clouds.
A break in the clouds arrived; the pitch, however, remained too wet for play.
A break in the clouds arrived, however the pitch remained too wet for play with only a comma before however.
Despite a break in the clouds arriving, several seats in the stand stayed empty.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mid-sentence "owing to" + noun phrase correctly states the cause.

Tip: A comma before owing to is common when the cause follows the result.

FALSE — Missing to: write "owing to a brief break."

Tip: End-of-sentence owing still needs its to.

TRUE — Parenthetical however between commas correctly contrasts the break with the wet pitch.

Tip: Mid-clause however with commas is allowed when it does not join two bare clauses with a weak comma alone.

FALSE — Using however as a coordinator with only a preceding comma remains poor formal style.

Tip: Distinguish parenthetical however (commas both sides) from clause-joining however (semicolon/period).

TRUE — Despite + -ing phrase correctly marks concession.

Tip: "Despite X arriving" ≈ "although X arrived."
highlights: Despite a break in the clouds arriving
tasks.solution_overview: Harder however items distinguish parenthetical mid-clause use from illegal comma splices. Pair that with a clean owing to check and a despite -ing concession.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because of how abruptly the trail narrowed, the group slowed to single file.
Because how abruptly the trail narrowed, the group slowed to single file.
Although how abruptly the trail narrowed surprised the guides, nobody turned back.
In spite of how abruptly the trail narrowed, nobody turned back.
The trail narrowed abruptly. Owing to that change, the group slowed to single file.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Because of + free relative noun clause ("how abruptly…") is grammatical.

Tip: Wh-clauses can act as nouns after because of / despite / in spite of.

FALSE — Bare because needs a normal clause, not "because how…" without of.

Tip: If a how/what clause follows, you usually need because of, not bare because.

TRUE — Although + clause including "how abruptly…surprised" is fine.

Tip: Here the how-clause sits inside a larger finite clause — although is satisfied.

TRUE — In spite of + how-clause (noun-like) correctly marks concession.

Tip: In spite of how / despite what are polished formal patterns.

TRUE — Sentence-initial Owing to + noun correctly links to the prior change.

Tip: Pointing back with "that change" keeps owing to attached to a noun.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced items use how-clauses as noun objects of because of / in spite of. Bare because still wants an ordinary subject–verb clause — do not drop of before how.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Notwithstanding the delayed train, the friends still made the exhibition opening — and despite the same delay, they refused to skip the café stop.
Despite delayed trains, they reached the gallery; however, several rooms had already closed for cleaning.
Although delayed trains, they reached the gallery, however several rooms had already closed for cleaning.
Owing to the delayed train, they walked the last kilometre along the canal.
Because of delayed trains were overcrowded, they walked the last kilometre along the canal.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Despite + noun works in the second half; the sentence remains grammatical (notwithstanding sits outside the core trap set but does not break the despite use).

Tip: Focus on the despite + noun chunk — it is correctly formed.

TRUE — Despite + noun and semicolon + however are both well formed.

Tip: Stacking two contrast tools is fine if each obeys its own rule.

FALSE — Although lacks a clause, and however is joined with only a weak comma.

Tip: Two linker errors can hide in one sentence — check each separately.

TRUE — Owing to + noun correctly states the reason for walking.

Tip: Travel delays often pair with owing to in formal notices.

FALSE — Because of + finite clause is illegal; write "Because trains were delayed" or "Because of overcrowded delayed trains."

Tip: If a verb like were sits after because of, rewrite immediately.
tasks.solution_overview: Dense sentences may contain two linkers. Score each linker on its own rule — noun versus clause, and however’s punctuation — rather than judging the sentence by overall "feel."

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whereas membership rose at the community garden, weekend volunteering fell — a split that, however, the organisers refused to call a failure.
Despite membership rose at the community garden, weekend volunteering fell.
In spite of membership rising at the community garden, weekend volunteering fell.
Because of membership rising at the community garden, the organisers ordered more tools.
Although membership rising at the community garden, the organisers ordered more tools.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whereas opens a proper clause contrast, and parenthetical however is correctly set off with commas.

Tip: Parenthetical however does not replace a missing verb after whereas.

FALSE — Despite cannot take the finite clause "membership rose…"

Tip: Change to although, or to "despite the rise in membership."

TRUE — In spite of + -ing phrase correctly compresses the contrast.

Tip: Rising turns the clause idea into a noun-like phrase for in spite of.

TRUE — Because of + -ing phrase correctly marks cause.

Tip: Same -ing phrase can follow because of (cause) or in spite of (contrast).

FALSE — Although still needs "Although membership rose…" with a finite verb.

Tip: Final check on every although: find the tensed verb or mark false.
tasks.solution_overview: The last set mixes whereas, despite, in spite of, because of, and although around one community-garden story. Name the linker, name what follows it, and the true/false call becomes mechanical even at exam speed.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup was hot, spicy, and fragrant.
She likes hiking mountain trails and to swim in cold lakes.
Volunteers must arrive early, sign the register, and wearing a badge.
The guide was both patient and she explained every landmark.
He enjoys reading crime novels, sketching street scenes, and baking bread.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three adjectives share the same form after "was," so the list is parallel.

Tip: When listing qualities, keep each item the same part of speech.

FALSE — A gerund ("hiking") is paired with an infinitive ("to swim").

Tip: After likes, stay with -ing throughout: hiking… and swimming…

FALSE — Two bare infinitives after "must" are followed by a participle ("wearing").

Tip: Shared modals need the same bare form: wear, not wearing.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins an adjective to a full clause.

Tip: Match structures after both…and: both patient and clear.

TRUE — Three gerund phrases after "enjoys" stay in matching -ing form.

Tip: Prefer reading…, sketching…, and baking… rather than mixing with to-infinitives.
highlights: reading crime novels, sketching street scenes, and baking
tasks.solution_overview: Read each sentence as a list or a paired construction. Ask whether every item shares the same grammatical shape. Correlatives such as both…and are correct only when the two sides match.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The playlist mixed jazz standards, folk ballads, and indie rock.
Their weekend plan was to visit museums, trying new cafés, and walk along the river.
Maya is good at repairing bikes but weak in organising toolkits.
The course aims to build stamina, improve balance, and boosting confidence.
Tom likes watering the garden and pruning the hedges.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three noun phrases sit in the same pattern after "mixed."

Tip: Noun lists are parallel when each item is the same kind of noun phrase.

FALSE — An infinitive series is broken by the gerund "trying."

Tip: After "to," keep bare infinitives: visit, try, and walk.

TRUE — Adjective + preposition + gerund appears on both sides.

Tip: Parallel comparisons often reuse the same preposition pattern (at… / in…).

FALSE — The final item shifts from infinitives to a gerund ("boosting").

Tip: Finish the series with boost, not boosting.

TRUE — Two gerund phrases after "likes" match cleanly.

Tip: Prefer watering… and pruning… rather than mixing -ing with to-infinitives.
highlights: jazz standards, folk ballads, and indie rock
tasks.solution_overview: Check lists of nouns, infinitives, and gerunds one item at a time. A single mismatched form is enough to mark the sentence false, even if the meaning is clear.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The leaflet explains how to book a seat, how to print a ticket, and how to find the platform.
Ideal flatmates should be tidy, considerate, and pay rent on time.
The club both renovated the court and installed new lights.
Our goals are finishing homework early, sleeping enough, and to exercise daily.
The judge asked whether the answers were complete, accurate, and fair.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three matching "how to" phrases keep the instructions parallel.

Tip: Repeat how to before each step when the shared frame is "explains how to."

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a verb phrase ("pay rent").

Tip: Use three adjectives, or rewrite the third as punctual with rent.

TRUE — "Both…and" links two matching past-tense verb phrases.

Tip: Place the same kind of phrase after each half of the correlative.

FALSE — Two gerunds are paired with an infinitive ("to exercise").

Tip: Keep the -ing series: finishing, sleeping, and exercising.

TRUE — Three adjectives after "were" form a clean parallel list.

Tip: After a linking verb, adjective chains should stay adjectives throughout.
highlights: how to book a seat, how to print a ticket, and how to find
both renovated the court and installed
tasks.solution_overview: Watch for adjective lists that suddenly become verbs, and for goals written as mixed gerunds and infinitives. Keep the opening pattern through the last item.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The film was long, confusing, and it bored the audience.
She not only packed the tent but also checked the weather forecast.
Passengers must queue calmly, show their tickets, and to board in groups.
Cooking requires patience, practice, and a sharp knife.
He spends weekends repairing bikes, coaching juniors, and to race himself.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a full clause.

Tip: Use three adjectives: long, confusing, and dull.

TRUE — "Not only…but also" joins two matching past-tense verb phrases.

Tip: Keep the same verb shape after each half of the correlative.

FALSE — Two bare infinitives after "must" are followed by a to-infinitive.

Tip: After must, stay bare: board, not to board.

TRUE — Three noun phrases after "requires" sit in parallel.

Tip: Noun lists after requires/needs are usually the safest parallel choice.

FALSE — Two gerunds are paired with an infinitive ("to race").

Tip: Use racing himself to keep the -ing pattern.
highlights: not only packed the tent but also checked
patience, practice, and a sharp knife
tasks.solution_overview: Warm-up items mix adjective lists, correlatives, and shared modals. Name the first item's form, then reject any ending that cannot wear the same grammatical clothes.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hike was rewarding because of the views, because of the fresh air, and the group was cheerful.
Either leave your bags in the locker or carry them with you at all times.
The recipe calls for chopping the onions, frying the spices, and to simmer the sauce.
Spectators clapped loudly, whistled in rhythm, and waved homemade banners.
She wants a laptop that is light, that is quiet, and affordable.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "because of + noun" phrases are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use because of the cheerful group so every reason stays a noun phrase.

TRUE — "Either…or" joins two matching bare infinitives with the same subject.

Tip: Keep leave… or carry… — same subject, same verb form.

FALSE — Two gerunds after "calls for" are followed by an infinitive.

Tip: Finish with simmering the sauce to keep the gerund list.

TRUE — Three past-tense verb phrases describe the crowd in parallel.

Tip: Shared tense and subject make verb lists easy to keep balanced.

FALSE — Two "that is" relatives are followed by an adjective missing "that is."

Tip: Write that is affordable, or drop that is before all three.
highlights: clapped loudly, whistled in rhythm, and waved
tasks.solution_overview: Repeated subordinators and correlatives fail when the last branch changes shape. Check that because of, either…or, and that is appear consistently—or rewrite the whole list.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: By stretching carefully, by drinking water, and by resting between sets, he avoided injury.
The museum tour was informative, interactive, and we learned about local pottery.
Parents asked the coach to explain the drills, to demonstrate each move, and feedback after practice.
Neither the rain nor the wind stopped the outdoor market.
Her weekend routine involves cycling to the bakery, collecting the newspaper, and she waters the plants.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three matching "by + gerund" phrases form a parallel means list.

Tip: Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal list balanced.

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a clause.

Tip: Use three adjectives: informative, interactive, and memorable.

FALSE — Two infinitives after "asked…to" are followed by a noun phrase.

Tip: Add to give feedback after practice to keep the infinitive series.

TRUE — "Neither…nor" joins two matching noun phrases as a compound subject.

Tip: Keep both sides the same category: noun + noun, not noun + clause.

FALSE — Two gerunds are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use watering the plants so every item stays a gerund.
highlights: By stretching carefully, by drinking water, and by resting
Neither the rain nor the wind
tasks.solution_overview: Means lists with by + gerund and correlatives like neither…nor are clean when the pattern repeats. Trailing clauses after adjective or gerund pairs are the usual false marks here.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The role of team captain involves motivating players, planning practices, and attendance at matches.
We are looking for someone who can think clearly, act calmly, and speak kindly.
The prize will be used both to buy new books and decorating the reading corner.
His strengths are curiosity, humour, and solving puzzles quickly.
The committee voted to approve the mural, to hire a local artist, and to schedule the unveiling.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two gerunds are followed by a noun phrase ("attendance").

Tip: Use attending matches to keep the gerund pattern.

TRUE — Three bare infinitives after "can" form a matching series.

Tip: Shared modals (can/must/should) demand the same bare verb form each time.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins an infinitive to a gerund.

Tip: Both to buy… and to decorate…, or both buying… and decorating…

FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a gerund phrase.

Tip: Use quick puzzle-solving so all three items are nouns.

TRUE — Three infinitives after "voted to" stay in parallel.

Tip: Repeating "to" before each verb is optional but often clearer.
highlights: think clearly, act calmly, and speak
both to buy new books and decorating
to approve the mural, to hire
tasks.solution_overview: Duty lists and "both…and" often hide mixed nouns, gerunds, and infinitives. Convert every item into the same type before you judge the sentence true.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The campaign was effective in raising awareness, in recruiting helpers, and donations increased.
Applicants must either enclose a sketchbook or they submit a link to an online gallery.
The chef is known for bold flavours, neat plating, and generous portions.
We aim not only to finish the trail but also the photos for the blog.
The workshop taught participants to define goals, to map their route, and to pack a first-aid kit.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "in + gerund" phrases are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Keep the preposition pattern: in raising…, in recruiting…, and in increasing donations.

FALSE — "Either…or" joins a bare infinitive to a full clause with a new subject.

Tip: Either enclose a sketchbook or submit a link — same subject, same verb form.

TRUE — Three noun phrases follow "known for" in parallel.

Tip: After "for," noun lists are usually the safest parallel choice.

FALSE — "Not only…but also" joins an infinitive to a bare noun.

Tip: Not only to finish the trail but also to edit the photos — match both halves.

TRUE — Three infinitives after "taught…to" match cleanly.

Tip: Repeat "to" when it keeps each learning outcome equally weighted.
highlights: bold flavours, neat plating, and generous portions
to define goals, to map their route, and to pack
tasks.solution_overview: Correlatives fail when one side is a phrase and the other is a clause, or when one side has "to" and the other does not. Balance the two halves before you look at meaning.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The contest requires entrants to submit a photo, to write a short caption, and a signed consent form.
Whether by bus, by bike, or on foot, students must reach the hall by nine.
The renovation plan is ambitious, controversial, and it may stall.
She speaks fluently in Spanish, in Italian, and Portuguese.
The app can track sleep, count steps, and remind users to drink water.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two infinitives are followed by a noun phrase without "to provide/submit."

Tip: Add to include a signed consent form, or turn all three into nouns after "submit."

TRUE — Three prepositional routes stay parallel after "whether."

Tip: Keep the same preposition pattern (by… / by… / on…) when listing channels.

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a clause.

Tip: Use three adjectives: ambitious, controversial, and risky.

FALSE — "In" appears before the first two languages but not the third.

Tip: Repeat in before Portuguese, or drop in before all three.

TRUE — Three bare infinitives after "can" form a matching list.

Tip: Shared auxiliaries make parallel verb lists especially clear.
highlights: by bus, by bike, or on foot
track sleep, count steps, and remind
tasks.solution_overview: Missing repeated prepositions and trailing clauses after adjective pairs are subtler errors. Read the list aloud; an abrupt change of rhythm usually signals a break in form.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach argued that fitness was improving, that teamwork was stronger, and morale was high.
She prefers walking in the park to cycle along the busy ring road.
The festival offered live music, outdoor workshops, and free sketching materials.
Not only did they repair the roof, but they also painted the shutters.
His advice was to arrive early, sitting near the aisle, and leave during the interval.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "that" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "that."

Tip: Repeat that before morale was high.

FALSE — "Prefer A to B" needs matching forms; walking is paired with cycle.

Tip: Prefer walking… to cycling… (two gerunds).

TRUE — Three noun phrases after "offered" stay parallel.

Tip: Event programmes often list noun objects cleanly when nothing switches to a clause.

TRUE — Inverted "not only" is balanced by "but…also" with a parallel past-tense verb phrase.

Tip: Keep both predicates finite and matching after not only…but also.

FALSE — An infinitive series is broken by a gerund ("sitting").

Tip: Use to sit near the aisle to keep the infinitive pattern.
highlights: live music, outdoor workshops, and free sketching materials
tasks.solution_overview: Repeated that-clauses and prefer…to constructions need matching markers on every branch. Prefer A to B fails when one side is -ing and the other is a bare infinitive.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The notice forbids smoking indoors, bringing pets, and to leave bicycles in the hallway.
As much as she loves painting landscapes, she loves photographing them too.
The librarian asked whether the books were returned, whether fines were paid, and cards renewed.
He is neither interested in chess nor in collecting stamps.
To cook well, to plate neatly, and cleaning the kitchen quickly are all part of the shift.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two gerunds after "forbids" are followed by an infinitive.

Tip: Use leaving bicycles… so every banned action is a gerund.

TRUE — "As much as…" balances two matching "loves + gerund" clauses.

Tip: Correlative as much as often needs mirrored verb + complement patterns.

FALSE — Two "whether" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "whether."

Tip: Repeat whether before cards were renewed.

TRUE — "Neither…nor" joins two matching "in + gerund/noun" phrases after "interested."

Tip: Keep the same preposition after neither and nor.

FALSE — Two infinitive subjects are followed by a gerund subject.

Tip: Use to clean the kitchen quickly so all three subjects are infinitives.
highlights: As much as she loves painting
neither interested in chess nor in collecting
tasks.solution_overview: Verb bans, whether-chains, and infinitive subjects look fine until the last item switches form. Treat the first branch as a template and force every later branch to copy it.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The brochure promises clearer maps, shorter queues, and that tickets will be refundable.
Whether to reschedule the match, whether to move indoors, or cancelling altogether was debated for hours.
She left early because of a headache, because of the noise, and because her phone battery had died.
The trainer emphasised warming up properly, cooling down slowly, and drinking enough water.
His reply was polite, brief, and unexpectedly helpful.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Use refundable tickets as a third noun phrase.

FALSE — Two "whether to" infinitives are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Or whether to cancel altogether keeps the pattern.

FALSE — Two "because of + noun" phrases are followed by a because-clause.

Tip: Use because of a dead phone battery so every reason stays a noun phrase—or rewrite all three as clauses.

TRUE — Three gerund phrases after "emphasised" stay parallel.

Tip: Long gerund objects remain correct when every item is -ing + complement.

TRUE — Three adjectives after "was" form a clean parallel list.

Tip: Adverbs like unexpectedly can modify an adjective without breaking the list.
highlights: and that tickets will be refundable
warming up properly, cooling down slowly, and drinking
tasks.solution_overview: Mid-band items mix brochure-style noun lists with whether-to chains and mixed reason frames. Pick one frame—nouns, whether to, or because of—and hold it through every item.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success on the course depended not so much on raw talent as practising every evening.
The neighbours debated whether to plant hedges, whether to build a fence, or installing a gate.
House rules forbid leaving dishes overnight, borrowing tools without asking, and using the roof terrace after midnight.
Her weekend is as much about cooking for friends as it is about catching up on sleep.
The motion was neither seconded promptly nor was it discussed on the merits.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Not so much…as" joins "on + noun" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Not so much on raw talent as on practising every evening — repeat on.

FALSE — Two "whether to" infinitives are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Or whether to install a gate keeps the pattern.

TRUE — Three gerund phrases after "forbid" stay parallel.

Tip: Long gerund objects remain correct when every item is -ing + complement.

TRUE — "As much…as" balances two "about + gerund" ideas with matching "it is."

Tip: Correlative as much…as often needs mirrored about-phrases.

FALSE — "Neither…nor" joins a past participle phrase to an inverted clause.

Tip: Neither seconded promptly nor discussed on the merits — two past participles.
highlights: leaving dishes overnight, borrowing tools without asking, and using
as much about cooking for friends as it is about
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced correlatives (not so much…as, as much…as, whether to…) fail when the second half drops a preposition or switches to a different verb form. Match the scaffolding, not just the topic.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The flyer promises visitors free entry, guided tours, and that parking will be available nearby.
By labelling drawers clearly, by colour-coding folders, and by clearing the desk nightly, she found her keys faster.
The candidate was praised for how she handled questions, how she framed answers, and her closing thank-you.
We will either finish the quilt this weekend or postpone the sewing circle until Friday.
The rule requires that guests sign in, that they leave keys at reception, and bikes be locked outside.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Use nearby parking as a third noun phrase.

TRUE — Three matching "by + gerund" phrases form a parallel means list.

Tip: Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal list balanced.

FALSE — Two "how" clauses are followed by a noun phrase.

Tip: Add how she delivered her closing thank-you to keep the how-pattern.

TRUE — "Either…or" joins two matching bare infinitives after "will."

Tip: Shared will + either…or needs the same bare verb form on both sides.

FALSE — Two "that" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "that."

Tip: Repeat that before bikes be locked outside.
highlights: and that parking will be available
By labelling drawers clearly, by colour-coding
either finish the quilt this weekend or postpone
tasks.solution_overview: Flyer language and house rules often stack that-clauses. If that appears twice, the third clause almost always needs it too—or all three should be rewritten as nouns.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The strategy rests less on expensive kit than practising basic drills.
Not only did attendance rise in spring, but energy levels also improved.
Readers asked for a guide that is clear, that is illustrated, and useful without jargon.
The club prefers meeting outdoors on Saturdays and to convene indoors on rainy Sundays.
A solid packing list must specify what to wear, what to carry, and when to leave.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Less…than" joins "on + noun" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Less on expensive kit than on practising basic drills.

TRUE — Inverted "not only" is balanced by "but…also" with a parallel past-tense verb phrase.

Tip: Keep both predicates finite and matching after not only…but also.

FALSE — Two "that is" relatives are followed by an adjective missing "that is."

Tip: Write that is useful without jargon.

FALSE — A gerund ("meeting") is paired with an infinitive ("to convene").

Tip: Prefer meeting… and convening…, or to meet… and to convene…

TRUE — Three matching wh-infinitive phrases specify wear, carry, and leave.

Tip: Parallel wh-phrases are ideal for lists that must answer what and when.
highlights: what to wear, what to carry, and when to leave
tasks.solution_overview: Comparative frames (less…than) and relative-clause chains demand the same marker on every branch. When in doubt, rewrite the last item so it could replace the first without changing structure.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The flatshare rules cover quiet hours, shared cleaning, and guests must leave by eleven.
She trains both in the gym and when the weather allows outdoor runs.
The quiz tracked page views, session duration, and how long users stayed on each question.
To attract volunteers, to retain helpers, and to protect their time are shared priorities.
The teacher advised against skipping warm-ups, against ignoring form, and against rushing the last set.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun objects are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use an eleven o'clock guest curfew so every item stays a noun phrase.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins a prepositional phrase to a when-clause.

Tip: Both in the gym and in the park — two prepositional phrases.

FALSE — Two noun objects are followed by a how-clause.

Tip: Use question dwell time so all three metrics are noun phrases.

TRUE — Three infinitive phrases function as a parallel compound subject.

Tip: Infinitive subjects can be parallel when every infinitive carries the same role.

TRUE — Three matching "against + gerund" phrases follow "advised."

Tip: Repeating against before each gerund locks the parallel pattern.
highlights: and guests must leave by eleven
both in the gym and when
To attract volunteers, to retain helpers, and to protect
against skipping warm-ups, against ignoring form, and against rushing
tasks.solution_overview: House rules and tracking language mix nouns, infinitives, and clauses freely in drafts. Your job is to refuse that mixing: pick one frame and hold it through every item.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The recovery hinged not so much on longer rests as rebuilding confidence through light sessions.
Organisers debated whether to delay the start, whether to shorten the route, or cancelling the race.
Hostel rules forbid accepting strangers' parcels, soliciting room swaps, and using the roof terrace after midnight.
Her weekend is as much about rebuilding trust with neighbours as it is about catching up on sleep.
The complaint was neither acknowledged promptly nor was it investigated in full.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Not so much…as" joins "on + noun" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Not so much on longer rests as on rebuilding confidence — repeat on.

FALSE — Two "whether to" infinitives are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Or whether to cancel the race keeps the pattern.

TRUE — Three gerund phrases after "forbid" stay parallel.

Tip: Long gerund objects remain correct when every item is -ing + complement.

TRUE — "As much…as" balances two "about + gerund/noun" ideas with matching "it is."

Tip: Correlative as much…as often needs mirrored about-phrases.

FALSE — "Neither…nor" joins a past participle phrase to an inverted clause.

Tip: Neither acknowledged promptly nor investigated in full — two past participles.
highlights: accepting strangers' parcels, soliciting room swaps, and using
as much about rebuilding trust with neighbours as it is about
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced correlatives (not so much…as, as much…as, whether to…) fail when the second half drops a preposition or switches verb form. Match the scaffolding, not just the topic.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival flyer promises clearer maps, shorter queues, and that shuttle buses will run until midnight.
By training marshals early, by publishing diversion signs, and by checking radios hourly, the walk reduced delays.
The speaker was praised for how she handled hecklers, how she timed jokes, and her encore story.
We will either finish the scrapbook this year or postpone the project until spring.
The campsite asks that visitors log arrivals, that they sort recycling carefully, and fires be extinguished by ten.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Use midnight shuttle buses as a third noun phrase.

TRUE — Three matching "by + gerund" phrases form a parallel means list.

Tip: Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal list balanced.

FALSE — Two "how" clauses are followed by a noun phrase.

Tip: Add how she delivered her encore story to keep the how-pattern.

TRUE — "Either…or" joins two matching bare infinitives after "will."

Tip: Shared will + either…or needs the same bare verb form on both sides.

FALSE — Two "that" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "that."

Tip: Repeat that before fires be extinguished by ten.
highlights: and that shuttle buses will run
By training marshals early, by publishing
either finish the scrapbook this year or postpone
tasks.solution_overview: Festival flyers and campsite rules often stack that-clauses. If that appears twice, the third clause almost always needs it too—or all three should be rewritten as nouns.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Good bread rests less on exotic flour than kneading the dough with patience.
Not only did attendance rise after Easter, but energy levels also improved.
Campers asked for a trail note that is realistic, that is waterproof, and useful without jargon.
The choir prefers rehearsing in person on Mondays and to rehearse online on Thursdays.
A solid itinerary must specify who books the tickets, what bags are allowed, and when the group will meet.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Less…than" joins "on + noun" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Less on exotic flour than on kneading the dough with patience.

TRUE — Inverted "not only" is balanced by "but…also" with a parallel past-tense verb phrase.

Tip: Keep both predicates finite and matching after not only…but also.

FALSE — Two "that is" relatives are followed by an adjective missing "that is."

Tip: Write that is useful without jargon.

FALSE — A gerund ("rehearsing") is paired with an infinitive ("to rehearse").

Tip: Prefer rehearsing… and rehearsing online…, or to rehearse… and to rehearse…

TRUE — Three matching wh-clauses specify who, what, and when.

Tip: Parallel wh-clauses are ideal for plans that must answer ownership, contents, and timing.
highlights: who books the tickets, what bags
tasks.solution_overview: Comparative frames (less…than) and relative-clause chains demand the same marker on every branch. When in doubt, rewrite the last item so it could replace the first without changing structure.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The landlord authorised tenants to repaint the hallway, to replace the hallway bulbs, and filing a repair request if leaks returned.
Just as the café invests in better beans, so too does it invest in staff training.
Progress will be judged on whether chores are finished, whether keys are returned, and communal lights are off.
The brief is neither to defend every habit nor to dismiss every suggestion wholesale.
She moved out because of limited daylight, because of noisy neighbours, and her commute had become unmanageable.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two infinitives after "authorised…to" are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Use to file a repair request to keep the infinitive series.

TRUE — "Just as…so too" balances two matching invest + in + noun patterns with inversion on the second clause.

Tip: Correlative just as…so too needs mirrored clause structure.

FALSE — Two "whether" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "whether."

Tip: Repeat whether before communal lights are off.

TRUE — "Neither…nor" joins two matching infinitives after "is."

Tip: Keep to + bare verb on both sides of neither…nor.

FALSE — Two "because of + noun" phrases are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use because of an unmanageable commute so every reason stays a noun phrase.
highlights: neither to defend every habit nor to dismiss
tasks.solution_overview: Final-band items combine correlatives, repeated subordinators, and long infinitive chains. Name the opening structure of each sentence, then reject any ending that cannot wear the same grammatical clothes.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach recommended that every player arrive forty minutes early.
It is essential that the lab notebook remains sealed overnight.
The landlord insisted that the tenant paints the hallway before moving out.
Friends suggested that she takes the night train to Lisbon.
It is crucial that the picnic baskets stays closed until noon.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After "recommended that," the formal subjunctive uses the base form "arrive."

Tip: Mandative verbs (recommend, insist, demand) want the bare verb, even after a singular subject.

FALSE — "It is essential that" requires "remain," not "remains."

Tip: Impersonal adjectives (essential, crucial, vital) still trigger the base-form pattern.

FALSE — After "insisted that," write "paint," not "paints."

Tip: Drop the third-person -s in any mandative that-clause.

FALSE — After "suggested that," use "take," not "takes."

Tip: Soft verbs like suggest still forbid indicative -s in exam English.

FALSE — Use "stay," not "stays," after "it is crucial that."

Tip: Stative verbs (stay, remain, keep) still lose -s in the formal subjunctive.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan for mandative triggers—recommend, insist, suggest, or "it is essential/crucial that." After the that-clause, expect a bare base form. Mark TRUE only when that base form is already there.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hiking club required that members bring spare batteries.
The gallery proposed that the exhibition is postponed until spring.
It is imperative that the recipe be followed exactly.
The librarian requested that each visitor returns borrowed maps today.
He suggested that Maya reconsiders the weekend itinerary.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Required that" correctly takes the base form "bring."

Tip: Require, request, and demand behave like recommend: that + base form.

FALSE — After "proposed that," write "be postponed," not "is postponed."

Tip: Indicative passive uses "is/are"; the subjunctive passive needs "be."

TRUE — "It is imperative that… be followed" uses the correct subjunctive passive.

Tip: Impersonal "it is + adjective + that" is a classic mandative frame.

FALSE — After "requested that," use "return," not "returns."

Tip: Do not add -s even when the that-clause subject is singular.

FALSE — After "suggested that," use "reconsider," not "reconsiders."

Tip: Suggest and propose are softer but still trigger the formal subjunctive here.
tasks.solution_overview: These items mix require, propose, request, suggest, and "it is imperative that." Treat them alike: look past the that-clause subject and check for a base form. Indicative -s and "is postponed" are the FALSE marks.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It was recommended that the mural remain unfinished until the festival.
The neighbourhood group insisted that the streetlights are repaired tonight.
The drama coach demanded that the understudy learn the monologue by Friday.
It is vital that every volunteer arrives before the doors open.
The flatmates asked that the Wi-Fi password be changed after the party.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past-tense "was recommended that" still takes present base form "remain."

Tip: The mandative subjunctive does not backshift with the main verb's tense.

FALSE — Use "be repaired," not "are repaired," after "insisted that."

Tip: A plural subject does not licence indicative "are" in this pattern.

TRUE — "Demanded that… learn" is correct base-form usage.

Tip: Active subjunctive often looks identical to the infinitive without "to."

FALSE — After "it is vital that," write "arrive," not "arrives."

Tip: Vital, essential, and necessary all suppress the third-person -s.

TRUE — "Asked that… be changed" correctly uses the subjunctive passive.

Tip: Ask that + clause (formal) follows the same rule as request that.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch past-tense reporting verbs and impersonal "it is vital that." Neither changes the rule: the that-clause verb stays in the base form. Flag any -s or "are/is" as incorrect.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The yoga instructor recommended that beginners stretch after every class.
It is necessary that the tent covers the sleeping bags completely.
The choir director insisted that the sheet music be photocopied tonight.
Parents demanded that the school issues clearer trip instructions.
The guide stressed that it is important that hikers report injuries promptly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Recommended that… stretch" is the expected base form.

Tip: Plural subjects still take bare verbs after recommend.

FALSE — Use "cover," not "covers," after "it is necessary that."

Tip: Necessary and essential never keep indicative agreement in careful exam usage.

TRUE — "Insisted that… be photocopied" is correct subjunctive passive.

Tip: Time adverbials do not change the verb form.

FALSE — After "demanded that," write "issue," not "issues."

Tip: A singular institution ("the school") still takes a bare verb in the that-clause.

TRUE — Nested "it is important that hikers report" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: The trigger can sit inside a larger sentence; find the that-clause first.
tasks.solution_overview: Most lines already use the mandative base form. The false ones keep ordinary present agreement ("covers," "issues") after necessary/demand—those are the traps to strike.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The referee ordered that both captains leave the pitch together.
Her tutor advised that the draft remains unread until Monday.
It is desirable that the survey be anonymous.
The campsite rules stipulated that guests extinguish fires by ten.
The flyer urges that each neighbour updates the shared calendar weekly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Ordered that… leave" follows the mandative pattern.

Tip: Order, stipulate, and insist are reliable subjunctive triggers.

FALSE — After "advised that" in this mandative sense, use "remain," not "remains."

Tip: Advise that + base form is the formal pattern tested here.

TRUE — "It is desirable that… be anonymous" correctly uses "be."

Tip: Desirable, advisable, and preferable work like essential.

TRUE — "Stipulated that… extinguish" is the correct bare form.

Tip: Rulebooks often hide subjunctives—check the that-clause carefully.

FALSE — After "urges that," write "update," not "updates."

Tip: Urge, recommend, and insist share the same base-form rule.
tasks.solution_overview: Sports, tutoring, camping, and neighbourhood notices still trigger the formal subjunctive. Read past the subject and verify that the that-clause verb is bare.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The student council moved that the talent show be cancelled this term.
Tourists requested that the guide explains the mosaic in more detail.
It is critical that spare keys be left with a neighbour.
The warden insisted that nobody enter the reserve after dusk.
The handbook recommends that each class consolidates notes weekly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Moved that… be cancelled" is correct meeting-style subjunctive.

Tip: "Move that" in minutes almost always takes the base form.

FALSE — Use "explain," not "explains," after "requested that."

Tip: A singular role ("the guide") is a frequent bait for -s.

TRUE — "It is critical that… be left" uses the right passive subjunctive.

Tip: Critical and crucial are interchangeable triggers for this pattern.

TRUE — "Insisted that nobody enter" correctly uses the bare verb after a negative indefinite.

Tip: Nobody/everybody still take base form, not "enters."

FALSE — After "recommends that," write "consolidate," not "consolidates."

Tip: Singular "each class" tempts -s—the subjunctive forbids it.
tasks.solution_overview: Meeting language ("moved that") and negative subjects ("nobody") still demand the base form. The errors here are ordinary present endings after request/recommend.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The lab protocol requires that each sample be labelled before freezing.
It is essential that the host opens the doors punctually.
Classmates proposed that the film night commence after exams.
Residents demanded that unsafe scaffolding were dismantled at once.
We recommended that the nominee not be shortlisted without references.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Requires that… be labelled" is correct.

Tip: Require that + passive subjunctive is standard in procedures.

FALSE — Use "open," not "opens," after "it is essential that."

Tip: Role nouns after essential/imperative still take the bare verb.

TRUE — "Proposed that… commence" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: Formal verbs like commence are fine; keep them bare after propose.

FALSE — After "demanded that," use "be dismantled," not "were dismantled."

Tip: Do not confuse mandative "be" with the unreal "were" subjunctive.

TRUE — Negation sits before the base form: "not be shortlisted."

Tip: Write "that X not + base," never "that X does not" in the formal pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: This set adds negation and a "were" trap. Mandative English wants "be," not past "were," and negatives use "not" + base form rather than "does not."

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The museum recommended that visitors apologise if they touch the exhibits.
It is advisable that travellers avoids unmarked mountain paths.
The lease provides that either tenant give thirty days' written notice.
The faculty insisted that the thesis is submitted in electronic form only.
Her coach urged that the ban be lifted pending a medical check.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Recommended that… apologise" uses the base form correctly.

Tip: Spelling (apologise/apologize) is separate from the subjunctive test—focus on the ending.

FALSE — After "it is advisable that," write "avoid," not "avoids."

Tip: Advisable and preferable suppress -s exactly like essential.

TRUE — "Provides that… give" is a formal mandative with a bare verb.

Tip: "Either tenant" still takes base form here, not "gives."

FALSE — Use "be submitted," not "is submitted," after "insisted that."

Tip: Academic instructions often hide indicative passives—swap "is" for "be."

TRUE — "Urged that… be lifted" is correct.

Tip: Sports and medical contexts still favour urge that + be + participle.
tasks.solution_overview: Lease wording and coach "urged that" sit beside recommend/insist frames. Correct items keep the bare verb; incorrect ones keep -s or indicative "is."

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The club secretary insisted that every gift above €50 is logged.
It is important that the appendix include the raw survey responses.
Fans demanded that ticket sales resumes immediately.
The allotment committee resolved that the shed be painted green.
The brief suggested that the designer prepares a mood board overnight.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — After "insisted that," use "be logged," not "is logged."

Tip: Threshold phrases (€50, 10%, etc.) distract—still check the verb form.

TRUE — "It is important that… include" correctly drops -s.

Tip: Important is among the highest-frequency impersonal triggers in exams.

FALSE — Use "resume," not "resumes," after "demanded that."

Tip: Plural "sales" can tempt agreement noise—subjunctive wants bare "resume" either way.

TRUE — "Resolved that… be painted" is correct committee English.

Tip: Resolve/move/order that + be + participle is a fixed formal pattern.

FALSE — After "suggested that," write "prepare," not "prepares."

Tip: Soft verbs (suggest, recommend) still forbid indicative -s in the that-clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Only two sentences already use the base form. Hunt for indicative "is" and third-person -s after insist, demand, and suggest—those are your FALSE marks.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The park ranger recommended that picnic leftovers be packed out.
It is mandatory that visitors wear closed shoes in the workshop.
The debate chair directed that both teams exchange notes by noon.
The hostel asked that laundry tickets is collected before checkout.
The handbook requires that the captain lay the route map on the table.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Recommended that… be packed" is correct.

Tip: Particle verbs still sit under the same "be" + participle rule in the passive.

TRUE — "It is mandatory that visitors wear" uses the bare plural verb correctly.

Tip: With plural subjects the base form looks like a normal present—confirm the trigger first.

TRUE — "Directed that… exchange" is the right base form.

Tip: Direct, order, and instruct that all behave mandatively.

FALSE — Use "be collected," not "is collected," after "asked that."

Tip: When the that-clause looks almost normal, still verify "be" versus "is."

TRUE — "Requires that the captain lay" correctly uses bare "lay."

Tip: Formal instructions still want the base form after require that.
tasks.solution_overview: Four items are already correct; the single error is an indicative passive ("is collected") after "asked that." When the that-clause looks almost normal, still verify "be" versus "is."

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The landlord insisted that the deposit remains refundable after repairs.
Researchers proposed that the pilot study be extended by six weeks.
It is preferable that feedback is collected anonymously.
The cycling club demanded that weekend rides be cancelled in high winds.
The editor requested that the author cite the primary dataset explicitly.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — After "insisted that," use "remain," not "remains."

Tip: "Remain refundable" is a set phrase—still strip the -s in mandative clauses.

TRUE — "Proposed that… be extended" is correct.

Tip: Research English frequently uses propose that + be + participle.

FALSE — Use "be collected," not "is collected," after "it is preferable that."

Tip: Preferable/advisable + that still demand the subjunctive passive with "be."

TRUE — "Demanded that… be cancelled" is correct.

Tip: Club rules often pack weather conditions around a clean "be" + participle core.

TRUE — "Requested that… cite" correctly uses the bare verb.

Tip: Academic request that + base form is standard formal style.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on "remain(s)" and passive "is/be collected." Indicative endings after insist and preferable are the FALSE answers; the rest already show proper base forms.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival board decreed that the murals be protected overnight.
It is essential that quiet hours is maintained throughout the hostel.
Neighbours agreed that the garden path be cleared before winter.
The coach insisted that every runner arrives forty minutes before the race.
Guidance notes recommend that applicants enclose certified translations.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Decreed that… be protected" is correct formal subjunctive.

Tip: Decree, ordain, and order are strong formal triggers.

FALSE — Use "be maintained," not "is maintained," after "it is essential that."

Tip: Abstract house rules still take "be," not "is," in the that-clause.

TRUE — "Agreed that… be cleared" correctly uses "be."

Tip: Agree that can be factual or mandative; here clearing is a prescribed action.

FALSE — After "insisted that," write "arrive," not "arrives."

Tip: Sports deadlines do not change the grammar rule.

TRUE — "Recommend that applicants enclose" uses the bare plural verb correctly.

Tip: When the subject is plural, correct forms often look ordinary—still confirm the trigger.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "decreed that" and softer "agreed/recommend that" share one test: base form after that. The two FALSE items keep indicative "is" and "arrives."

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The mentor recommended that the intern not receive further tasks this week.
It was vital that the vaccine were stored below eight degrees.
The panel insisted that discrepancies be reconciled before sign-off.
Kitchen staff required that inventory counts takes place under dual control.
She asked that the embargo remain in place until the filing date.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negated subjunctive "not receive" is correctly formed.

Tip: Place "not" immediately before the base verb; do not insert "do/does."

FALSE — After "it was vital that," use "be stored," not "were stored."

Tip: Past-tense "was vital" does not licence past "were"; mandative still wants "be."

TRUE — "Insisted that… be reconciled" is correct.

Tip: Plural abstract subjects still take "be," not "are."

FALSE — Use "take," not "takes," after "required that."

Tip: Subject–verb lookalikes ("counts takes") are noise—strip to "counts take."

TRUE — "Asked that… remain" correctly keeps the base form.

Tip: "Remain in place" after ask/insist is a frequent correct pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder traps appear: negation without "do," and past "were" after "it was vital that." Remember the mandative form is tenseless "be" / bare verb, not a past indicative or unreal "were."

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The charter provides that the club publish fixture lists annually.
It is crucial that no one tamper with the sealed sample bags.
The festival committee directed that banners be withheld pending the vote.
Her solicitor recommended that the client waive the interview recording.
The notice requires that complaints be lodged within fourteen days.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Provides that… publish" is bare-form formal English.

Tip: Singular institutional subjects still take no -s here.

TRUE — After "it is crucial that," "no one tamper" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: Indefinites (no one, everyone, anybody) still suppress -s in mandative clauses.

TRUE — "Directed that… be withheld" correctly uses the subjunctive passive.

Tip: Plural objects still take "be," not "are," after direct that.

TRUE — "Recommended that… waive" is correct.

Tip: Formal "waive" after recommend is a high-frequency exam item.

TRUE — "Requires that… be lodged" correctly uses "be" + participle.

Tip: Plural "complaints" still take "be" in the passive subjunctive.
tasks.solution_overview: Every sentence here already uses the mandative base form or "be" + participle. Confirm the trigger, confirm the bare verb, and mark all five TRUE—do not invent errors that are not on the page.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The committee moved that standing orders be suspended for the vote.
It is imperative that the nominee declares all related hobbies.
Organisers required that the programme be amended before printing.
The mediator suggested that each side makes one further concession.
Clinicians insisted that the dosage remain constant during the trial.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Moved that… be suspended" is correct.

Tip: Procedural motions almost always use the formal subjunctive.

FALSE — After "it is imperative that," use "declare," not "declares."

Tip: Nominee/applicant/candidate after imperative are classic -s traps.

TRUE — "Required that… be amended" is correct.

Tip: Event planning loves require that + be + participle.

FALSE — Use "make," not "makes," after "suggested that."

Tip: "Each side" is singular in form—exam writers plant -s here deliberately.

TRUE — "Insisted that… remain" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: Clinical protocols often keep "remain" after insist/require.
tasks.solution_overview: Three correct mandatives and two indicative -s errors after imperative and suggest. "Each" and role-title subjects are the usual bait for an unwanted ending.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rules stipulated that volunteers not solicit donations door-to-door.
It is necessary that the shared fridge be emptied before the holiday.
Supporters demanded that the captain steps down after the match.
The brief urged that exhibits be paginated consecutively.
IT guidance recommends that remote staff uses only the college VPN.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negated mandative "not solicit" is correctly formed.

Tip: After stipulate/require, "that X not + verb" is the formal negative.

TRUE — "It is necessary that… be emptied" is correct.

Tip: Everyday chores recycle the same "be" + participle frame.

FALSE — After "demanded that," write "step," not "steps."

Tip: Dramatic verbs (step down, resign) still lose -s in the that-clause.

TRUE — "Urged that… be paginated" is correct.

Tip: Exhibition and catalogue English favour urge that + be + participle.

FALSE — Use "use," not "uses," after "recommends that."

Tip: Collective "staff" may take singular agreement in BrE—but the subjunctive still wants bare "use."
tasks.solution_overview: Negation without do-support and collective nouns (staff) raise the difficulty. Correct sentences already use "not" + base or "be" + participle; FALSE ones keep ordinary -s.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The safety notice provides that the cleaner not enter the lab alone.
It is desirable that the questionnaire were bilingual from the outset.
Flatmates insisted that cleaning rotas be recalculated after the move.
The assessor recommended that the candidate retakes the oral component.
The ranger directed that contingency supplies remain untouched this season.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Formal "provides that… not enter" is a correct negated subjunctive.

Tip: Notices and orders are prime territory for "that X not + base."

FALSE — After "it is desirable that," use "be bilingual," not "were bilingual."

Tip: Do not import the unreal "were" into mandative clauses.

TRUE — "Insisted that… be recalculated" is correct.

Tip: Household planning still uses clean "be" + participle forms.

FALSE — Use "retake," not "retakes," after "recommended that."

Tip: Exam/assessment vocabulary is a favourite place to hide -s.

TRUE — "Directed that… remain" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: "Remain untouched/unchanged" after direct/insist is a high-yield pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: At this level, watch unreal "were" bleeding into mandative frames and -s after recommend. Negated formal "not + base" is grammatical; "were" after desirable is not.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The society charter requires that the secretary keep minutes of every meeting.
It was insisted that the rehearsal starts before the hall closes.
External mentors advised that settlement talks be reopened quietly.
The club proposed that membership fees is raised next autumn.
The protocol states that it is vital that specimens reach the lab within four hours.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Requires that… keep" is correct bare-form usage.

Tip: Officer titles (secretary, treasurer) after require are classic test items.

FALSE — After "it was insisted that," use "start," not "starts."

Tip: Passive reporting ("it was insisted") does not change the that-clause rule.

TRUE — "Advised that… be reopened" is correct.

Tip: Advise that + be + participle is formal advisory English.

FALSE — Use "be raised," not "is raised," after "proposed that."

Tip: Plural "fees" still take "be" in the passive subjunctive.

TRUE — "It is vital that specimens reach" correctly uses the bare plural verb.

Tip: Nested "states that it is vital that…" still ends in a mandative clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Reporting shells ("it was insisted," "the protocol states that it is vital") bury the real trigger. Unwrap to the innermost that-clause and test for base form versus indicative.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board resolved that interim prizes not be declared this half.
It is essential that whoever chairs the panel has no prior conflict.
Organisers demanded that stage cues be tightened after the dress run.
The examiner insisted that each script is double-marked independently.
Guidance recommends that the risk register be reviewed after every incident.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negated passive "not be declared" is correctly formed.

Tip: Resolutions often negate with "not be" + participle.

FALSE — After "it is essential that," use "have," not "has," even after "whoever."

Tip: Free relatives (whoever) still sit under the mandative rule—no -s.

TRUE — "Demanded that… be tightened" is correct.

Tip: Theatre and event language still uses demand that + be + participle.

FALSE — Use "be double-marked," not "is double-marked," after "insisted that."

Tip: Exam-administration passives are a favourite "is" trap.

TRUE — "Recommends that… be reviewed" is correct.

Tip: Safety and ops manuals recycle this frame constantly.
tasks.solution_overview: The sharpest trap is "whoever… has": the free relative does not cancel the mandative. Strip -s / swap "is" for "be" wherever essential, insist, or recommend governs the clause.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The articles provide that directors declare interests at the first opportunity.
It is critical that the spill kit remains sealed until an incident occurs.
The tribunal ordered that costs be reserved pending written submissions.
Her supervisor suggested that the abstract emphasises policy implications only.
Class reps requested that management provide a clearer exam timetable.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Provide that directors declare" correctly uses the bare plural verb.

Tip: Articles and constitutions are full of silent mandatives—spot the that-clause.

FALSE — After "it is critical that," use "remain," not "remains."

Tip: Safety manuals often leave an indicative -s by mistake.

TRUE — "Ordered that costs be reserved" is correct.

Tip: Costs/orders after order that almost always take "be."

FALSE — Use "emphasise," not "emphasises," after "suggested that."

Tip: Academic suggest that + -s is one of the most common exam errors.

TRUE — "Requested that management provide" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: Collective "management" still takes a bare verb in mandative English.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with constitutional "provide that," tribunal "ordered that," and academic "suggested that." Only the critical/suggest items keep unwanted -s; the rest already show proper base forms.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not only she arrived late, but she also forgot her keys.
Seldom the café opens before seven on Sundays.
Never the neighbours had complained about the noise.
No sooner had the kettle boiled than the toast burned.
Under no circumstances the children will stay home alone.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Fronted "not only" needs inversion: "Not only did she arrive late…".

Tip: If "not only" sits at the start, treat it like a question for the auxiliary: did/does/had + subject.

FALSE — Needs "Seldom does the café open…".

Tip: Negative frequency words (seldom, rarely, never) at the start almost always trigger inversion.

FALSE — Fronted "never" needs "Never had the neighbours complained…", not subject–verb order.

Tip: With past perfect after "never", move "had" before the subject.

TRUE — "No sooner…than" with past perfect inversion is the classic pattern here.

Tip: Pair "no sooner" with "than" (not "when") and invert: "had + subject".

FALSE — Needs "Under no circumstances will the children stay…".

Tip: Modal + subject swaps after a negative prepositional phrase at the front.
tasks.solution_overview: These openers look formal, but the test is mechanical: a negative or restrictive phrase at the front usually forces auxiliary–subject order. Scan each line for that swap first, then check the correlative word (than/when) if "no sooner" or "hardly" appears.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly had the film started when the fire alarm went off.
Rarely we see such clear skies in November.
Little did the guests realise how long the queue would be.
Not only did the recipe look simple, but it also tasted great.
Seldom the library stays open past nine on weekdays.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Hardly had…when…" is the standard inverted past-perfect pattern.

Tip: After hardly/scarcely/barely, prefer "when" (or "before"), not "than".

FALSE — Needs "Rarely do we see…".

Tip: No auxiliary visible? Add do/does/did and place it before the subject.

TRUE — "Little did…" correctly inverts after a restrictive opener.

Tip: "Little" meaning "not at all" behaves like a negative fronting word.

TRUE — Fronted "not only" takes inversion, and "but also" keeps the second clause parallel.

Tip: Check both halves: inversion after "not only", then a matching "but also" clause.

FALSE — Requires "Seldom does the library stay…".

Tip: "Seldom" + present simple → does/do before the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Task 2 drills the core set: hardly, rarely, little, not only, seldom. Correct lines already invert; wrong ones leave ordinary subject–verb order after a fronted negative. Fix those by inserting or moving the auxiliary.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Under no circumstances should this door be left unlocked overnight.
No sooner the bus pulled away than Marta realised she had left her bag.
Never has the school cancelled sports day for such a light drizzle.
Scarcely the match had begun before the referee stopped play.
At no time the coach authorised a change of kit colour.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negative adverbial + modal inversion is clean: "should this door be left".

Tip: After "under no circumstances", expect will/should/can before the subject.

FALSE — Needs "No sooner had the bus pulled away than…".

Tip: "No sooner" almost always pairs with past perfect and inversion of "had".

TRUE — "Never has the school cancelled…" correctly inverts present perfect.

Tip: Keep the participle after the subject: Never + has/have + subject + past participle.

FALSE — Needs "Scarcely had the match begun…".

Tip: Scarcely/hardly/barely fronting → had + subject + past participle.

FALSE — Needs "At no time did the coach authorise…".

Tip: "At no time" is a full negative fronting phrase; invert like a question.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on stock fronting phrases: under no circumstances, no sooner, never, scarcely, at no time. If the phrase is negative and sits first, the next word should be an auxiliary, not the subject.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only after the rain stopped did the picnic become possible.
Not until the train doors closed did Alex notice the wrong platform.
Hardly the hikers had reached the ridge when fog rolled in.
On no account may visitors feed the animals in this enclosure.
Nowhere in the guidebook does it mention the Monday closure.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Only after…" inverts the main clause: "did the picnic become".

Tip: With only + time clause, leave the time clause alone and invert the main clause.

TRUE — "Not until…" likewise inverts only the main clause.

Tip: Do not invert inside the "not until" clause itself.

FALSE — Needs "Hardly had the hikers reached the ridge when…".

Tip: Hardly + past perfect: had before the subject.

TRUE — "On no account may visitors…" is a correct formal prohibition with inversion.

Tip: "On no account" and "under no circumstances" behave the same way.

TRUE — "Nowhere…does it mention…" correctly inverts after a negative place adverbial.

Tip: Nowhere/no place at the front → does/do/did + subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these already invert correctly after only after, not until, on no account, and nowhere. The odd one out is "hardly" without "had" before the subject—fix that pattern and the rest fall into place.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No longer does the bakery deliver to our street.
Barely had the concert begun when the lights failed.
In no way can the warranty cover water damage from floods.
Not only was the hotel full, but the next town was booked out too.
Seldom have we eaten such fresh bread from a roadside stall.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "No longer" at the front takes "does the bakery deliver".

Tip: No longer + present simple → do/does before the subject.

TRUE — "Barely had…when…" mirrors the hardly pattern.

Tip: Barely/hardly/scarcely share the same inversion + "when" template.

TRUE — "In no way can the warranty…" correctly inverts the modal.

Tip: In no way / under no circumstances / on no account all pull the modal forward.

TRUE — Fronted "not only" with "was" before the subject is right, and the second clause completes the contrast.

Tip: With be-verbs, invert be itself: Not only was the hotel…

TRUE — "Seldom have we eaten…" is clean present-perfect inversion.

Tip: Frequency negative + have/has + subject + past participle.
tasks.solution_overview: Every sentence here is already inverted. Use them as models: spot the fronted negative, confirm the auxiliary sits next, then note the correlative (when/but also) where relevant.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No sooner had the dishwasher finished than the sink filled again.
Rarely does a local team win away in such weather.
Not only the chef objected, but the waiters also complained.
Under no circumstances will pets be allowed in the exhibition hall.
Never the museum had displayed so many private loans at once.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past-perfect inversion after "no sooner" plus "than" is exact.

Tip: Memorise the trio: no sooner + had + subject + than.

TRUE — "Rarely does…" correctly adds do-support for present simple.

Tip: If there is no auxiliary, invent do/does/did for the inversion.

FALSE — Needs "Not only did the chef object, but…".

Tip: Fronted not only without an auxiliary still needs did/does/do.

TRUE — Modal inversion after "under no circumstances" is correct.

Tip: will/must/should jumps before the subject after this phrase.

FALSE — Needs "Never had the museum displayed…".

Tip: Never + past perfect → Never had + subject + past participle.
tasks.solution_overview: Three lines already invert; two leave the subject right after not only / never. Mentally flip those into question order and you will see the repair immediately.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly had the snow melted when another frost arrived.
Little the tourists understood about the ferry timetable.
Only when the power returned did the fridge start humming again.
Scarcely had the paint dried on the fence when rain began.
Seldom the post office updates its holiday opening hours early.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Hardly + had + subject + when is textbook.

Tip: Keep "when" (not "than") after hardly/scarcely/barely.

FALSE — Needs "Little did the tourists understand…".

Tip: Little as a fronting restrictor needs did/does/do + subject.

TRUE — Only when + clause, then invert the main clause.

Tip: Invert after the time clause ends, not inside it.

TRUE — Scarcely had…when… matches the hard/barely family.

Tip: Same skeleton for scarcely, hardly, and barely.

FALSE — Needs "Seldom does the post office update…".

Tip: Present-simple after seldom → does/do before the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Hardly, scarcely, and only when are shown correctly; little and seldom are missing their auxiliaries. Add did/does and the pattern locks in.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not until the referee blew the whistle the players left the pitch.
Under no circumstances are bikes permitted inside the shopping centre.
No sooner had the oven preheated than the dough was ready.
At no point did the guide admit that the path was closed.
Rarely a quiet carriage stays quiet for the whole journey.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Needs "…did the players leave the pitch" after the not-until clause.

Tip: Not until + time clause → invert the main clause with did/does/do or an auxiliary.

TRUE — Be-verb inversion after "under no circumstances" is fine: "are bikes permitted".

Tip: With be, invert be itself; no extra do-support.

TRUE — No sooner + had + than is correct again.

Tip: Watch the correlative: than after no sooner.

TRUE — "At no point did the guide admit…" is solid inversion.

Tip: At no point / at no time are interchangeable triggers.

FALSE — Needs "Rarely does a quiet carriage stay…".

Tip: Rarely + present simple → does/do + subject + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Most lines invert cleanly. The traps are "not until" without main-clause inversion and "rarely" without do-support—both classic exam misses.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only by booking early can we secure seats near the stage.
No sooner had the parcel arrived when the courier rang again.
Not only did traffic jam the bridge, but the tunnel closed as well.
Under no circumstances should raw chicken sit on the worktop.
Never before has the festival sold out in a single morning.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Only by…" inverts the main clause: "can we secure".

Tip: Only + prepositional phrase at the front still forces inversion.

FALSE — "No sooner" takes "than", not "when": "…arrived than the courier rang again".

Tip: Correlative pairs: no sooner→than; hardly/scarcely→when.

TRUE — Not only + did + but…as well is correctly inverted and balanced.

Tip: Keep both verbs parallel after not only / but also.

TRUE — Modal inversion after under no circumstances is right.

Tip: should/must/will before the subject after this opener.

TRUE — "Never before has…" correctly inverts present perfect.

Tip: Never before / never again behave like never for inversion.
tasks.solution_overview: Inversion is mostly done right; the subtle miss is the correlative after "no sooner". Word order can look perfect and still fail if than/when is swapped.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly had the teacher finished speaking than phones started buzzing.
Not until the keys were found did the family leave the flat.
Seldom do neighbourhood shops stay open past midnight.
On no account the intern may unlock the storeroom alone.
Little did the runners know a shortcut waited behind the hill.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Hardly pairs with "when", not "than": "…speaking when phones started buzzing".

Tip: Swap than→when after hardly/scarcely/barely even if inversion looks fine.

TRUE — Not until + clause, then "did the family leave".

Tip: Main-clause inversion only; leave the time clause in normal order.

TRUE — Seldom + do-support is correct.

Tip: Frequency negatives need do/does/did when no other auxiliary exists.

FALSE — Needs "On no account may the intern unlock…".

Tip: Move the modal before the subject after on no account.

TRUE — Little did… is a stock restrictive inversion.

Tip: Little + did + subject + base verb is the usual template.
tasks.solution_overview: Two errors here mix correlative choice (hardly…than) with missing modal inversion (on no account). Check both word order and the linking word after the fronted phrase.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only after the laundry dried the sheets were folded and stacked.
Nowhere else will you find cherries this sweet in late summer.
Scarcely had the guests sat down when dessert appeared.
Not only did the app crash, it also wiped the draft message.
Under no circumstances the cleaner will mix bleach with ammonia.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Needs "…were the sheets folded and stacked" (or "…did anyone fold the sheets").

Tip: Only after + time clause → invert the main clause.

TRUE — Nowhere else + will + subject is correct.

Tip: Nowhere / nowhere else at the front always invert.

TRUE — Scarcely had…when… is the right pair.

Tip: Keep when after scarcely; keep had before the subject.

TRUE — Not only… with inversion is acceptable; "it also" can finish the contrast.

Tip: "But also" can appear as "it also" if the second clause still matches.

FALSE — Needs "Under no circumstances will the cleaner mix…".

Tip: will must precede the subject after this fronting phrase.
tasks.solution_overview: Only after and under no circumstances still trap people who invert late or not at all. The other three already show the target shapes—use them as anchors.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No sooner had the curtains opened than applause filled the hall.
Rarely have gardens recovered so quickly after a late frost.
Not only was the suitcase heavy, but the zip was broken.
At no time were passengers told about the platform change.
Barely had the bakery opened when the first queue formed.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — No sooner + had + than is perfect.

Tip: Drill the correlative than until it is automatic.

TRUE — Rarely + present perfect inversion is correct.

Tip: Rarely have/has + subject + past participle.
