TRUE — Not only was…but… keeps be inverted and the contrast clear.

Tip: With was/were, invert be; no do-support needed.

TRUE — At no time + were + subject is correct be-inversion.

Tip: Passive or be-main verbs invert be itself.

TRUE — Barely had…when… matches the hard/scarcely family.

Tip: Barely = hardly for inversion purposes.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean model set: no sooner, rarely, not only, at no time, barely. If your own answers miss any of these shapes, rewrite the wrong ones to match these templates.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only if the weather clears will the outdoor market go ahead.
The notice not only lists opening times but also warns about roadworks.
No sooner had breakfast ended than the day trip coaches arrived.
Hardly the ink had dried on the consent form when surgery was cancelled.
Under no circumstances are personal heaters permitted in the office.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Only if + clause, then invert the main clause: "will the outdoor market go".

Tip: Conditional "only if" at the front still triggers main-clause inversion.

TRUE — Mid-sentence "not only…but also" needs no inversion.

Tip: Invert only when "not only" is fronted; otherwise keep normal order.

TRUE — No sooner…than with past perfect inversion is correct.

Tip: Confirm than after no sooner every time.

FALSE — Needs "Hardly had the ink dried…when…".

Tip: had must sit before the subject after hardly.

TRUE — Under no circumstances + are + subject is correct.

Tip: Be-inversion after this phrase is standard in policies.
tasks.solution_overview: The key sophistication here is knowing when not to invert: mid-clause "not only…but also" is fine. The only hard fail is hardly without had-before-subject.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not until did the plumber fix the leak the floorboards were dry.
In no circumstances should leftover rice sit out overnight.
Seldom has a village fete drawn such a crowd in midweek.
No longer the tram line serves the old factory estate.
Only after did the museum reopen were tickets put on sale.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Do not invert inside the not-until clause; say "Not until the plumber fixed the leak were the floorboards dry" (or "…did the floorboards dry").

Tip: Invert the main clause only—never invert the not-until/time clause itself.

TRUE — "In no circumstances should…" is the same family as under no circumstances.

Tip: In/under no circumstances both pull the modal forward.

TRUE — Seldom + present perfect inversion is correct.

Tip: Seldom has/have + subject + past participle.

FALSE — Needs "No longer does the tram line serve…".

Tip: No longer + present simple → does/do before the subject.

FALSE — Wrong placement of did; use "Only after the museum reopened were tickets put on sale".

Tip: Keep the only-after clause normal; invert the main clause alone.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced traps put the auxiliary in the wrong clause (not until / only after). Remember: time/condition clause stays normal; the following main clause inverts.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not only did the soup burn, but the bread went stale as well.
Scarcely had the rehearsal ended than the costume call began.
Never again will the club host fireworks without a fire marshal.
Little does the neighbourhood appreciate how quiet the park becomes at dusk.
Under no circumstances the lifeguard may leave the pool unattended.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Fronted not only + did, completed by but…as well, is acceptable.

Tip: "But also / but…as well" both work if the first half inverts.

FALSE — Scarcely takes "when", not "than".

Tip: Correlative check: scarcely/hardly/barely → when; no sooner → than.

TRUE — Never again + will + subject is correct.

Tip: Never again / never before behave like never.

TRUE — Little does… correctly inverts present simple with do-support.

Tip: Little + does/do + subject + base verb.

FALSE — Needs "Under no circumstances may the lifeguard leave…".

Tip: Modal before subject after under no circumstances.
tasks.solution_overview: Inversion looks right on the scarcely line, but the correlative is wrong. Pair that check with the modal-order miss on under no circumstances.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only when the Wi-Fi returned did the online class continue.
No sooner the suitcase was packed than the taxi horn sounded.
At no stage were residents told about the water shut-off.
Rarely do we publish the newsletter without a photo gallery.
Not only the soundtrack disappointed; the plot disappointed too.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Only when + clause, then "did the online class continue".

Tip: Invert after the when-clause finishes.

FALSE — Needs "No sooner was the suitcase packed than…" or "No sooner had the suitcase been packed than…".

Tip: No sooner requires inversion of be/had immediately after it.

TRUE — At no stage + were + subject is correct be-inversion.

Tip: At no stage / at no point / at no time are equivalent triggers.

TRUE — Rarely + do-support is correct.

Tip: Rarely do/does + subject + base verb.

FALSE — Fronted not only needs inversion: "Not only did the soundtrack disappoint…".

Tip: If not only leads the sentence, insert did/does/do before the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Two failures omit inversion after no sooner and not only. The survivors show only when, at no stage, and rarely done properly—mirror those.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not until the fridge was emptied the movers wheeled it downstairs.
Under no circumstances may allergy medication be shared between guests.
Seldom has a community garden produced such a crop of tomatoes.
Only by rearranging the furniture can the sofa fit through the door.
Hardly had the babysitter arrived than the toddler woke up crying.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Needs "…did the movers wheel it downstairs".

Tip: Not until → invert the main clause; do not leave subject–verb order there.

TRUE — Under no circumstances + may + subject is correct modal inversion.

Tip: After this phrase, expect may/will/should before the subject.

TRUE — Seldom + present perfect inversion is correct.

Tip: Seldom has/have + subject + past participle.

TRUE — Only by + -ing, then modal inversion in the main clause.

Tip: Only by / only with / only through all invert the following clause.

FALSE — Hardly takes "when", not "than".

Tip: Even with perfect inversion, wrong correlative still fails the item.
tasks.solution_overview: Top-band items stay inside negative/restrictive inversion: not until, under no circumstances, seldom, only by, hardly. Judge each line by whether the auxiliary moved—and whether than/when is the right partner.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Under no circumstances is smoking permitted near the playground.
No sooner had the ferry docked than foot passengers streamed ashore.
Not only were tickets refunded, but free drinks were offered as well.
Seldom does a weekday market feel this crowded before noon.
Little did neighbours expect the street party to last past midnight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Under no circumstances + is + subject is correct.

Tip: Be-main verbs invert be after this phrase.

TRUE — No sooner…than with past perfect is exact.

Tip: had + subject + than remains the gold standard.

TRUE — Not only were…but… correctly inverts were.

Tip: Plural subject → were before it after not only.

TRUE — Seldom does… is clean do-support inversion.

Tip: Frequency negative + does/do + subject + base verb.

TRUE — Little did… is the classic restrictive inversion.

Tip: Little + did + subject + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are model answers across the core triggers. Treat this task as a checklist of shapes you should be able to produce under exam pressure.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only after the gym closed members were allowed to collect belongings.
Not until the vet confirmed the results did the owners relax.
Barely had the campsite been booked when a storm warning arrived.
On no account should unfinished cakes leave the kitchen counter.
Never the caretaker had unlocked every classroom before dawn.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Needs "…were members allowed to collect belongings" or "…did members become free to collect belongings".

Tip: Only after + clause → invert the main clause.

TRUE — Not until…did… is correctly inverted in the main clause.

Tip: Keep the not-until clause in normal order.

TRUE — Barely had…when… is right.

Tip: Passive past perfect still inverts had: Barely had the campsite been booked…

TRUE — On no account should… is correct modal inversion.

Tip: should/must/may before the subject after on no account.

FALSE — Needs "Never had the caretaker unlocked…".

Tip: Never + past perfect → Never had + subject + past participle.
tasks.solution_overview: Two lines forget to invert after only after and never. The others show not until, barely, and on no account in full working order—match those repairs to the same templates.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nowhere in the hiking leaflet does it mention the Monday trail closure.
Not only did the hostel refill the kettle, but it also left fresh towels.
Hardly had the blackout ended when the street lights flickered back on.
Under no circumstances the landlord will enter without written notice.
No sooner had the suitcases been labelled than the taxi pulled up.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nowhere…does it mention… correctly inverts after a negative place adverbial.

Tip: Nowhere / no place at the front → does/do/did + subject.

TRUE — Not only did…but also… is fully inverted and parallel.

Tip: Match verb forms across both halves after not only / but also.

TRUE — Hardly had…when… is the standard pattern.

Tip: when after hardly; had before the subject.

FALSE — Needs "Under no circumstances will the landlord enter…".

Tip: Final check on every under-no-circumstances item: modal before subject.

TRUE — No sooner had…than… closes the set correctly.

Tip: than after no sooner; had before the subject.
highlights: Nowhere in the hiking leaflet does
tasks.solution_overview: Four model inversions and one classic miss: under no circumstances without modal–subject swap. If you catch that last pattern every time, this topic is exam-ready.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having packed the tent, Maya set off before sunrise.
Walking into the kitchen, the smell of coffee filled the room.
Exhausted after the hike, the sofa looked inviting.
Hoping to catch the early train, Leo left without breakfast.
Covered in mud, the boots were left by the door.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Maya is the logical subject of Having packed, so the opener attaches cleanly.

Tip: Ask who did the -ing / having action — that person must be the grammatical subject.

FALSE — The smell was not walking; rewrite as Walking into the kitchen, she noticed the smell of coffee.

Tip: If the subject cannot perform the participle, it is dangling.

FALSE — A sofa cannot feel exhausted; Exhausted after the hike, they sank onto the sofa.

Tip: Past participles of emotion still need a human or animate logical subject.

TRUE — Leo hoped to catch the train and is the subject after the comma.

Tip: Hoping / Wanting / Trying openers need the hoper as subject.

TRUE — The boots were covered in mud; the passive participle matches the subject.

Tip: Covered / Damaged / Painted can attach to things that underwent the state.
tasks.solution_overview: For each opener, name the implied doer of the participle, then check whether that doer is the grammatical subject. Only three sentences match; the kitchen smell and the sofa dangle.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Delayed by fog, the ferry arrived two hours late.
Having tasted the soup, several spices were added.
Surprised by the score, the fans cheered louder.
Reading the map carefully, a shortcut became obvious.
Bored during the lecture, Mira started doodling.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The ferry is a logical patient of Delayed; the participle attaches correctly.

Tip: Passive -ed openers are fine when the subject was delayed, damaged, or approved.

FALSE — Spices did not taste the soup; Having tasted the soup, the cook added several spices.

Tip: Having + past participle needs the taster as subject, not the ingredients.

TRUE — The fans are surprised; subject and participle align.

Tip: Surprised / Relieved / Thrilled almost always need a person as subject.

FALSE — A shortcut cannot read; Reading the map carefully, she spotted a shortcut.

Tip: Present participles imply an agent who can act.

TRUE — Mira is bored and starts doodling; the attachment is clean.

Tip: Keep the experiencer as subject across the comma.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan for Having + past participle and bare -ing openers. Three sentences keep a matching subject; spices and a shortcut wrongly sit in the doer slot.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having crossed the bridge, the cyclists paused for water.
Startled by the alarm, the rehearsal was cancelled at once.
Published last year, the novel still sells well.
Hoping to improve her serve, tennis lessons were booked online.
Soaked by the rain, Tom's jacket hung by the radiator.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The cyclists crossed the bridge; Having crossed matches the subject.

Tip: Having + past participle is safe when the subject did that prior action.

FALSE — A rehearsal cannot be startled; Startled by the alarm, the cast cancelled the rehearsal.

Tip: Emotion participles need an animate experiencer.

TRUE — The novel was published last year; the passive participle fits.

Tip: Published / Written / Filmed can modify the work itself.

FALSE — Lessons cannot hope; Hoping to improve her serve, she booked tennis lessons online.

Tip: Hoping always points to a person with a goal.

TRUE — The jacket was soaked; Covered/Soaked openers can modify things.

Tip: Physical state on an object is usually grammatical.
tasks.solution_overview: Warm up on clean matches versus classic dangles: startled rehearsal and hoping lessons. Published novel and soaked jacket show when things, not people, can carry a participle.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Running down the pitch, the ball slipped past the keeper.
Confused by the instructions, Ana asked for help.
Having finished dessert, the plates were cleared away.
Written in pencil, the note was hard to read.
Looking for a quiet spot, the park bench seemed perfect.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The ball was not running; Running down the pitch, the striker saw the ball slip past the keeper.

Tip: Sport scenes often dangle the ball or the score instead of the player.

TRUE — Ana is confused and asks; attachment is correct.

Tip: Confused / Puzzled + human subject is a safe pattern.

FALSE — Plates did not finish dessert; Having finished dessert, they cleared the plates away.

Tip: Having finished needs the eater, not the crockery.

TRUE — The note was written in pencil; the participle modifies the note.

Tip: Written / Typed / Printed can modify a document.

FALSE — A bench cannot look for a spot; Looking for a quiet spot, they chose the park bench.

Tip: Looking / Searching openers need a searcher as subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Only two lines work. The rest put a ball, plates, or a bench where a person should sit after the comma.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having studied all night, Priya still felt unprepared.
Arriving late, seats near the stage were taken.
Burnt at the edges, the toast was scraped into the bin.
Thrilled by the invitation, a reply was sent immediately.
Wandering through the market, they bought fresh herbs.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Priya studied and still felt unprepared; the subject matches.

Tip: Having + past participle + same person in the main clause is the standard pattern.

FALSE — Seats did not arrive late; Arriving late, we found the seats near the stage taken.

Tip: Arriving / Entering needs the arriver as subject.

TRUE — The toast was burnt; the passive participle fits the food.

Tip: Burnt / Overcooked / Undercooked can modify dishes.

FALSE — A reply cannot feel thrilled; Thrilled by the invitation, she sent a reply immediately.

Tip: Emotion + inanimate subject = classic dangling trap.

TRUE — They wandered and bought herbs; clean attachment.

Tip: Wandering / Strolling openers need the wanderer after the comma.
tasks.solution_overview: Three correct attachments and two dangles: seats that arrive and a reply that feels thrill. Keep asking who or what the participle really describes.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Built in the 1890s, the library still has wooden floors.
Hearing the doorbell, the cake was taken out of the oven.
Tired of waiting, the queue finally moved forward.
Having lost her keys, Jess borrowed her flatmate's spare.
Painted bright yellow, the door cheered up the hallway.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The library was built in the 1890s; Built modifies the building.

Tip: Built / Designed / Restored often modify places or objects.

FALSE — A cake cannot hear; Hearing the doorbell, she took the cake out of the oven.

Tip: Hearing / Seeing / Smelling need a perceiver.

FALSE — A queue cannot feel tired of waiting; Tired of waiting, the passengers finally moved forward.

Tip: Tired of… needs a person, not the line itself.

TRUE — Jess lost her keys and borrowed a spare; perfect match.

Tip: Having lost / Having forgotten needs the loser as subject.

TRUE — The door was painted yellow; the participle attaches to the door.

Tip: Painted / Decorated / Lined can modify objects.
tasks.solution_overview: Object-friendly participles (Built, Painted) pass; perception and emotion openers fail when cake or a queue sits as subject.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Jogging along the canal, a heron took off from the reeds.
Convinced she was right, Omar refused to change his answer.
Having been washed overnight, the shirts hung neatly on the line.
Opening the fridge, cold air rushed out.
Based on true events, the film kept audiences guessing.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The heron was not jogging; Jogging along the canal, she saw a heron take off from the reeds.

Tip: Nature scenes often dangle wildlife instead of the walker.

TRUE — Omar is convinced and refuses; the participle matches.

Tip: Convinced / Determined + person is usually safe.

TRUE — The shirts had been washed; Having been + past participle fits the clothes.

Tip: Passive perfect participles can modify things that underwent the process.

FALSE — Cold air did not open the fridge; Opening the fridge, he felt cold air rush out.

Tip: Opening / Closing needs the person who opened it.

TRUE — The film is based on true events; Based on… correctly modifies the film.

Tip: Based on / Inspired by often modify books, films, or stories.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch wildlife and weather rush into the subject slot after -ing openers. Three lines attach correctly; the heron and the cold air do not.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having missed the bus, a taxi seemed the only option.
Wrapped in foil, the leftovers stayed fresh until Friday.
Worried about the forecast, umbrellas were packed in every bag.
Climbing the stairs two at a time, Dan reached the flat first.
Known for its spicy sauce, the street stall draws long queues.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A taxi did not miss the bus; Having missed the bus, she decided a taxi was the only option.

Tip: Having missed needs the misser, not the alternative plan.

TRUE — The leftovers were wrapped; Wrapped modifies the food.

Tip: Wrapped / Sealed / Stored can modify leftovers and packages.

FALSE — Umbrellas cannot worry; Worried about the forecast, they packed umbrellas in every bag.

Tip: Worried / Anxious always need a person.

TRUE — Dan climbed and reached the flat; clean match.

Tip: Climbing / Running + person subject is straightforward.

TRUE — The stall is known for its sauce; Known for… attaches to the stall.

Tip: Known for / Famous for can modify places and things.
tasks.solution_overview: Two dangles put a taxi and umbrellas in the experiencer role. The other three keep leftovers, Dan, and a stall as logical subjects.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been postponed twice, the match finally went ahead on Sunday.
Turning the corner, a sudden gust nearly knocked her over.
Delighted with the results, the students shared their project online.
Growing in a sunny window, the herbs thrived all summer.
Expecting a quiet evening, the doorbell rang again and again.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The match had been postponed; Having been postponed correctly modifies it.

Tip: Having been + past participle works for events that underwent delay or change.

FALSE — A gust cannot turn the corner; Turning the corner, she was nearly knocked over by a sudden gust.

Tip: Turning / Rounding needs the walker or driver.

TRUE — The students are delighted; attachment is clean.

Tip: Delighted / Pleased + people is a reliable pattern.

TRUE — The herbs grow in the window; Growing modifies the herbs.

Tip: Growing / Blooming can modify plants.

FALSE — A doorbell cannot expect an evening; Expecting a quiet evening, they heard the doorbell ring again and again.

Tip: Expecting / Hoping need a human subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Passive perfect on an event and plant-friendly Growing pass. Gusts and doorbells cannot turn corners or expect evenings.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Stolen from a museum decades ago, the painting was finally recovered.
Whistling a tune, the pavement glistened after the shower.
Having reheated the stew, leftovers never tasted better.
Shocked by the ending, viewers sat in silence for a moment.
Parked under a tree, the bicycle stayed cool in the heat.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The painting was stolen; Stolen modifies the artwork.

Tip: Stolen / Lost / Found can modify objects that underwent those events.

FALSE — Pavement cannot whistle; Whistling a tune, he noticed the pavement glistening after the shower.

Tip: Whistling / Humming need a person.

FALSE — Leftovers did not reheat the stew; Having reheated the stew, she thought leftovers never tasted better.

Tip: Having reheated needs the cook as subject.

TRUE — Viewers are shocked; the participle matches.

Tip: Shocked / Moved / Inspired + audience is fine.

TRUE — The bicycle was parked; Parked attaches to the bike.

Tip: Parked / Locked / Chained can modify vehicles and bikes.
tasks.solution_overview: Object states (Stolen, Parked) and shocked viewers work. Whistling pavement and reheating leftovers swap the real agent out of the subject slot.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having trained for months, the marathon still felt brutal.
Filled with old photographs, the album sat on the shelf.
Realising the mistake, a corrected draft was emailed at once.
Accompanied by a guide, the hikers crossed the ridge safely.
Sitting by the window, rain streaked the glass for hours.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The marathon did not train; Having trained for months, she still found the marathon brutal.

Tip: Having trained needs the athlete, not the race.

TRUE — The album was filled with photographs; Filled modifies the album.

Tip: Filled / Packed / Lined can modify containers and spaces.

FALSE — A draft cannot realise a mistake; Realising the mistake, he emailed a corrected draft at once.

Tip: Realising / Noticing need a thinker.

TRUE — The hikers were accompanied; Accompanied by… matches them.

Tip: Accompanied / Joined by can modify people.

FALSE — Rain was not sitting by the window; Sitting by the window, she watched rain streak the glass for hours.

Tip: Sitting / Standing openers need the sitter.
tasks.solution_overview: Two pass; three fail by putting a race, a draft, or rain where a person should be. Mental verbs (Realising) are especially strict.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been invited late, a seat near the back was all that remained.
Carved from oak, the table dominated the dining room.
Frustrated with the slow Wi-Fi, several restarts were tried.
Watching from the stands, they spotted their friend on the pitch.
Frozen solid overnight, the pond looked safe enough to skate on.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A seat was not invited; Having been invited late, she found only a seat near the back remained.

Tip: Having been invited needs the invitee.

TRUE — The table was carved from oak; Carved modifies the table.

Tip: Carved / Made / Assembled can modify furniture and objects.

FALSE — Restarts cannot feel frustrated; Frustrated with the slow Wi-Fi, he tried several restarts.

Tip: Frustrated / Annoyed need a person, not the remedy.

TRUE — They watched and spotted their friend; clean attachment.

Tip: Watching / Listening from… needs the observer as subject.

TRUE — The pond was frozen; Frozen solid overnight fits.

Tip: Frozen / Thawed / Flooded can modify places and surfaces.
tasks.solution_overview: Passive invitation and frustrated restarts dangle. Carved table, watching fans, and a frozen pond show when objects and people attach correctly.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having mixed the batter too quickly, lumps remained in the cake.
Driven by curiosity, the children opened the attic door.
Stored in a cool cupboard, the spices kept their flavour for years.
Hearing the final whistle, celebrations spilled onto the pitch.
Located near the harbour, the café fills up every weekend.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Lumps did not mix the batter; Having mixed the batter too quickly, she left lumps in the cake.

Tip: Having mixed needs the baker.

TRUE — The children are driven by curiosity; Driven by… matches them.

Tip: Driven by / Motivated by can modify people with motives.

TRUE — The spices were stored cool; Stored modifies the spices.

Tip: Stored / Kept / Aged can modify food and goods.

FALSE — Celebrations cannot hear a whistle; Hearing the final whistle, the fans spilled onto the pitch in celebration.

Tip: Hearing needs ears — put the hearers as subject.

TRUE — The café is located near the harbour; Located attaches to the place.

Tip: Located / Situated / Nestled often modify buildings and venues.
tasks.solution_overview: Abstract results (lumps, celebrations) steal the subject after Having and Hearing. Driven children and located café keep the logic straight.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been repaired poorly, the zipper jammed again within a week.
Crossing the busy square, street musicians played near the fountain.
Impressed by the choir, tickets for the next concert sold out.
Drying on the balcony, the sheets flapped in the breeze.
Hoping for clearer skies, the picnic was moved to Saturday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The zipper had been repaired poorly; Having been repaired matches it.

Tip: Having been + past participle can modify objects that underwent a process.

FALSE — Musicians were not crossing (or the subject is ambiguous); Crossing the busy square, they heard street musicians near the fountain.

Tip: Crossing / Entering must describe the grammatical subject, not a nearby scene.

FALSE — Tickets cannot be impressed; Impressed by the choir, fans bought tickets until the next concert sold out.

Tip: Impressed / Amazed need an experiencer.

TRUE — The sheets were drying; Drying modifies the sheets.

Tip: Drying / Hanging / Airings can modify laundry and cloth.

FALSE — A picnic cannot hope; Hoping for clearer skies, they moved the picnic to Saturday.

Tip: Hoping always needs a person with a wish.
tasks.solution_overview: Only two attach cleanly. Scene-setting Crossing, impressed tickets, and a hoping picnic are the traps.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having checked the timetable twice, the platform still looked empty.
Buried under autumn leaves, the path was easy to miss.
Amused by the cartoon, laughter filled the living room.
Using only leftover vegetables, they made a surprisingly good soup.
Designed for beginners, the course starts with simple chords.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The platform did not check the timetable; Having checked the timetable twice, she still found the platform empty.

Tip: Having checked needs the checker.

TRUE — The path was buried under leaves; Buried modifies the path.

Tip: Buried / Hidden / Covered can modify places and paths.

FALSE — Laughter cannot be amused; Amused by the cartoon, they filled the living room with laughter.

Tip: Amused / Entertained need people.

TRUE — They used leftovers and made soup; Using… matches the cooks.

Tip: Using / Following + person subject is clean when the person does the using.

TRUE — The course was designed for beginners; Designed modifies the course.

Tip: Designed for / Intended for often modify products and courses.
tasks.solution_overview: Platforms and laughter cannot check or feel amusement. Buried path, cooking Using, and Designed course show correct object and agent matches.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been woken by birdsong, coffee seemed urgently necessary.
Sewn by hand, the costume took three weeks to finish.
Confused about the homework, several questions were emailed to the tutor.
Standing on tiptoe, she could just reach the top shelf.
Inspired by the podcast, a long walk through the city followed.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Coffee was not woken by birdsong; Having been woken by birdsong, he decided coffee seemed urgently necessary.

Tip: Having been woken needs the sleeper.

TRUE — The costume was sewn by hand; Sewn modifies the costume.

Tip: Sewn / Knitted / Woven can modify garments and crafts.

FALSE — Questions cannot feel confused; Confused about the homework, she emailed several questions to the tutor.

Tip: Confused + inanimate subject is a dangling classic.

TRUE — She stood on tiptoe and reached; attachment is exact.

Tip: Standing / Kneeling + person subject is straightforward.

FALSE — A walk cannot be inspired; Inspired by the podcast, he took a long walk through the city.

Tip: Inspired / Motivated need a person, not the resulting activity.
tasks.solution_overview: Coffee, emailed questions, and a walk steal the experiencer role. Only the sewn costume and standing reacher attach correctly.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been warned about the tide, the beach was abandoned before dusk.
Balancing the tray carefully, not a single glass spilled.
Written for young readers, the story still amuses adults.
Exhausted but determined, the team finished the relay.
Glancing at her watch, the meeting seemed endless.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The beach was not warned; Having been warned about the tide, they abandoned the beach before dusk.

Tip: Having been warned needs the people who received the warning.

FALSE — A glass did not balance the tray; Balancing the tray carefully, she spilled not a single glass.

Tip: Balancing / Carrying need the balancer as subject.

TRUE — The story was written for young readers; Written for… fits.

Tip: Written for / Aimed at can modify books and stories.

TRUE — The team is exhausted but determined; both participles match the team.

Tip: Paired adjectives/participles still need one logical subject.

FALSE — A meeting cannot glance at a watch; Glancing at her watch, she felt the meeting seemed endless.

Tip: Glancing / Peering need a person with eyes.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder dangles: warned beach, balancing glass, glancing meeting. Only the story and the exhausted team keep logical subjects.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having reduced sugar in the recipe, the muffins tasted less sweet.
Caught in traffic, patience wore thin before the lights changed.
Hidden behind the curtains, the cat watched the room in silence.
Relying on memory alone, several steps in the dance were skipped.
Charged overnight, the phone lasted through the whole trip.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Muffins did not reduce the sugar; Having reduced sugar in the recipe, she found the muffins tasted less sweet.

Tip: Having reduced needs the cook, not the result.

FALSE — Patience cannot be caught in traffic; Caught in traffic, they felt patience wear thin before the lights changed.

Tip: Caught in… needs the travellers.

TRUE — The cat was hidden; Hidden behind… matches the cat.

Tip: Hidden / Crouched / Nestled can modify animals and people.

FALSE — Steps cannot rely on memory; Relying on memory alone, they skipped several steps in the dance.

Tip: Relying / Depending need a person.

TRUE — The phone was charged overnight; Charged modifies the phone.

Tip: Charged / Updated / Reset can modify devices.
tasks.solution_overview: Abstract patience and dance steps, plus muffins as cook, are the traps. Hidden cat and charged phone show clean object/animal attachment.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been delayed by roadworks, arrival at the campsite came after midnight.
Folded neatly into the envelope, the letter waited for days.
Unsure which path to take, a coin was tossed in the clearing.
Waving from the platform, her friends disappeared as the train pulled out.
Torn at the corner, the poster still advertised the festival clearly.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Arrival was not delayed on the road; Having been delayed by roadworks, they reached the campsite after midnight.

Tip: Having been delayed needs the travellers, not the abstract arrival.

TRUE — The letter was folded; Folded neatly… modifies the letter.

Tip: Folded / Sealed / Stamped can modify mail and paper.

FALSE — A coin cannot feel unsure; Unsure which path to take, they tossed a coin in the clearing.

Tip: Unsure / Uncertain need a decision-maker.

FALSE — Her friends were not waving from the platform if they disappeared as the train pulled out — the waver should be the subject: Waving from the platform, she watched her friends disappear…

Tip: Check who is actually doing the waving; do not let the wrong noun sit after the comma.

TRUE — The poster was torn; Torn at the corner attaches correctly.

Tip: Torn / Faded / Crumpled can modify posters and paper.
tasks.solution_overview: Abstract arrival, an unsure coin, and a mismatched waving subject fail. Folded letter and torn poster keep object logic intact.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having tasted every sample, a clear favourite emerged among the cheeses.
Stacked against the wall, the canvases leaned at a dangerous angle.
Relieved the exam was over, celebration plans were made on the spot.
Following the river upstream, they found a quieter swimming spot.
Damaged in the storm, several tiles still clung to the roof.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A favourite did not taste the samples; Having tasted every sample, she found a clear favourite among the cheeses.

Tip: Having tasted needs the taster, not the outcome.

TRUE — The canvases were stacked; Stacked against… modifies them.

Tip: Stacked / Leaning / Piled can modify objects in space.

FALSE — Plans cannot feel relieved; Relieved the exam was over, they made celebration plans on the spot.

Tip: Relieved / Glad need a person.

TRUE — They followed the river and found a spot; Following… matches the hikers.

Tip: Following / Tracing a path needs the followers as subject.

TRUE — The tiles were damaged; Damaged in the storm fits.

Tip: Damaged / Cracked / Bent can modify parts and objects.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with a tasting favourite and relieved plans as dangles, then three solid matches: stacked canvases, following hikers, and storm-damaged tiles.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup was hot enough to warm us after the hike.
The soup was enough hot to warm us after the hike.
It was such a noisy café that we could barely talk.
It was so a noisy café that we could barely talk.
The trail was too steep for beginners.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Adjective + enough before a to-infinitive is the standard order. Hot enough to warm us is natural and grammatical.

Tip: After adjectives, put enough last: adj + enough (+ to…).

FALSE — Enough cannot sit before the adjective here. Flip to hot enough (or too hot if you mean excess).

Tip: Never write enough + adjective; reverse it.

TRUE — Such a + adjective + singular countable noun + that-clause is the classic pattern.

Tip: Such takes the noun phrase; so takes the adjective alone.

FALSE — So does not combine with a before a noun. Use such a noisy café, or so noisy that… without the noun.

Tip: So a / so an is almost always wrong — use such a/an.

TRUE — Too + adjective (+ for…) correctly marks excess relative to a purpose or audience.

Tip: Too = excess; enough = sufficiency.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan for the intensifier first: so, such, too, or enough. Then check what follows — adjective alone, noun phrase, or word-order with enough. Easy traps are so a… and enough + adjective.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The fog was so thick that the ferry stayed in harbour.
There was such excitement that the crowd started cheering early.
There was so excitement that the crowd started cheering early.
He is not tall enough for the roller coaster.
He is not enough tall for the roller coaster.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + adjective + that-clause intensifies and links a result.

Tip: So + adj/adv (+ that…); keep the noun out of that slot.

TRUE — Such + uncountable noun (excitement) + that needs no article.

Tip: Such + noun; no a/an with uncountables.

FALSE — So cannot modify a bare noun. Use such excitement or so much excitement.

Tip: So + noun needs much/many (or a determiner phrase).

TRUE — Tall enough places enough after the adjective before for.

Tip: Adj + enough + for / to…

FALSE — Enough tall reverses the required order.

Tip: If enough comes first, check whether a noun follows (enough time) — not an adjective.
tasks.solution_overview: Pair each intensifier with its partner: so with adjectives, such with nouns, enough after adjectives. When so sits before a noun with no much/many, mark it false.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It was such an early train that half the carriages were empty.
It was so an early train that half the carriages were empty.
The suitcase is too heavy to lift alone.
The lecture was too much technical for first-year students.
She sang so beautifully that the hall went silent.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Such an before a vowel-sound adjective + noun is correct (early → an).

Tip: Such a/an agrees with the following sound, not with so.

FALSE — So an is ungrammatical; replace with such an early train or so early that…

Tip: Article + noun belongs with such, not so.

TRUE — Too + adjective + to-infinitive expresses excess preventing a result.

Tip: Too…to often means "so…that not".

FALSE — Do not insert much between too and a single adjective. Too technical is enough; too much modifies nouns (too much noise).

Tip: Too much + noun; too + adjective.

TRUE — So + adverb + that-clause is parallel to so + adjective.

Tip: Beautifully is an adverb, so so beautifully that… is fine.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on article choice with such and the too much trap. If the word after too is an adjective, much should not be there unless you are quantifying a noun.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We had enough daylight to finish photographing the mural.
The path was so icy that cyclists walked their bikes.
She typed so quickly notes that nobody could read them.
The film was such gripping that we stayed until the credits.
The kitchen is large enough for a second fridge.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Enough + noun is correct when enough quantifies a noun (enough daylight).

Tip: Enough + noun vs adjective + enough — two different slots.

TRUE — So + adjective + that correctly builds cause and result.

Tip: Icy is adjectival; so icy that… fits.

FALSE — So quickly notes mixes adverb pattern with a noun. Use so quickly that… or such quick notes that…

Tip: Do not park a noun right after so + adverb.

FALSE — Such needs a noun phrase: such a gripping film, not such gripping alone before that.

Tip: Such + (a/an) + (adj) + noun.

TRUE — Adjective + enough + for + noun phrase is grammatical.

Tip: Enough for X / enough to V — both common after adjectives.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate noun-quantifying enough from adjective-modifying enough. Then catch hybrid errors like so + adverb + noun and such + bare adjective without a noun.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There was so much rain that the cricket match was abandoned.
There were so many volunteers that the charity ran out of badges.
The recipe is too vaguely to follow without a video.
The offer was not generous enough to tempt her back.
It was such bad weather that the outdoor market closed early.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So much + uncountable noun (+ that) is the correct so + noun pattern.

Tip: Uncountable → so much; plural countable → so many.

TRUE — So many + plural countable noun is parallel to so much.

Tip: Count the noun before choosing much/many.

FALSE — Too must modify an adjective after be: too vague to follow, not too vaguely when you mean the recipe itself.

Tip: After linking be, use too + adjective, not too + -ly adverb.

TRUE — Generous enough to… places enough correctly after the adjective.

Tip: Not + adj + enough to… is a common exam pattern.

TRUE — Such + adjective + uncountable noun (weather) needs no article.

Tip: Such bad weather / such good news — no a/an.
tasks.solution_overview: When so modifies quantity, check much vs many. When too follows be, prefer an adjective. Such before uncountable noun phrases usually drops the article.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The app loads too slowly to be useful during live quizzes.
The photos were such blurry that we deleted the whole roll.
We do not have enough flour to bake a second loaf.
It was so narrow a bridge that only one car could cross.
The library was enough quiet for evening revision.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Too + adverb + to-infinitive correctly marks excess manner blocking a purpose.

Tip: Too slowly to… parallels too small to…

FALSE — Such blurry lacks a noun head. Use such blurry photos or so blurry that…

Tip: Such wants a noun; so wants an adjective.

TRUE — Enough + uncountable noun (flour) is correct before to.

Tip: Enough flour / enough time — noun after enough.

TRUE — So + adjective + a + noun (+ that) is a formal but grammatical pattern (so narrow a bridge).

Tip: So adj a noun ≈ such a adj noun; both appear in careful English.

FALSE — Quiet is an adjective, so use quiet enough, not enough quiet.

Tip: Enough before adjectives is a word-order error.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch for such + bare adjective and enough + adjective. The formal so + adj + a + noun pattern is acceptable — do not mark it false just because such a… is more common.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The deadline is tight enough that any delay will cost us the slot.
It was so clever puzzle that the whole class stayed late.
The courier arrived too late for us to catch the evening train.
Such were the crowds that the museum opened an extra wing.
The essay is too much short for a full literature review.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Adj + enough + that-clause is acceptable alongside enough to…

Tip: Enough that… and enough to… both appear; meaning stays "sufficient".

FALSE — So clever puzzle misses the article/noun patterning. Use such a clever puzzle or so clever that…

Tip: So + adj + countable noun without a is a classic miss.

TRUE — Too + adverb/adjective + for + object + to-infinitive is a solid excess pattern.

Tip: Too late for X to V = X cannot V in time.

TRUE — Inversion such were the crowds that… is formal but grammatical.

Tip: Such + be + noun phrase + that is literary/formal, not an error.

FALSE — Too much short wrongly inserts much before an adjective. Use too short.

Tip: Too much ≠ intensifier before adjectives.
tasks.solution_overview: Most items still hinge on word order and partners of so/such/too. One formal inversion with such is correct — do not reject unusual word order if the grammar holds.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The map was not clear enough for hikers to follow in mist.
They made so rapid progress that the language course finished early.
They made such rapid progress that the language course finished early.
The backpack is too heavily to carry up the ridge.
We kept enough spare batteries to last the whole festival.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Not + adj + enough + for + noun + to-infinitive is fully grammatical.

Tip: Enough often licenses a for…to… complement.

TRUE — So + adjective + uncountable noun (progress) without a is acceptable; progress is uncountable.

Tip: So + adj + uncountable noun can work; contrast so clever puzzle (countable needs a).

TRUE — Such + adjective + uncountable noun is the safer textbook twin of the previous pattern.

Tip: Such rapid progress is the exam-safe default.

FALSE — Too heavily is an adverb where an adjective is needed after be: too heavy / too heavily loaded…

Tip: Linking verb → too + adjective.

TRUE — Enough + adjective + plural noun quantifies how many of that type you have.

Tip: Enough spare batteries = a sufficient number of that kind.
tasks.solution_overview: Distinguish countable vs uncountable after so/such, and adjective vs adverb after be. Enough before a noun phrase (enough spare batteries) is fine — that is not the enough + adjective error.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.
The view was such stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.
The oven is not hot enough to crisp the pastry.
It was too a complicated route for a first visit.
There has been such an upsurge in tickets that the box office stayed open late.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + adjective + as to + infinitive is a formal result pattern parallel to so…that.

Tip: So…as to… ≈ so…that someone does…

FALSE — Such does not take as to after a bare adjective. Use so stunning as to… or such a stunning view that…

Tip: Such pairs with nouns; so…as to pairs with adjectives.

TRUE — Not + adjective + enough + to… is correct.

Tip: Participial and ordinary adjectives both take enough after them.

FALSE — Too a complicated is wrong; use too complicated a route or such a complicated route.

Tip: Too + adj + a + noun is possible (too complicated a route), but too a… never is.

TRUE — Such an + noun (+ that) correctly intensifies a countable singular.

Tip: Upsurge is countable → such an upsurge.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal so…as to… is fair game. Check that such is not forced into that frame, and that too never precedes the article directly (too a…).

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The novel is too dense a book for a single weekend.
Fans left because the queue was such long.
We arrived early enough to claim seats near the stage.
The coach found the warm-up so rushed that she ordered another lap.
She is enough experienced to lead the climbing group.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is a formal pattern matching so adj a noun.

Tip: Too dense a book = such a dense book in meaning of excess.

FALSE — Such long needs a noun: such a long queue, or so long that…

Tip: Bare such + adjective without noun is incomplete.

TRUE — Adverb early + enough + to-infinitive is correct (enough after the adverb).

Tip: Adv + enough mirrors adj + enough.

TRUE — So + adjective + that after a reporting verb is clean.

Tip: Found X so adj that… keeps so on the adjective.

FALSE — Experienced is an adjective → experienced enough, not enough experienced.

Tip: Same flip rule as enough hot.
tasks.solution_overview: Accept the formal too/so + adj + a + noun shapes when articles land after the adjective. Reject such + bare adjective and enough + adjective.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The storm was so fierce as that ferries cancelled sailings.
The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings.
We lacked enough evidence to challenge the referee's call.
It was such a poorly printed map that hikers took wrong turns.
The hills are too steep for the juniors finish before dusk.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — So…as that mixes two patterns. Choose so…that or so…as to, not both markers.

Tip: Never stack as and that after so.

TRUE — Clean so + adjective + that result clause.

Tip: One linker only: that or as to.

TRUE — Enough + noun (evidence) before to-infinitive is correct.

Tip: Uncountables still take enough + noun.

TRUE — Such a + adverb + adjective + noun is fine when the adverb modifies the adjective inside the noun phrase.

Tip: Such a poorly printed X = noun phrase after such.

FALSE — Missing to before the infinitive: too steep for the juniors to finish…

Tip: For + object needs to before the verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Hunt blended patterns (as that) and missing to after for + object. Such a + heavily modified noun phrase can still be correct.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Practice stopped because the heat became so intense.
Practice stopped because the heat became such intense.
The clause is worded carefully enough to avoid confusion.
There were too few lifeguards to watch every lane.
The gallery hung so few paintings that the room felt empty.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + adjective can stand without a that-clause when the result is implied by context.

Tip: That-clause is common but not obligatory after so/such/too/enough.

FALSE — Such intense needs a noun (such intense heat) or switch to so intense.

Tip: After become, prefer so + adjective.

TRUE — Carefully enough places enough after the adverb modifying the participle/adjective phrase.

Tip: Adv + enough + to… works like adj + enough.

TRUE — Too few + plural noun expresses insufficiency (excess of scarcity).

Tip: Too few ≈ not enough; grammar differs from too much + adj.

TRUE — So few + plural noun + that is grammatical and parallel to so many.

Tip: Few/little pair with so the same way many/much do.
tasks.solution_overview: Result clauses are optional. Focus on whether such has a noun and whether few/little sit correctly after so/too.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour.
The rule is so that latecomers wait for the next tour.
Runners pulled out, the course having become too muddy to race.
She left enough of a gap to let the next cyclist pass.
The trail is not enough marked for night walking.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Such that meaning "of a kind that" is a fixed formal pattern without an adjective.

Tip: Noun + is such that… = the nature of X means…

FALSE — So that expresses purpose ("in order that"), not the "of a kind that" reading. Here such that is required.

Tip: So that ≠ such that; different jobs.

TRUE — Too + adjective + to-infinitive inside a participial absolute is still grammatical.

Tip: Too…to… keeps its shape in reduced clauses.

TRUE — Enough of a + singular countable noun is idiomatic.

Tip: Enough of a gap / enough of an issue — of a(n) before singular count nouns.

FALSE — Marked is adjectival here → not marked enough, not not enough marked.

Tip: Flip enough after adjectives even with not.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder items distinguish such that (nature/result) from so that (purpose), and test enough of a… plus adjective–enough order under negation.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Attendance fell so low as volunteers began cancelling shifts.
Attendance fell so low that volunteers began cancelling shifts.
The visa proved too costly a requirement for the exchange student.
We cannot cook without such spices as the recipe lists.
The rebuild was enough extensive that the gallery closed for a year.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — So…as without to needs a comparative/manner reading or as to; here a result clause should use that (or so low as to cause…).

Tip: So adj as + finite clause is not standard for result.

TRUE — So + adjective + that correctly states the result.

Tip: Default result linker after so/such is that.

TRUE — Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is grammatical formal English.

Tip: Too costly a requirement ≈ an excessively costly requirement.

TRUE — Such…as meaning "the kind that" with a relative-like clause is correct.

Tip: Such spices as X lists = the spices that X lists.

FALSE — Enough extensive reverses order; need extensive enough that…

Tip: Enough never precedes the adjective in this frame.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate result that from faulty so…as + clause, and recognise formal such…as and too adj a noun. Keep policing enough + adjective.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The playlist was so arranged as to build toward the finale.
Cash on hand is barely enough for bus fare, let alone a taxi.
It was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.
There was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.
The dish became such favourite with locals that tourists queued daily.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + past participle/adjective + as to + infinitive expresses designed result.

Tip: So arranged as to… = arranged in such a way that…

TRUE — Enough for + noun works; barely intensifies sufficiency without breaking grammar.

Tip: Modifiers like barely/almost can precede enough.

FALSE — It was too little time is awkward/wrong; time needs there was / we had too little time, or too little time remained.

Tip: Watch dummy it with quantity noun phrases.

TRUE — There was too little + uncountable noun (+ to…) is the natural existential pattern.

Tip: Prefer there-insertion with too little/much + noun.

FALSE — Needs an article: such a favourite with… (or so popular with…).

Tip: Countable singular after such almost always needs a/an.
tasks.solution_overview: Judge existential framing with too little + noun, article requirements after such, and formal so…as to…. Surface similarity can hide a missing there or a/an.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The experiment is designed such that temperature stays constant.
The experiment is designed so that temperature stays constant.
The dough proved elastic enough that it stretched without tearing.
He spoke with so a confident tone that doubts faded.
We kept the talk short enough not to overrun the lunch break.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Designed such that… means "in such a way that" and is standard in scientific English.

Tip: Verb + such that ≈ configured so that.

TRUE — Designed so that… expressing purpose/result is also grammatical.

Tip: Here so that and such that can both work with slightly different nuance.

TRUE — Adj + enough + that-clause is acceptable.

Tip: Elastic enough that… = sufficiently elastic that…

FALSE — So a confident tone is wrong; use such a confident tone or so confidently that…

Tip: So a… returns as a trap even in longer NPs.

TRUE — Adj + enough + not to-infinitive correctly encodes avoidance.

Tip: Enough not to… = sufficiently… to avoid…
tasks.solution_overview: Both so that and such that can be right after verbs of designing. Still fail so a…, and accept enough not to… as a valid negative infinitive pattern.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Seldom is a coastline so eroded that no beach remains.
The tent proved insufficiently sturdy enough to survive the gale.
Her complaint was not so much unfair as poorly timed.
The delay was such that, had we waited, the concert would have started.
They priced the tickets too steeply for students to attend weekly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Inversion with seldom does not break the inner so…that pattern.

Tip: Judge the so/such/too/enough core even inside inversion shells.

FALSE — Insufficiently sturdy enough doubles the sufficiency marker. Use insufficiently sturdy or not sturdy enough — not both.

Tip: One sufficiency tool per adjective phrase.

TRUE — Not so much X as Y is an established correlative; so is required in this idiom.

Tip: Not so much…as… ≠ ordinary so + adjective, but it is grammatical.

TRUE — Such that introducing a counterfactual continuation is formal and correct.

Tip: Such that can host complex follow-ons, including inverted conditionals.

TRUE — Too + adverb + for + noun + to-infinitive marks excess manner/cost.

Tip: Too steeply for X to V parallels too steep for X to V (adv vs adj depends on what is modified).
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced packaging: inversion, correlative not so much…as…, and stacked markers. Reject double intensifiers like insufficiently…enough while keeping legitimate idioms with so.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No other runner moved so swiftly as to claim the lead overnight.
No other runner moved such swiftly as to claim the lead overnight.
The rule is drawn tightly enough that substitutions need consent.
We had rather too little daylight for a full summit attempt.
The interface was so intuitive a design as users needed no tutorial.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + adverb + as to + infinitive correctly states result after a comparative frame.

Tip: So…as to… works with adverbs as well as adjectives.

FALSE — Such does not modify adverbs; such swiftly is impossible.

Tip: Such → noun phrases only (or such that).

TRUE — Adv/adj + enough + that remains grammatical in careful register.

Tip: Tightly enough that… = sufficiently tightly that…

TRUE — Rather too + adjective/determiner phrase is idiomatic mild criticism.

Tip: Rather/a bit/far can modify too.

FALSE — So intuitive a design as + finite clause mismatches; use so intuitive a design that… or so intuitive that…, or so intuitive as to need…

Tip: So adj a noun pairs with that or as to, not bare as + clause.
highlights: so intuitive a design as users
tasks.solution_overview: Stress-test so…as to… with adverbs, block such + adverb, and require the right linker after so adj a noun. Degree modifiers before too are allowed.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only then did the river become high enough for kayaking to look safe.
The study was based on so biased a sample that the conclusions collapsed.
The study was based on such biased a sample that the conclusions collapsed.
Supplies look healthy enough; still, they may prove too thin under strain.
He is too much of a perfectionist to submit an unfinished draft.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Inversion only then did… leaves high enough for… intact and grammatical.

Tip: Embedded enough patterns survive fronting and inversion.

TRUE — So + adjective + a + noun + that is the formal pattern inside a prepositional phrase.

Tip: So biased a sample = such a biased sample.

FALSE — Such biased a sample mis-orders the article; need such a biased sample (article before the adjective).

Tip: Such a + adj + noun, never such adj a noun.

TRUE — Two coordinated judgments: adj + enough, and too + adj, both well formed.

Tip: Enough and too can contrast in one sentence without clashing.

TRUE — Too much of a + noun + to-infinitive is a fixed evaluative idiom.

Tip: Too much of a X to V = excessively X-like to V.
tasks.solution_overview: Article placement separates so adj a noun (correct) from such adj a noun (incorrect). Also recognise the idiom too much of a… to…

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had the ice been thick enough, the skaters would have crossed the lake.
The rehearsal grew so protracted as nobody could finalise the cues.
Whatever the poster promises, service is seldom swift enough to match it.
It remains too early a stage for full automation of bookings.
Their reply was so that we cancelled the booking at once.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Adj + enough inside an inverted third conditional is grammatical.

Tip: Enough keeps adjective-final order even in had-conditionals.

FALSE — So…as + finite clause is wrong for result; use so protracted that… or so protracted as to prevent…

Tip: As to + infinitive, or that + clause — not as + clause after so + adj.

TRUE — Seldom… enough to… correctly denies sufficiency.

Tip: Frequency adverb + enough pattern is fine.

TRUE — Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is formal but correct.

Tip: Too early a stage = an excessively early stage.

FALSE — So that marks purpose ("in order that"), not the nature/result reading needed here. Use such that we cancelled… or Their reply was so blunt that we cancelled…

Tip: Reply/situation + such that = character/result; so that = purpose.
tasks.solution_overview: Final set mixes conditionals, formal too adj a noun, and result-linker discipline after so. Prefer that or as to for results, and keep such that vs so that distinct.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success depends of careful practice before the recital.
She is responsible of watering the neighbour's plants.
They are interested on learning Portuguese this summer.
Despite of the rain, the picnic went ahead.
He was accused of cheating in the board-game tournament.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use depends on, not depends of, for this fixed dependency pattern.

Tip: After depend, lock in on — of is a common L1 transfer trap.

FALSE — Use responsible for, not responsible of.

Tip: Pair responsible with for + noun/gerund; of is wrong here.

FALSE — The fixed pattern is interested in, not interested on.

Tip: Interest takes in; on belongs with focus/concentrate.

FALSE — Despite never takes of; write Despite the rain or In spite of the rain.

Tip: Despite of is always wrong — drop of or switch to in spite of.

TRUE — Accused of + gerund/noun is the standard collocation.

Tip: Accuse/charge of wrongdoing; do not swap in for after accused.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan each sentence for a fixed verb/adjective + preposition lock. Ask whether the preposition matches the standard pattern, and watch for the classic despite of false friend.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He insisted on seeing the raw score sheets.
Her recipe differs of last year's version.
We apologised about spilling juice on the carpet.
The documentary focuses to ocean plastics.
She participated in the weekend pottery workshop.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Insist on + gerund is the fixed pattern here.

Tip: After insist, use on + -ing, not a bare infinitive.

FALSE — Use differs from, not differs of.

Tip: Differ/different → from; do not write differ of.

FALSE — Prefer apologised for spilling… in careful exam English.

Tip: Apologise for a fault or inconvenience; about is weaker and often marked wrong.

FALSE — Use focuses on, not focuses to.

Tip: Focus/concentrate take on, never to.

TRUE — Participated in correctly names involvement in an event.

Tip: Participate/join/engage → in an event or activity.
tasks.solution_overview: These items test high-frequency everyday collocations. Match each verb to its locked preposition, and rewrite any false friend before deciding TRUE or FALSE.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They objected against the new quiet-hours rule.
The volunteer is capable of handling the front desk.
She is good in swimming long distances.
We look forward to meeting your cousins.
He succeeded to repair the bicycle chain.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Object takes to, not against: objected to the rule.

Tip: Object to X; protest against is a different verb.

TRUE — Capable of + gerund is the fixed ability pattern.

Tip: Capable of doing; able to do — different frames.

FALSE — Use good at swimming, not good in for skills.

Tip: Good/bad/skilled at activities; in is for subjects like good in maths only in some varieties — exam English prefers at for skills.

TRUE — Look forward to + gerund (meeting) is correct; to is a preposition here.

Tip: After look forward to, use a noun or -ing, never a bare infinitive.

FALSE — Succeed in repairing, not succeed to repair.

Tip: Succeed in + -ing; manage to + infinitive is the other pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Check object to, capable of, good at, look forward to + -ing, and succeed in. Wrong prepositions or infinitives after these heads are almost always FALSE.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The salad consists from tomatoes, cucumber, and feta.
This jacket belongs to my older brother.
You can rely of her to bring the tent.
They complained for the noisy neighbours upstairs.
A locked gate prevented them from entering the park.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Consist of lists the parts; consist from is wrong.

Tip: Consist of / be made of — not from after consist.

TRUE — Belong to correctly marks ownership.

Tip: Belong to someone; never belong of.

FALSE — Use rely on, not rely of.

Tip: Rely/depend/count → on.

FALSE — Complain about a problem; complain for is non-standard here.

Tip: Complain about noise/service; complain to a person.

TRUE — Prevent someone from + gerund is the fixed restraint pattern.

Tip: Prevent/stop/keep from doing; not to do after prevent.
tasks.solution_overview: Everyday ownership and hindrance verbs lock tightly: consist of, belong to, rely on, complain about, prevent from. Mark any swapped preposition false.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Lisbon is famous for its tiled façades.
This trail is similar with the one near the lake.
My playlist is different than yours in every genre.
She has been married with her partner for twelve years.
The children are afraid of thunderstorms at night.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Famous for + noun phrase is the standard reputation pattern.

Tip: Famous/known for a feature; famous as a role.

FALSE — Similar to, not similar with.

Tip: Similar/identical/comparable → to.

FALSE — In careful exam English prefer different from (or different to in BrE); different than is often marked down.

Tip: Different from is the safest exam choice.

FALSE — Married to a person, not married with.

Tip: Married to someone; with belongs in other frames (live with).

TRUE — Afraid of + noun is correct.

Tip: Afraid of something; frightened of works the same way.
tasks.solution_overview: Adjective + preposition pairs are rigid: famous for, similar to, different from, married to, afraid of. Swap the preposition and the sentence fails.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We arrived to the station just before midnight.
Please listen to the podcast episode I sent.
They waited the bus for twenty minutes in the rain.
Look at the mural behind the café.
We talked the film for almost an hour.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Arrive at a station/building; arrive in a city/country — not arrive to.

Tip: Arrive at/in; get to is the to-pattern.

TRUE — Listen to + object is obligatory in standard English.

Tip: Hear can take a direct object; listen needs to.

FALSE — Wait for the bus; wait cannot take a bare object here.

Tip: Wait for someone/something.

TRUE — Look at correctly directs visual attention.

Tip: Look at / stare at; watch can take a direct object.

FALSE — Talk about the film; talk needs about (or to a person).

Tip: Talk about a topic; discuss a topic (no about).
tasks.solution_overview: Perception and movement verbs often need a preposition English learners drop: arrive at/in, listen to, wait for, look at, talk about.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She goes to work by foot every morning.
They travelled to the coast by train.
The match starts in Monday evening.
I usually read in night when the house is quiet.
We met on a cold Friday afternoon.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — On foot, not by foot.

Tip: By + vehicle (by bus/train/car); on foot is the walking exception.

TRUE — By train correctly names the means of transport.

Tip: By + vehicle is the default transport pattern.

FALSE — On Monday / on Monday evening, not in Monday.

Tip: On + days and dated times; in + months/years/parts of day (in the evening).

FALSE — At night is the fixed time phrase; in night is wrong.

Tip: At night / in the night (rarer); never bare in night.

TRUE — On + day/date phrases is standard.

Tip: On Friday / on Friday afternoon both work.
tasks.solution_overview: Time and transport prepositions are closed sets: by + vehicle, on foot, on + day, at night. Memorise the exceptions rather than translating.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We congratulated her for winning the baking contest.
Don't blame me about the burnt toast.
Thanks for helping me move the sofa.
The hostel provided us with clean towels.
Police charged him of vandalising the bus stop.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Congratulate someone on winning; for is weaker/wrong in exam English after congratulate.

Tip: Congratulate on an achievement.

FALSE — Blame someone for something, not about.

Tip: Blame for / accuse of — different heads, different prepositions.

TRUE — Thank(s) for + gerund/noun is correct.

Tip: Thank for help; thank someone for doing X.

TRUE — Provide someone with something is the classic ditransitive pattern.

Tip: Provide with / supply with; provide something to someone is also possible.

FALSE — Charge someone with an offence, not of.

Tip: Charge with; accuse of — do not mix them.
tasks.solution_overview: Speech-act verbs split carefully: congratulate on, blame for, thank for, provide with, charge with. Mixing for/of/about across these heads is a common trap.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is keen on early-morning runs along the canal.
She is fond from old jazz records.
They take pride of their community garden.
I'm tired of waiting for the plumber.
He gets bored of the same playlist every day.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Keen on + noun/gerund expresses enthusiasm.

Tip: Keen on ≈ interested in / enthusiastic about.

FALSE — Fond of, not fond from.

Tip: Fond of people and things you like.

FALSE — Take pride in, not pride of.

Tip: Pride in / proud of — related meaning, different prepositions.

TRUE — Tired of + gerund/noun is fixed.

Tip: Tired of doing X; exhausted from effort is a different idea.

FALSE — Prefer bored with (or by) in careful English; bored of is informal/non-standard for many exams.

Tip: Bored with the routine; fed up with is the of-cousin.
tasks.solution_overview: Attitude adjectives and nouns lock to one preposition: keen on, fond of, pride in, tired of, bored with. Near-synonyms do not share prepositions.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: According to the weather app, storms arrive tonight.
We stayed home because of the flooding.
She chose tea instead coffee after dinner.
In addition of stretching, he iced his knee.
As a result of the delay, they missed the opening act.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — According to + source is the reporting preposition phrase.

Tip: According to X; never according with for this meaning.

TRUE — Because of + noun phrase correctly gives a reason.

Tip: Because of + noun; because + clause.

FALSE — Instead of coffee; instead alone cannot take a bare noun like this.

Tip: Instead of X; instead (adverb) stands alone.

FALSE — In addition to stretching, not in addition of.

Tip: In addition to / as well as — both take to, not of.

TRUE — As a result of + noun phrase is a fixed causal pattern.

Tip: As a result of X; as a result (alone) needs a comma and a clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Multi-word prepositions are all-or-nothing: according to, because of, instead of, in addition to, as a result of. Missing or swapped final prepositions make the item false.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She insisted that we leave the campsite before dawn.
The coach discouraged them to swim after dark.
Warm soup helped him recover from the cold.
Nothing will stop her to finish the marathon.
He specialised in marine biology at university.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Insist that + clause is a separate fixed pattern from insist on + -ing.

Tip: Insist that (clause) vs insist on (gerund) — both valid, different frames.

FALSE — Discourage someone from swimming, not to swim.

Tip: Discourage/prevent/keep from + -ing.

TRUE — Recover from an illness is the standard medical collocation.

Tip: Recover from; recover of is wrong.

FALSE — Stop her from finishing / stop her finishing; not stop her to finish for prevention.

Tip: Stop to do = pause in order to; stop from doing = prevent.

TRUE — Specialise in a field is fixed.

Tip: Specialise/major in a subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch verbs that look like they take infinitives but actually take from + -ing (discourage, stop for prevention). Keep insist that and specialise in intact.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'm used to waking up before sunrise.
She used to waking up before sunrise when she worked nights.
They are accustomed with long bus rides.
He prefers walking to cycling in the city.
We prefer walking than cycling when it rains.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Be used to + gerund means accustomed to a habit.

Tip: Be/get used to + noun/-ing.

FALSE — Used to + base verb for past habits: used to wake, not used to waking.

Tip: Used to V (past habit) ≠ be used to V-ing (accustomed).

FALSE — Accustomed to, not accustomed with.

Tip: Accustomed/used → to.

TRUE — Prefer X to Y correctly compares two options.

Tip: Prefer A to B; not prefer A than B.

FALSE — Prefer … than is wrong; use prefer walking to cycling, or would rather walk than cycle.

Tip: Prefer to; rather than.
highlights: used to waking up before sunrise when
tasks.solution_overview: Separate past-habit used to + V from be used to + -ing, keep accustomed to, and compare preferences with prefer A to B — never prefer … than.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of the heat, they finished the hike.
In spite the heat, they finished the hike.
Notwithstanding the late start, the choir sounded polished.
She refrained to comment during the argument.
Please refrain from posting spoilers online.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — In spite of + noun phrase equals despite.

Tip: In spite of keeps of; despite drops it.

FALSE — In spite must be followed by of before a noun.

Tip: Never write in spite the… — insert of.

TRUE — Notwithstanding takes a noun phrase with no extra of.

Tip: Notwithstanding X ≈ despite X.

FALSE — Refrain from commenting, not refrain to comment.

Tip: Refrain/abstain from + -ing.

TRUE — Refrain from + gerund is the fixed restraint pattern.

Tip: From + -ing after refrain.
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast markers split: despite / notwithstanding (no of) versus in spite of (needs of). Restraint verbs take from + -ing, not to-infinitives.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The outcome of the experiment depends on temperature.
Access to the roof terrace is restricted after dusk.
She has no intention to cancel the trip.
There is no point of arguing about the score.
What's the point in staying if the museum is closed?
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Depend on correctly links outcome to a condition.

Tip: Outcome of X; depend on Y — two different prepositions in one sentence can both be right.

TRUE — Access to a place is the fixed pattern.

Tip: Access to; entrance to; not access of for places.

FALSE — Intention of cancelling / no intention of -ing is preferred; intention to is often marked wrong in exams.

Tip: Have no intention of doing X.

FALSE — No point in arguing, not point of arguing in this frame.

Tip: No point in + -ing; what's the point of is a related but different pattern.

TRUE — Point in + gerund is acceptable in this rhetorical question.

Tip: Point in / point of both appear; match the whole fixed frame.
