tasks.solution_overview: Abstract nouns pick locked prepositions: access to, intention of, point in/of. Do not assume to after every noun that feels "future-facing."

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She was angry with her brother for borrowing her headphones.
He was angry about the cancelled ferry.
They were pleased of the surprise birthday brunch.
I'm delighted with how the garden turned out.
We were surprised from the sudden snowfall.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Angry with a person + for a reason is a solid double pattern.

Tip: Angry with people; angry about situations.

TRUE — Angry about a situation/event is correct.

Tip: About for things; with for people.

FALSE — Pleased with/by, not pleased of.

Tip: Proud of vs pleased with — do not swap.

TRUE — Delighted with a result is natural and grammatical.

Tip: Delighted with/by; delighted to hear that…

FALSE — Surprised by/at, not surprised from.

Tip: Surprised by news; shocked at/by.
tasks.solution_overview: Emotion adjectives split people vs situations (angry with / about) and reject of/from transfers (pleased with, surprised by).

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup tastes of garlic and lemon.
This jacket smells like woodsmoke.
She reminded me of my primary-school teacher.
Can you remind me of locking the back door?
Please remind him to bring the picnic blanket.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Taste of a flavour is a fixed sensory pattern.

Tip: Taste of / smell of a substance.

TRUE — Smell like is acceptable for resemblance.

Tip: Smell of a substance; smell like a comparison — both can work.

TRUE — Remind someone of a person/thing (resemblance or memory trigger).

Tip: Remind of a memory; remind to do a duty.

FALSE — For a future action use remind me to lock, not remind me of locking.

Tip: Remind of = memory/resemblance; remind to = instruction.

TRUE — Remind someone to + infinitive correctly issues a prompt.

Tip: Reminder for actions → to + V.
tasks.solution_overview: Sensory of/like patterns are fine; remind splits into of (memory) versus to (future action). Mixing those two frames is the hard trap.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival was cancelled owing to high winds.
Owing the high winds, the festival was cancelled.
The hike was postponed due to flooding on the trail.
Due the flooding, the hike was postponed.
Thanks to a clear sky, we saw the meteor shower.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Owing to + noun phrase is a formal causal preposition.

Tip: Owing to = because of.

FALSE — Owing needs to before the noun phrase.

Tip: Never drop to from owing to.

TRUE — Due to + noun is widely accepted as a causal preposition in modern exam English.

Tip: Due to X / because of X.

FALSE — Due the… is incomplete; insert to.

Tip: Due to, not bare due before a noun cause.

TRUE — Thanks to + noun credits a positive cause.

Tip: Thanks to (positive); owing to / due to (neutral/negative).
tasks.solution_overview: Causal multi-word prepositions all keep their final to: owing to, due to, thanks to. Any stripped to is an automatic false.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She accused him for leaving the gate open.
They suspected her of feeding the stray cats.
He was convicted for trespassing on farmland.
The club banned him from using the tennis courts.
Nothing can compensate the loss of the old oak.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Accuse someone of doing, not for.

Tip: Accuse of; blame for.

TRUE — Suspected of + gerund is the fixed collocation.

Tip: Suspected/accused of wrongdoing.

FALSE — Convicted of an offence is the standard legal/exam pattern (for appears in some loose usage but of is safer here).

Tip: Convicted of; charged with.

TRUE — Ban someone from + gerund/noun is correct.

Tip: Ban/prohibit from; forbid someone to is different.

FALSE — Compensate for a loss; compensate cannot take the loss as a bare object in this sense.

Tip: Compensate for damage/loss.
tasks.solution_overview: Fault and restriction vocabulary is preposition-heavy: accuse/suspect/convict of, ban from, compensate for. Swapping for/of or dropping the preposition fails the item.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The plan is contingent on dry weather this weekend.
Approval is contingent of dry weather this weekend.
She prides herself in finishing every crossword.
She takes pride in finishing every crossword.
He is proud for his daughter's science prize.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Contingent on + noun/gerund matches depend on.

Tip: Contingent on conditions.

FALSE — Contingent of is a depend-of style transfer error.

Tip: On, not of, after contingent.

FALSE — Pride oneself on doing, not in, after the reflexive verb.

Tip: Pride oneself on; take pride in — different verbs, different prepositions.

TRUE — Take pride in + gerund is fixed.

Tip: Take pride in / be proud of.

FALSE — Proud of an achievement, not proud for.

Tip: Proud of someone/something.
tasks.solution_overview: Near-identical pride frames diverge: pride oneself on vs take pride in vs be proud of. Contingent follows depend → on, never of.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: By the time we arrived, the café had run out of cups.
The café had run out from cups before noon.
I'm looking forward for the weekend hike.
She objects to being photographed without consent.
He succeeded on repairing the leaky tap.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Run out of + noun is the depletion pattern.

Tip: Run out of supplies; run out (intransitive) for time.

FALSE — Run out from cups is wrong; use run out of.

Tip: Of after run out for materials.

FALSE — Looking forward to the hike, not for.

Tip: Look forward to + noun/-ing.

TRUE — Object to + gerund is correct.

Tip: Object to being/doing; not object against.

FALSE — Succeeded in repairing, not on.

Tip: Succeed in + -ing; insist on is a different verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with high-frequency exam traps: run out of, look forward to, object to, succeed in. Wrong satellite prepositions are the only thing that separates TRUE from FALSE here.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wonder where he is.
I wonder where is he.
Could you tell me what time the train leaves?
Could you tell me what time does the train leave?
She asked whether the bakery was still open.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After wonder, the clause keeps statement order: where + subject + verb (where he is), not question inversion.

Tip: Embedded wh-clauses look like statements, not questions.

FALSE — where is he inverts auxiliary and subject, which belongs in a direct question, not after I wonder.

Tip: Drop the inversion: where he is.

TRUE — Polite frame Could you tell me… embeds what time the train leaves with subject before the verb.

Tip: No does inside the embedded clause.

FALSE — does the train leave is direct-question word order jammed into an indirect question.

Tip: Use what time the train leaves.

TRUE — whether correctly introduces a yes/no embedded clause with statement order (the bakery was).

Tip: whether/if + subject + verb — never invert.
tasks.solution_overview: Indirect questions keep statement word order after the question word or whether/if. Scan for stray do/does/did or swapped auxiliary–subject pairs — those belong only in direct questions.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Do you know if the library has opened yet?
Do you know if has the library opened yet?
Please explain why the soup burned.
Please explain why did the soup burn.
They could not decide which route was safer.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — if embeds a yes/no clause with normal order: the library has opened yet.

Tip: After if/whether, never move has/is/will before the subject.

FALSE — if has the library… wrongly inverts the auxiliary into the embedded clause.

Tip: Keep if the library has…

TRUE — why the soup burned is statement order after explain; no auxiliary is needed.

Tip: Embedded why-clauses do not take did unless the original had do-support for another reason.

FALSE — why did the soup burn mirrors a direct question; the embedding verb already carries the interrogative force.

Tip: why + subject + past: why the soup burned.

TRUE — which route was safer keeps subject–verb order inside the embedded choice question.

Tip: which + noun + verb — no extra it.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on if/whether and wh-clauses after know, explain, and decide. Correct items keep subject before the finite verb; wrong ones smuggle direct-question inversion (has…?, did…?) into the subordinate clause.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The question is how the team will respond.
The question is how will the team respond?
I am not sure what caused the blackout.
I am not sure what did cause the blackout.
She asked whether were the tickets still valid.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After The question is, how the team will respond uses statement order (subject team before will).

Tip: Noun-phrase frames still take embedded statement order.

FALSE — how will the team respond? is a direct question glued onto The question is.

Tip: how + subject + modal: how the team will respond.

TRUE — what is the subject of caused, so no do-support is required or allowed.

Tip: Subject wh-clauses never need did.

FALSE — what did cause forces unnecessary do-support into an embedded subject question.

Tip: what caused, not what did cause.

FALSE — whether were the tickets… inverts were and the subject after whether.

Tip: whether the tickets were…
tasks.solution_overview: Watch two classic traps: modal inversion after how (will the team…) and fake did in subject questions (what did cause…). Correct embedded clauses read like calm statements inside a larger sentence.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They could not decide which option was it safer.
I'd like to know when the guests arrive.
I'd like to know when do the guests arrive.
Can you remind me where the spare keys are kept?
Can you remind me where are the spare keys kept?
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Extra pronoun it after was breaks the clause; which option was safer is already complete.

Tip: Never add a dummy it after the verb in an embedded which-clause.

TRUE — when the guests arrive keeps subject–verb order after I'd like to know.

Tip: Softeners like I'd like to know still take statement order.

FALSE — when do the guests arrive inserts do-support as if the clause were a direct question.

Tip: Delete do: when the guests arrive.

TRUE — where the spare keys are kept is passive statement order inside a polite question.

Tip: are stays after the subject keys.

FALSE — where are the spare keys… flips are before the subject inside the embedded clause.

Tip: where + subject + are/is…
highlights: where the spare keys are kept
tasks.solution_overview: Polite frames (I'd like to know, Can you remind me) do not license inversion inside the embedded clause. Also reject dummy it after which… was — the option is already the subject.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nobody could say who had locked the gate.
Nobody could say who had the gate been locked by.
We need to establish whether the courier can arrive by noon.
We need to establish whether can the courier arrive by noon.
Tell me how much the tickets will cost.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — who is subject of had locked; statement order is natural and correct.

Tip: Subject who/what never invert with the verb.

FALSE — who had the gate been… forces awkward inversion and a stranded by that belongs in a rewritten object question.

Tip: Prefer who had locked… or by whom the gate had been locked.

TRUE — whether the courier can arrive… keeps modal can after the subject.

Tip: whether + subject + modal + verb.

FALSE — whether can the courier… is direct yes/no inversion after whether.

Tip: Never put the modal before the subject in an embedded clause.

TRUE — how much the tickets will cost is statement order after Tell me.

Tip: how much/how many + noun phrase + verb — no will-fronting.
highlights: how much the tickets will cost
tasks.solution_overview: Subject wh-words (who locked…) stay simple; modal yes/no embeds keep can/will after the subject. Reject any whether can… or how much will… fronting inside the subordinate clause.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tell me how much will the tickets cost.
The note does not say how long the delay lasted.
The note does not say how long did the delay last.
Parents asked what the school intended to do next.
Parents asked what did the school intend to do next.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — how much will the tickets cost inverts will and the subject after Tell me.

Tip: how much the tickets will cost.

TRUE — how long the delay lasted keeps statement order after say.

Tip: how long + subject + past verb — no did.

FALSE — how long did the delay last smuggles do-support into the embed.

Tip: Delete did: how long the delay lasted.

TRUE — what the school intended… is object-wh with subject before the verb.

Tip: After asked, keep what + subject + verb.

FALSE — what did the school intend… is a direct question sitting inside asked.

Tip: Drop did and keep intended after school.
highlights: how much will the tickets cost
how long did the delay last
tasks.solution_overview: how much/how long and object what-clauses fail when will or did jumps before the subject. Correct embeds keep the finite verb after the subject noun.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I can't remember where I put my passport.
I can't remember where did I put my passport.
Have you found out whether the museum opens on Mondays?
Have you found out whether does the museum open on Mondays?
She wondered why everyone was whispering.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — where I put my passport is statement order after remember.

Tip: Memory verbs still take embedded statement order.

FALSE — where did I put… is direct-question do-support inside an embedded clause.

Tip: where + subject + past: where I put…

TRUE — whether the museum opens… keeps opens after the subject.

Tip: whether + subject + verb — no does.

FALSE — whether does the museum open… invents do-support after whether.

Tip: whether the museum opens…

TRUE — why everyone was whispering keeps was after the subject.

Tip: After wonder, why + subject + verb.
tasks.solution_overview: remember, find out, and wonder all embed statement order. Reject did/does fronting after where or whether — those forms belong only in stand-alone questions.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She wondered why was everyone whispering.
Let me know which bus you are taking.
Let me know which bus are you taking.
We still don't know who broke the window.
We still don't know who did break the window.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — why was everyone… inverts was before the subject after wondered.

Tip: why everyone was whispering.

TRUE — which bus you are taking keeps you before are.

Tip: which + noun + subject + verb.

FALSE — which bus are you taking flips are before you inside the embed.

Tip: which bus you are taking.

TRUE — who broke the window is a clean subject question with no do-support.

Tip: Subject who + past verb — no did.

FALSE — who did break adds unnecessary emphatic/wrong do to a subject question.

Tip: who broke, not who did break.
tasks.solution_overview: be-inversion after why and are-fronting after which both mark direct-question order. Subject who stays simple: who broke, never who did break in this embed.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'm curious how often she practises the piano.
I'm curious how often does she practise the piano.
Can anyone say where the nearest pharmacy is?
Can anyone say where is the nearest pharmacy?
They asked if we had packed enough water.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — how often she practises… keeps subject–verb order after curious.

Tip: Frequency wh-phrases still take statement order.

FALSE — how often does she practise… inserts do-support as in a direct question.

Tip: how often she practises…

TRUE — where the nearest pharmacy is places is after the subject.

Tip: where + noun phrase + is/are.

FALSE — where is the nearest pharmacy flips is before the subject inside say.

Tip: where the nearest pharmacy is.

TRUE — if we had packed… is a yes/no embed with statement order.

Tip: if/whether + subject + verb — never invert.
tasks.solution_overview: how often and where…is embeds fail when does or is jumps before the subject. if-clauses stay calm: subject then verb, no fronted auxiliary.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They asked if had we packed enough water.
Nobody knows how many people will show up.
Nobody knows how many people will show up will.
Please check whether the oven has preheated.
Please check whether has the oven preheated.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — if had we packed… inverts had before we after asked.

Tip: if we had packed…

TRUE — how many people will show up keeps will after the subject people.

Tip: how many + noun + subject/verb cluster — no will-fronting.

FALSE — Extra will at the end is garbled; the clause is already complete after show up.

Tip: Stop at how many people will show up.

TRUE — whether the oven has preheated keeps has after the subject.

Tip: whether + subject + auxiliary + participle.

FALSE — whether has the oven… flips has before the subject.

Tip: whether the oven has…
highlights: how many people will show up
tasks.solution_overview: Reject had-fronting after if and has-fronting after whether. how many… will… is fine once; an extra trailing will is noise, not grammar.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide explained how the bridge had been built.
The guide explained how had the bridge been built.
I need to find out whose jacket this is.
I need to find out whose is this jacket.
Did anyone mention when the concert starts?
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — how the bridge had been built keeps passive statement order after explained.

Tip: Passive embeds still place had after the subject.

FALSE — how had the bridge been… inverts had into direct-question order.

Tip: how the bridge had been built.

TRUE — whose jacket this is keeps this before is.

Tip: whose + noun + subject + be.

FALSE — whose is this jacket flips is before this inside find out.

Tip: whose jacket this is.

TRUE — when the concert starts is statement order after mention; the outer Did anyone… is the direct question.

Tip: Outer inversion does not license inner inversion.
highlights: how the bridge had been built
tasks.solution_overview: Passive how-clauses and whose…is patterns both fail when the auxiliary precedes the subject. A direct outer question (Did anyone…) never licenses inversion inside the embed.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Did anyone mention when does the concert start?
We're trying to work out what the noise is coming from.
We're trying to work out what is the noise coming from.
He refused to say whether he would join us later.
He refused to say whether would he join us later.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — when does the concert start inserts do-support inside the embedded clause.

Tip: when the concert starts.

TRUE — what the noise is coming from keeps is after the subject noise.

Tip: Object what + subject + verb (+ stranded preposition).

FALSE — what is the noise coming from flips is before the subject inside work out.

Tip: what the noise is coming from.

TRUE — whether he would join… keeps would after the subject.

Tip: whether + subject + modal + verb.

FALSE — whether would he join… is modal inversion after whether.

Tip: whether he would join…
highlights: what the noise is coming from
what is the noise coming from
tasks.solution_overview: Stranded-preposition embeds (coming from) and whether + modal clauses both require subject before the finite verb. Reject does-fronting and would-fronting inside the subordinate clause.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It remains unclear which neighbour complained first.
It remains unclear which neighbour did complain first.
Could you clarify how far the campsite is from here?
Could you clarify how far is the campsite from here?
The coach asked who would captain the side on Saturday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — which neighbour complained first is a subject which-clause with no do-support.

Tip: Subject which + noun + past verb — no did.

FALSE — which neighbour did complain adds fake do to a subject question.

Tip: which neighbour complained…

TRUE — how far the campsite is… keeps is after the subject.

Tip: how far/how tall + subject + be.

FALSE — how far is the campsite… inverts is before the subject after clarify.

Tip: how far the campsite is…

TRUE — who would captain… keeps would after subject who.

Tip: Subject who + modal + verb — no inversion.
tasks.solution_overview: Subject which and subject who need no did or inversion. Degree phrases like how far keep be after the subject noun — not before it.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach asked who would the side be captained by on Saturday.
I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether the Wi-Fi password has changed.
I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether has the Wi-Fi password changed.
No one could remember how the recipe went.
No one could remember how did the recipe go.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — who would the side be captained by… forces awkward inversion; prefer who would captain… or by whom the side would be captained.

Tip: Avoid inverting inside a passive who-embed.

TRUE — whether the Wi-Fi password has changed keeps has after the subject inside a polite frame.

Tip: Long softeners still take statement order in the embed.

FALSE — whether has the Wi-Fi password… flips has before the subject.

Tip: whether the Wi-Fi password has…

TRUE — how the recipe went is statement order after remember.

Tip: how + subject + past — no did.

FALSE — how did the recipe go inserts do-support into the embed.

Tip: how the recipe went.
tasks.solution_overview: Awkward passive who-inversion and has-fronting after whether are both wrong. Everyday how-clauses after remember stay subject–verb: how the recipe went, not how did…

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The review depends on whether the supplier can meet the deadline.
The review depends on whether can the supplier meet the deadline.
She couldn't decide whom she should invite first.
She couldn't decide whom should she invite first.
Tell us what made the engine stall.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — whether the supplier can meet… keeps can after the subject (rare economy item).

Tip: Preposition + whether still takes statement order.

FALSE — whether can the supplier… is modal inversion after whether.

Tip: whether the supplier can…

TRUE — whom she should invite keeps she before should.

Tip: Object whom + subject + modal + verb.

FALSE — whom should she invite flips should before she inside decide.

Tip: whom she should invite.

TRUE — what made the engine stall is a subject what-clause with no do-support.

Tip: what + past verb when what is the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: depends on whether… and object whom… should… both keep the subject before the modal. Subject what made… needs no did — do not invent one.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tell us what did make the engine stall.
I'm still unsure of how the app works offline.
I'm still unsure of how does the app work offline.
They wanted to know to whom the parcel should be delivered.
They wanted to know to whom should the parcel be delivered.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — what did make… adds unnecessary do to a subject question.

Tip: what made, not what did make.

TRUE — how the app works offline keeps works after the subject after unsure of.

Tip: Preposition + how still takes statement order.

FALSE — how does the app work… inserts do-support inside the embed.

Tip: how the app works…

TRUE — to whom the parcel should be delivered keeps should after the subject in a formal prepositional wh-clause.

Tip: to whom + subject + modal + verb.

FALSE — to whom should the parcel… inverts should before the subject.

Tip: to whom the parcel should be…
tasks.solution_overview: Subject what never takes did in embeds. After of how and to whom, keep the subject before the finite verb or modal — never front does or should.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The puzzle is figuring out under what conditions the yeast activates.
The puzzle is figuring out under what conditions does the yeast activate.
We never learned why the lights flickered every evening.
We never learned why did the lights flicker every evening.
Ask her which shelf the spices belong on.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — under what conditions the yeast activates keeps the subject before the verb after a prepositional wh-opener.

Tip: Preposition + wh + subject + verb.

FALSE — under what conditions does the yeast… adds do-support as in a direct question.

Tip: under what conditions the yeast activates.

TRUE — why the lights flickered… is statement order after learned.

Tip: why + subject + past — no did.

FALSE — why did the lights flicker… smuggles do-support into the embed.

Tip: why the lights flickered…

TRUE — which shelf the spices belong on keeps the spices before belong.

Tip: which + noun + subject + verb (+ stranded preposition).
highlights: under what conditions the yeast activates
under what conditions does the yeast
which shelf the spices belong on
tasks.solution_overview: Complex openers (under what conditions) and stranded which…on still demand statement order. Any does/did inside the subordinate clause is a direct-question scar.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Ask her which shelf do the spices belong on.
It is hard to say whether or not the weather will clear by noon.
It is hard to say whether or not will the weather clear by noon.
The children kept asking where Father Christmas lived.
The children kept asking where did Father Christmas live.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — which shelf do the spices… inserts do before the subject inside Ask her.

Tip: which shelf the spices belong on.

TRUE — whether or not the weather will clear… keeps will after the subject; or not does not change order.

Tip: whether (or not) + subject + verb.

FALSE — whether or not will the weather… inverts will before the subject.

Tip: whether or not the weather will…

TRUE — where Father Christmas lived is classic storybook statement order after asking.

Tip: where + subject + past.

FALSE — where did Father Christmas live is direct-question order inside kept asking.

Tip: where Father Christmas lived.
highlights: whether or not the weather will
whether or not will the weather
tasks.solution_overview: or not after whether never licenses modal fronting. Storybook where-clauses and which…belong on both stay subject–verb; drop do/did from the embed.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The minutes do not record on what basis the exemption had been granted.
The minutes do not record on what basis had the exemption been granted.
Partners remain divided over which vendor we should engage.
Partners remain divided over which vendor should we engage.
I wonder who seconded the motion.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — on what basis the exemption had been granted keeps had after the subject (rare economy/formal item).

Tip: Prepositional wh-openers still take statement order.

FALSE — on what basis had the exemption… inverts had before the subject.

Tip: on what basis the exemption had…

TRUE — which vendor we should engage keeps we before should (rare economy item).

Tip: which + noun + subject + modal + verb.

FALSE — which vendor should we engage flips should before we.

Tip: which vendor we should engage.

TRUE — who seconded the motion is a clean subject who-clause.

Tip: Subject who + past — never invert or add did.
highlights: on what basis the exemption had
on what basis had the exemption
tasks.solution_overview: Prepositional wh-openers (on what basis) and object which-clauses (which vendor we should…) both fail when the auxiliary precedes the subject. Subject who remains the simplest correct pattern.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The minutes do not record who did second the motion.
Friends remain divided over whether the trip itself makes sense.
Friends remain divided over whether does the trip itself make sense.
I wonder where the caretaker is during the blackout.
I wonder where is the caretaker during the blackout.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — who did second… adds emphatic/wrong do to a subject question.

Tip: who seconded — never who did second in this embed.

TRUE — whether the trip itself makes… keeps makes after the subject; itself is just a focusing pronoun.

Tip: Extra focus words do not change embedded order.

FALSE — whether does the trip… invents do-support after whether.

Tip: whether the trip makes…

TRUE — where the caretaker is… is the classic wonder pattern with statement order.

Tip: I wonder where + subject + is.

FALSE — where is the caretaker… reverts to direct-question inversion after wonder.

Tip: where the caretaker is — the core contrast of this topic.
tasks.solution_overview: Close on the signature contrast: wonder where the caretaker is (statement order) versus where is the caretaker (direct inversion). Along the way, reject fake do after who or whether — embeds do not need it.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Pass the remote to whoever finds it under the sofa.
The neighbour, who's garden we borrowed tools from, waved hello.
Late nights affect my concentration in morning classes.
Between you and I, the reunion dinner felt awkward.
Fewer guests arrived than we had expected.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is the subject of finds, so the nominative form is required even after to.

Tip: Ignore the preposition; judge case inside the clause.

FALSE — Use possessive whose, not who's (= who is/has): whose garden.

Tip: If you cannot expand to who is, write whose.

TRUE — Affect as a verb correctly means influence.

Tip: Most exam sentences want the verb affect, not the noun effect.

FALSE — After the preposition between, use object case: Between you and me.

Tip: Strip you and — you would never say between I.

TRUE — Fewer correctly modifies the countable plural guests.

Tip: Countable plural → fewer; mass noun → less.
tasks.solution_overview: Work through each sentence as a quick case check: which form fits the grammar slot? Look for subject vs object, possession vs contraction, influence vs result, object pronouns after prepositions, and countable vs mass nouns.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Give the spare ticket to whomever arrives at the gate first.
The coach, whose whistle broke mid-match, borrowed another.
Too much sugar will effect your energy after lunch.
Between you and me, the playlist needs more variety.
The selection criteria is printed on the club noticeboard.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The relative is the subject of arrives, so use whoever, not whomever.

Tip: Find the verb in the clause; if the wh-word does the action, choose whoever.

TRUE — Whose correctly marks possession before whistle.

Tip: Whose works for people and things in formal English.

FALSE — For influence, use the verb affect: will affect your energy.

Tip: Reserve verb effect for bring about / cause to happen.

TRUE — Object pronouns after between are correct: you and me.

Tip: Formal speech still uses me here — I is the hypercorrection.

FALSE — Criteria is plural; use are: The selection criteria are printed.

Tip: Singular form is criterion.
tasks.solution_overview: These five hinge on classic swap traps. Ask: is the wh-word a subject? Is the 's a contraction or a possessive? Does the sentence mean influence or bring about? Is the pronoun after a preposition? Is criteria treated as plural?

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whoever finishes the puzzle should claim the prize.
Who's responsible for locking the studio tonight?
The committee hopes the new rule will effect a change in attendance.
Less messages were left on the noticeboard this week.
The entry criteria are clear and posted online.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever correctly acts as the subject of finishes.

Tip: Start-of-sentence subject slots almost always need whoever.

TRUE — Who's expands cleanly to who is before responsible.

Tip: Test expansion before you accept who's.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about is correct with a change.

Tip: Effect a change/reform/improvement is the rare but valid pattern.

FALSE — Messages are countable; use Fewer messages.

Tip: If you can count the noun, prefer fewer.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes are.

Tip: Formal exam English keeps criteria plural.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these are standard correct forms; one countable/mass slip remains. Confirm each pair quickly: whoever subject, who's = who is, effect = bring about, fewer with countables, criteria + plural verb.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Invite whomever the class nominates as quiz master.
Please name the classmate who's notes we borrowed.
Cold weather can affect joint pain overnight.
Keep this secret between you and me.
We need less luggage before we board the train.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of nominates, so the object form is traditionally correct.

Tip: If another subject does the verb, the wh-word is often the object.

FALSE — Need possessive whose notes, not who's (= who is).

Tip: Who's notes never expands sensibly.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence.

Tip: Ask whether something influences something else.

TRUE — Object pronouns after between are required.

Tip: Everyday English still marks between you and I wrong.

TRUE — Luggage is uncountable, so less is appropriate.

Tip: Mass nouns (time, luggage, advice) take less.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch the one genuine object-case whomever and the mass-noun less. The rest are possession, influence, and prepositional object pronouns — mark false only where the wrong member of a pair appears.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Forward the parcel to whomever is at the front desk.
The café whose windows fog up in winter serves great soup.
Loud music will effect the baby's nap downstairs.
This argument stays between my sister and I.
One key criterion is still missing from the checklist.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Is needs a subject: use whoever is at the front desk.

Tip: To + whomever + is is almost always wrong.

TRUE — Possessive whose correctly links the café to windows.

Tip: Whose is fine with inanimate subjects in formal prose.

FALSE — Meaning is influence → will affect the baby's nap.

Tip: No a change/result noun after the verb? Prefer affect.

FALSE — Object of between must be me: between my sister and me.

Tip: Same rule as between you and me.

TRUE — Singular criterion correctly pairs with is.

Tip: One item → criterion; several → criteria.
tasks.solution_overview: Difficulty steps up slightly: check clause subjects after to, possessive whose with places, affect vs effect, object pronouns after between, and criterion vs criteria.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We will ask whoever the tutor recommends.
Who's been watering the plants while we were away?
The announcement had little effect on the waiting queue.
Fewer than twelve seats were still free.
These criteria was written after the rehearsal.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is widely accepted as the object of recommends and is the safer exam default when case is contested.

Tip: Markers rarely accept whomever as a subject; they often accept whoever as an object.

TRUE — Who's = who has before the past participle been.

Tip: Who's been is a standard contraction.

TRUE — Noun effect meaning result/impact is correct after little.

Tip: Article/quantifier + effect usually signals the noun.

TRUE — Countable seats take fewer than.

Tip: Fewer than + number + plural noun is the careful form.

FALSE — Plural criteria needs were, not was.

Tip: Never pair criteria with a singular verb in formal answers.
tasks.solution_overview: Four statements are solid; one plural agreement error with criteria. Confirm contractions, the noun effect, fewer with numbers of countable items, and plural verb agreement.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Assign the chore to whoever the rota lists as free.
The runner who's shoes came untied lost several seconds.
Spicy food can affect sleep if you eat late.
Less volunteers signed up for the clean-up.
The judging criteria remain unchanged this year.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever functions acceptably as the object of lists in modern exam English.

Tip: Prefer whoever unless the object case is unmistakable and required.

FALSE — Possessive needed: whose shoes, not who's (= who is).

Tip: Expand every who's before you accept it.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence.

Tip: Subject influences object → affect.

FALSE — Volunteers are countable people: Fewer volunteers signed up.

Tip: Headcount plurals → fewer.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes plural remain.

Tip: Watch subject–verb number with Latin plurals.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan for the possessive/contraction slip and the fewer/less headcount error. The affect and criteria lines should read clean if you keep influence and plural agreement in mind.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Congratulate whomever you choose for the lead role.
A bakery whose ovens failed closed early on Friday.
Management intends to effect several schedule changes.
Please discuss the surprise only between you and me.
We noticed less delays on the morning bus route.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of choose, so the object form is traditionally correct.

Tip: Subject you + verb choose → object whomever.

TRUE — Whose ovens correctly shows possession for a place.

Tip: Whose + noun is the safe possessive pattern.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about fits schedule changes.

Tip: Effect + concrete result noun is the cue.

TRUE — Between you and me uses correct object pronouns.

Tip: Hypercorrect I fails after prepositions.

FALSE — Delays are countable: fewer delays.

Tip: Plural -s nouns almost always take fewer.
tasks.solution_overview: Most lines are carefully correct, including a legitimate object-case whomever and verb effect. The single miss is less with a countable plural — swap it mentally to fewer.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hand the microphone to whomever finishes speaking next.
Tell me who's attending the farewell picnic.
The rumour did not affect her mood for long.
The dispute should stay between the landlord and I.
Each criterion carries equal weight in the scorecard.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Subject of finishes must be whoever.

Tip: Verb immediately after the wh-word usually signals subject case.

TRUE — Who's = who is before attending.

Tip: Progressive after who's → contraction is fine.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence her mood.

Tip: Feelings and habits are typically affected.

FALSE — Use me: between the landlord and me.

Tip: Coordinated pronouns keep the same case.

TRUE — Singular criterion correctly takes singular carries.

Tip: Each + singular noun reinforces criterion.
tasks.solution_overview: Two traps are classic: whomever used as a subject, and I after between. The remaining three are clean contractions, affect-as-influence, and singular criterion agreement.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Support will go to whoever presents the clearest plan.
Name the cousin who's suitcase we found at the station.
The new timetable may effect parents with early starts.
Fewer sunny days remain before the school trip.
The admission criteria have been tightened again.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is the subject of presents.

Tip: Subject + verb right after whoever is the clean pattern.

FALSE — Possessive required: whose suitcase.

Tip: Who's suitcase cannot mean who is suitcase.

FALSE — Influence meaning needs may affect parents.

Tip: Adverbial after the verb often follows affect, not effect.

TRUE — Countable sunny days take fewer.

Tip: Calendar units in the plural prefer fewer.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes have.

Tip: Have/are/were are the safe plural partners.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on the two false lines: a who's/whose possession error and affect miswritten as effect. The whoever-subject, fewer-days, and criteria-have lines should all read true.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We contacted whomever the host had invited to speak.
The club, whose chair resigned yesterday, postponed the vote.
Heavy rain can affect outdoor matches across the region.
Between you and me and the rest of the team, morale is fragile.
There is less evidence than we expected in the file.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of had invited, so object case is traditionally right.

Tip: Past perfect clauses often bury the object — find who receives the action.

TRUE — Non-defining whose chair correctly marks possession.

Tip: Commas do not change the whose/who's rule.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence outdoor matches.

Tip: Weather/events affect plans and people.

TRUE — All coordinated pronouns after between stay in object case; me is correct.

Tip: Adding more nouns does not license I.

TRUE — Uncountable evidence takes less.

Tip: Evidence, information, and research are mass nouns.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are carefully correct. Use this set to lock in the right members of each pair: object whomever, possessive whose, verb affect, object me, and less with a mass noun.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Award the points to whomever meets the weekly target.
Who's signature appears on the permission slip?
The mediation failed to effect an early settlement.
Less than forty applications arrived before noon.
Several criteria needs revision before publication.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Subject of meets requires whoever.

Tip: Target-meeting clauses are subject cases.

FALSE — Ask whose signature, not who's (= who is).

Tip: Noun after the wh-word → almost always whose.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about fits a settlement.

Tip: Effect + indefinite article + result noun is classic.

FALSE — Countable applications prefer Fewer than forty applications.

Tip: Exam English still prefers fewer with countable plurals after numbers.

FALSE — Plural subject needs need: Several criteria need revision.

Tip: Several + plural noun → plural verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Only one sentence is true — the effect a settlement pattern. The other four mix subject/object, possession/contraction, fewer/less with numbers, and criteria agreement.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Delegate the keys to whoever you believe can lock up safely.
A neighbour who's driveway floods after storms asked for help.
Bright screens affect how well I sleep at night.
The apology must remain between the claimant and me.
We have fewer furniture than last year after the move.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is the subject of can lock inside the nested clause.

Tip: Case is decided in the innermost clause, not by to.

FALSE — Possessive needed: whose driveway.

Tip: Driveway/garden after the wh-word → whose.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence sleep.

Tip: Subject influences object → affect.

TRUE — Object pronoun me after between is correct.

Tip: Between X and me is standard.

FALSE — Furniture is typically uncountable here → less furniture (or fewer pieces of furniture).

Tip: Do not use fewer with a mass noun.
tasks.solution_overview: Nested clauses and mass/count swaps raise the difficulty. Decide case inside you believe can…, fix the who's/whose slip, keep affect and between…me, and reverse the fewer/furniture mismatch.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Offer the spare ticket to whomever the mentors shortlist.
The school whose hall was flooded suspended two concerts.
The announcement will effect audience confidence tomorrow.
Keep the draft between you and I until Friday.
The scoring criteria are applied uniformly to all entries.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of shortlist.

Tip: Mentors shortlist someone → object case.

TRUE — Whose hall correctly shows possession.

Tip: Organisation/place + whose + noun is fine.

FALSE — Confidence is influenced → will affect audience confidence.

Tip: Abstract reactions (confidence, mood) take affect.

FALSE — Object case required: between you and me.

Tip: Until Friday does not change pronoun case.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes are applied.

Tip: Passive voice still needs plural agreement.
tasks.solution_overview: Two false lines misuse effect for influence and I after between. Confirm the object-case whomever, the possessive whose, and plural criteria in the passive.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Promote whoever has delivered consistent results this season.
Who's been responsible for the overdue library fines?
Late nights are beginning to effect my morning runs.
There were fewer discrepancies in the second sample.
This single criteria determines eligibility on its own.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is the subject of has delivered.

Tip: Perfect aspect does not change the case rule.

TRUE — Who's been = who has been.

Tip: Been after who's almost always means who has.

FALSE — Influence meaning → beginning to affect my morning runs.

Tip: Progressive frames usually host affect.

TRUE — Countable discrepancies take fewer.

Tip: Count nouns in samples prefer fewer.

FALSE — Singular is criterion: This single criterion determines…

Tip: Single/one/each before the noun forces criterion.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch the subtler affect/effect slip inside a progressive construction and the false plural criteria after single. The whoever, who's been, and fewer lines are sound.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We will brief whomever is appointed as interim captain.
A neighbour whose parcels arrived late complained.
The coach hopes to effect lasting improvements in fitness.
Please keep the surprise between the organisers and me.
Managers reported less absences after flexible hours began.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Subject of is appointed must be whoever.

Tip: Passive is appointed still needs a subject form.

TRUE — Whose parcels correctly marks possession.

Tip: Neighbour/person + whose is standard.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about fits improvements.

Tip: Lasting/major + noun after effect is a good cue.

TRUE — Object pronoun me after between is correct.

Tip: Parallel organisers and me, never I.

FALSE — Countable absences need fewer absences.

Tip: Attendance counts are countable.
tasks.solution_overview: Passive clauses hide subject-case whoever traps, and countable absences tempt less. Hold onto whose, effect-as-bring-about, and between…me as the true anchors.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Allocate overtime to whoever the roster shows as available.
Identify the officer who's remit covers weekend shifts.
Sudden storms quickly affect outdoor festival plans.
The negotiation is strictly between you and me at this stage.
Fewer patience was left after the third delay.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is acceptable as the object of shows; when object case is unclear, whoever remains the safer exam form.

Tip: When object case is unclear, whoever rarely costs marks.

FALSE — Possessive whose remit is required.

Tip: Remit/mandate/role after the wh-word → whose.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence festival plans.

Tip: Weather events affect outdoor schedules.

TRUE — Between you and me is the correct object-case pair.

Tip: At this stage is irrelevant to case.

FALSE — Uncountable patience takes Less patience.

Tip: Patience, advice, and information are mass nouns.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder items flip the usual fewer/less intuition: patience is mass, so fewer is wrong. Also catch the remit possession error while confirming whoever, affect, and between you and me.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Send the draft to whomever you think should review it first.
The hotel whose rooms were renovated issued a statement.
Further delays will effect the project timeline severely.
Confidential seating stays between the ushers and me.
The shortlisting criteria leave little room for discretion.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Innermost clause: who should review — subject case → whoever you think should review it.

Tip: Ignore you think; case belongs to the embedded verb.

TRUE — Whose rooms correctly expresses possession.

Tip: Place nouns after whose are routine.

FALSE — Influence on the timeline → will affect the project timeline.

Tip: Severely/significantly after the verb often follows affect.

TRUE — Object pronoun me after between is correct.

Tip: Role names do not change pronoun case.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes plural leave.

Tip: Criteria + plural verb is the default formal choice.
tasks.solution_overview: The nested you think should… clause is the main trap — the wh-word is a subject, so whoever is required. Pair that with an affect/effect influence error; the remaining three are solid.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We interviewed whomever the agency had shortlisted for the role.
Who's attending on behalf of the parents' association?
The redesign may effect a reduction in overlapping duties.
Between you and I, the seating plan is flawed.
One of the criteria are inconsistent with the handbook.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of had shortlisted.

Tip: Agency shortlisted someone → object case.

TRUE — Who's attending = who is attending.

Tip: Expansion test passes cleanly.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about fits a reduction.

Tip: Effect + a + noun of result is intentional formal diction.

FALSE — Object case: Between you and me.

Tip: Informal tone does not excuse I.

FALSE — One of the criteria takes a singular verb: is inconsistent.

Tip: One of + plural noun → singular verb for one.
tasks.solution_overview: Two advanced traps: hypercorrect between you and I, and singular agreement after one of the criteria. The object-case whomever, who's contraction, and effect-a-reduction lines are correctly written.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Appoint whoever the club considers capable of leading the project.
A guest who's bags remain unpacked will miss the bus.
Humidity continues to affect drying times for the paint.
All discussions must stay between the counsel and me.
We now require less formal approvals than before the overhaul.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — With consider X capable, prefer whoever in careful exam answers.

Tip: Nested complements after consider usually favour whoever.

FALSE — Possessive whose bags is required.

Tip: Bags/luggage after the wh-word → whose.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence drying times.

Tip: Continues to + affect is a common formal stem.

TRUE — Object pronoun me after between is correct.

Tip: Counsel and me is a frequent formal stem.

FALSE — Approvals are countable → fewer formal approvals.

Tip: If the noun is plural and countable, choose fewer even with adjectives in between.
tasks.solution_overview: Finish with a dense mix: a club-considers clause, a who's/whose slip, solid affect and between…me, and a sneaky less before a countable plural. Only mark true when each confusable pair is already the right member.
